docs.title: About this book
docs.text: A complete first course in signals and systems for engineering students. It starts from the classification of continuous-time and discrete-time signals and the properties of systems, develops convolution for linear time-invariant systems, and then builds the frequency-domain toolkit: Fourier series, the continuous-time and discrete-time Fourier transforms, the DFT and FFT, sampling and aliasing, the Laplace transform and the z-transform. It closes with frequency response and filter design, an introduction to state-space models, and applications in audio, communication and control. Every chapter has worked numerical examples, figures, short NumPy programs with their output, exercises with answers and a quiz.

docs.title: Chapter 14: Applications: Audio, Communication and Control
docs.text:
The tools of the book at work in three fields of engineering

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • model echoes and reverberation as comb filters and read their frequency responses;
  • explain the short-time Fourier transform and read a spectrogram;
  • describe amplitude modulation, synchronous and envelope demodulation, and frequency-division multiplexing in terms of spectra;
  • explain how bandwidth, intersymbol interference and the FFT enter digital communication;
  • analyse a simple feedback loop: closed-loop poles, steady-state error with proportional and integral control, and stability margins;
  • implement a controller as a difference equation.

docs.title: 14.1 One toolkit, many fields
docs.text: Every application in this chapter follows the same pattern. A physical quantity becomes a signal; a system (a room, a radio channel, a motor) acts on it; and an engineer designs another system (an equaliser, a receiver, a controller) to get the desired result. The language is always the language of this book: convolution, frequency response, poles and zeros, sampling. Only the vocabulary of each field changes. The three sections below are short introductions, intended to show the ideas at work and to point the way to further study.

docs.title: Digital audio in numbers
docs.text: Sound is a pressure wave; a microphone turns it into a voltage; an anti-aliasing filter and an analog-to-digital converter turn the voltage into samples (Figure 9.4). Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz, so the compact disc format samples at 44.1 kHz with 16 bits per sample, giving a quantization SNR of about 98 dB (Section 9.7). Professional recording commonly uses 48 kHz or more and 24 bits, which leaves room for processing without adding audible noise. Speech for telephony needs much less: the classic telephone channel passes about 300 Hz to 3.4 kHz and is sampled at 8 kHz.

docs.title: Echo and reverberation as comb filters
docs.text:
A single echo, a copy of the sound delayed by \(D\) samples and scaled by \(\alpha\), is the FIR system

\[ y[n] = x[n] + \alpha\,x[n - D], \qquad H(e^{j\Omega}) = 1 + \alpha e^{-j\Omega D}. \]

Its magnitude \(|1 + \alpha e^{-j\Omega D}|\) swings between \(1 + |\alpha|\) and \(1 - |\alpha|\), with peaks at \(\Omega = 2\pi k/D\), that is every \(f_s/D\) Hz. Plotted against frequency, the response looks like the teeth of a comb, which gives the system its name, the comb filter. A delay of 0.25 s at 8 kHz (\(D = 2000\)) puts the teeth only 4 Hz apart: we hear such an echo as a distinct repetition, not as a change of tone. A very short delay (a few milliseconds) spreads the teeth hundreds of hertz apart and colours the sound audibly, the "hollow" quality of a voice next to a hard wall.

Feeding the delayed output back gives the recursive comb

\[ y[n] = x[n] + \alpha\,y[n - D], \qquad H(z) = \frac{1}{1 - \alpha z^{-D}}, \]

whose impulse response is an endless train of echoes \(\delta[n] + \alpha\delta[n - D] + \alpha^2\delta[n - 2D] + \cdots\), decaying by \(\alpha\) each time. Its \(D\) poles lie on a circle of radius \(|\alpha|^{1/D}\), inside the unit circle when \(|\alpha| < 1\). Artificial reverberation combines several such combs, with different delays, and some all-pass sections that scatter the echoes in time, to imitate the dense, decaying echo pattern of a hall. A real room is itself an LTI system to a good approximation: recording its impulse response (with a sharp clap or a specially designed test signal) and convolving dry recordings with it, usually by FFT, places the music in that room.

docs.title: Equalisers
docs.text: An equaliser adjusts the balance of frequencies: more bass, less harshness, a notch at a feedback frequency. Digital equalisers are almost always built from cascaded second-order IIR sections ("biquads"), each with two poles and two zeros, placed by the reasoning of Section 11.7: poles near the unit circle at a chosen angle make a boost, zeros near it make a cut, and the radii set the width. A graphic equaliser with ten bands is ten such sections in cascade, and by Section 4.5 their order does not matter.

docs.title: The spectrogram
docs.text:
A Fourier transform of a whole recording says which frequencies occur but not when. Music and speech change from moment to moment, so audio analysis uses the short-time Fourier transform (STFT): slide a window (Section 8.5) along the signal, take an FFT of each windowed segment, and stack the spectra side by side. The magnitude, drawn as brightness against time and frequency, is a spectrogram.

Figure 14.2 A spectrogram. Spectrogram of a 2-second signal sampled at 8 kHz: a chirp sweeping from 100 Hz to 3500 Hz appears as a rising diagonal line, and a steady 1 kHz tone as a horizontal line. Darker cells carry more energy.

The choice of window length is the time-bandwidth trade-off of Section 6.7 in practical form. A long window gives fine frequency resolution (bins \(f_s/L\) apart) but blurs events in time; a short window catches rapid changes but smears frequencies. Speech analysis typically uses windows of 20 to 30 ms. The spectrogram is the everyday instrument of audio engineers, phoneticians and anyone who studies birdsong or machine vibration.

Perceptual audio coders, which shrink music files by a large factor, are built on the same foundation: they split the signal into frequency bands with a transform closely related to the DFT (the modified discrete cosine transform), and spend bits only where the ear will notice the quantization noise.

docs.title: The channel as a system
docs.text:
A communication channel (a cable, an optical fibre, the radio path between two antennas) is modelled, to a first approximation, as an LTI system followed by additive noise:

\[ r(t) = (s * h_c)(t) + w(t), \]

where \(s\) is the transmitted signal, \(h_c\) the channel impulse response and \(w\) the noise. The frequency response \(H_c(j\omega)\) says which frequencies the channel passes; its bandwidth limits how fast information can be sent. Much of communication engineering is the design of signals that suit the channel, and of receivers that undo its effects.

docs.title: Amplitude modulation
docs.text:
Section 6.6 showed that multiplying a message \(m(t)\) by a carrier \(\cos\omega_ct\) moves its spectrum to \(\pm\omega_c\). This is double-sideband suppressed-carrier (DSB-SC) modulation. A message of bandwidth \(W\) occupies \(2W\) around the carrier: the upper sideband above \(\omega_c\) and the lower sideband below it. The receiver recovers the message by synchronous demodulation (Example 6.7): multiply by the same carrier and low-pass filter. The catch is that the receiver's carrier must match the transmitter's in frequency and phase; a phase error \(\theta\) scales the recovered message by \(\cos\theta\), and an error of \(90°\) makes it vanish.

Conventional AM, used for medium-wave broadcasting, avoids that difficulty by sending the carrier as well:

\[ s(t) = A_c\left[1 + \mu\,m(t)\right]\cos\omega_ct, \qquad |m(t)| \le 1, \]

with modulation index \(0 < \mu \le 1\). Because \(1 + \mu m(t)\) never goes negative, the message rides on the peaks of the carrier as its envelope (Figure 14.3). A simple envelope detector (a diode, a capacitor and a resistor) follows the peaks and recovers the message without any local carrier. The cost is power: with \(\mu = 1\) and a sinusoidal message, two-thirds of the transmitted power is in the carrier, which carries no information.

Figure 14.3 Amplitude modulation. Left: a conventional AM signal, a 1 kHz carrier whose amplitude follows 1 + 0.5cos(2π·50t); the dashed red curves are the envelope. Right: single-sided amplitude spectra of a message with components at 50 Hz and 120 Hz (green), and of the DSB-SC signal obtained by multiplying it by the 1 kHz carrier (blue): lines at 1000 ± 50 Hz and 1000 ± 120 Hz, each at half the message amplitude.

Frequency-division multiplexing (FDM) puts many messages on one channel by giving each its own carrier, spaced far enough apart that the spectra do not overlap. A receiver selects one with a band-pass filter, then demodulates it. Broadcast radio and television, and the original long-distance telephone networks, are all FDM systems, and the design of the filters that separate the channels is a direct application of Chapter 12.

docs.title: Digital communication
docs.text:
In digital communication the message is a sequence of symbols (bits, or groups of bits), each sent as a pulse \(p(t)\) whose amplitude or phase encodes the symbol: \(s(t) = \sum_k a_k\,p(t - kT_s)\), with one symbol every \(T_s\) seconds. Two signals-and-systems facts govern the design.

  • Bandwidth and symbol rate. By the time-bandwidth trade-off, shorter symbols need more bandwidth. A channel of bandwidth \(B\) Hz can carry at most about \(2B\) independent pulses per second without mutual interference, a limit that is the sampling theorem read in reverse. Pulses are shaped (with spectra that roll off smoothly, such as the raised-cosine family) to use the band efficiently.
  • Intersymbol interference. The channel convolves each pulse with \(h_c\), spreading it in time so that it overlaps its neighbours. This intersymbol interference (ISI) is removed by an equaliser, a filter that approximates the inverse of the channel (Section 3.6), often adapted continuously as the channel changes.

Modern wireless and wired systems (Wi-Fi, 4G and later cellular systems, many digital television systems, and DSL over telephone lines) use orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM), which is the DFT put to work. The transmitter places data symbols on \(N\) closely spaced subcarriers and generates the sum of all the modulated subcarriers with a single inverse FFT; the receiver separates them with a forward FFT. A short cyclic prefix, a copy of the end of each block placed before it, turns the channel's linear convolution into a circular one (Section 8.4), so that the channel becomes a simple multiplication of each subcarrier by \(H_c\) at its frequency, which one complex division per subcarrier undoes.

docs.title: The feedback loop
docs.text:
A control system makes a physical plant (a motor, a heater, an aircraft, a chemical process) follow a desired reference \(r(t)\). Figure 14.4 shows the standard loop: a sensor measures the output \(y\), the error \(e = r - y\) is formed, and a controller \(C(s)\) computes the input \(u\) to the plant \(G(s)\). By Section 10.5 the closed-loop transfer function is

\[ T(s) = \frac{Y(s)}{R(s)} = \frac{C(s)G(s)}{1 + C(s)G(s)} . \]

The product \(L(s) = C(s)G(s)\) is the loop transfer function. The closed-loop poles are the roots of \(1 + L(s) = 0\).

Figure 14.4 A feedback control loop. Left: a unity-feedback loop. The error e = r − y drives the controller C(s), whose output u drives the plant G(s) = 1/(s + 1). Right: unit-step responses with proportional control, C = 4 (orange), which settles at 0.8, and with proportional-integral control, C = 4 + 10/s (blue), which overshoots slightly and settles at 1.

Feedback offers three benefits that no open-loop arrangement can match. It reduces sensitivity to the plant: if \(|L| \gg 1\), then \(T \approx 1\) whatever the exact \(G\), so an ageing motor or a change of load hardly affects the result. It rejects disturbances: a disturbance entering at the plant output is reduced by the factor \(1/(1 + L)\). And it can stabilise an unstable plant (Example 10.7). The price is the risk of instability, because a loop with too much gain and too much delay oscillates.

docs.title: Steady-state error: proportional and integral control
docs.text:
Take the plant \(G(s) = \frac{1}{s + 1}\), a first-order lag with unit DC gain.

Proportional control, \(C(s) = K_p\), gives \(T(s) = \frac{K_p}{s + 1 + K_p}\). The closed-loop pole moves from \(-1\) to \(-(1 + K_p)\), so the response is faster. For a unit step reference, the final value theorem gives

\[ y(\infty) = T(0) = \frac{K_p}{1 + K_p}, \qquad e(\infty) = \frac{1}{1 + K_p}. \]

With \(K_p = 4\) the output settles at 0.8, a steady-state error of 20%. Raising the gain reduces the error but never removes it, and in a real system large gains amplify noise and excite unmodelled dynamics.

Proportional-integral (PI) control, \(C(s) = K_p + \frac{K_i}{s}\), adds a term proportional to the integral of the error. Then

\[ T(s) = \frac{K_ps + K_i}{s^2 + (1 + K_p)s + K_i}, \qquad T(0) = 1 . \]

The steady-state error to a step is zero: as long as any error remains, the integral keeps growing and pushes the output on, so the loop can come to rest only when the error is zero. With \(K_p = 4\) and \(K_i = 10\) the closed-loop poles are the roots of \(s^2 + 5s + 10\), namely \(-2.5 \pm 1.94j\), with \(\zeta \approx 0.79\). The response (Figure 14.4) overshoots by about 10%, more than \(\zeta\) alone would suggest, because the closed-loop zero at \(s = -2.5\) speeds up the initial rise. Adding a derivative term gives the PID controller, the workhorse of industrial control.

docs.title: Stability margins
docs.text:
How close is a feedback loop to instability? The loop goes unstable when \(1 + L(j\omega) = 0\) for some \(\omega\), that is when \(L(j\omega) = -1\): a gain of exactly 1 together with a phase of \(-180°\). The Bode plot of \(L\) measures the distance from that point:

  • the gain margin is the factor by which the gain could rise, at the frequency where the phase of \(L\) is \(-180°\), before \(|L|\) reached 1;
  • the phase margin is the additional phase lag that could be tolerated, at the frequency where \(|L| = 1\), before the phase reached \(-180°\).

Designers commonly aim for a phase margin of roughly 45° to 60°, which (for loops that behave like second-order systems) corresponds to well-damped responses. A pure time delay \(e^{-sT_d}\) in the loop (in sensing, computation or transport) adds phase lag \(-\omega T_d\) without changing the gain, and eats into the phase margin; this is why delays are the enemy of control.

docs.title: Digital implementation
docs.text:
Today almost every controller is a program. The error is sampled every \(T\) seconds, the control law runs as a difference equation, and the output is held by a DAC (a zero-order hold) until the next sample. A PI controller, for example, becomes

\[ u[n] = K_p\,e[n] + K_i\,T\sum_{k=0}^{n}e[k], \qquad\text{or recursively}\qquad u[n] = u[n-1] + K_p\big(e[n] - e[n-1]\big) + K_iT\,e[n], \]

which replaces the integral by a running sum. The sampling rate must be well above the bandwidth of the loop (often 10 to 30 times), because the hold and the computation add delay, and delay costs phase margin. For more exact designs, the plant is discretised as in Section 13.6 and the controller designed directly in the z-domain, with the closed-loop poles placed inside the unit circle.

docs.title: 14.5 Applications in NumPy
docs.text:
The program below checks three statements of this chapter: the comb response of a 0.25 s echo, DSB-SC modulation and synchronous demodulation (using the FFT as an ideal low-pass filter), and the final values of the P and PI loops of Figure 14.4, simulated with small Euler steps.

import numpy as np

# 1. Echo: y[n] = x[n] + 0.5 x[n - D] is a comb filter with peaks every fs/D Hz
fs, D = 8000, 2000                        # a 0.25 s echo at 8 kHz
f = np.array([0, 2, 4, 6])                # Hz
H = 1 + 0.5 * np.exp(-2j * np.pi * f / fs * D)
print("echo |H| at 0, 2, 4, 6 Hz:", np.round(np.abs(H), 3))

# 2. Amplitude modulation and synchronous demodulation, using the FFT as an ideal filter
fs, N = 10_000, 10_000                    # 1 s of signal, 1 Hz bins
t = np.arange(N) / fs
m = np.cos(2 * np.pi * 50 * t) + 0.5 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * 120 * t)    # message
c = np.cos(2 * np.pi * 1000 * t)                                      # 1 kHz carrier
s = m * c                                                             # DSB-SC signal
S = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(s)) * 2 / N
print("spectral lines of s(t) at:", np.flatnonzero(S > 0.1), "Hz")
v = 2 * s * c                             # mix down again: m + m cos(2 wc t)
V = np.fft.rfft(v)
V[200:] = 0                               # ideal low-pass filter at 200 Hz
m_hat = np.fft.irfft(V, n=N)
print(f"largest error in recovered message: {np.max(np.abs(m_hat - m)):.1e}")

# 3. Feedback control of G(s) = 1/(s + 1): proportional versus proportional-integral
def simulate(Kp, Ki, T=10.0, h=1e-3):
    y, integ, out = 0.0, 0.0, []
    for _ in range(int(T / h)):
        e = 1.0 - y                       # unit-step reference
        integ += e * h
        u = Kp * e + Ki * integ
        y += h * (-y + u)                 # plant y' = -y + u (Euler step)
        out.append(y)
    return np.array(out)
for Kp, Ki in ((4, 0), (4, 10)):
    y = simulate(Kp, Ki)
    print(f"Kp = {Kp}, Ki = {Ki:2d}: final value {y[-1]:.4f}, peak {y.max():.3f}")
print("closed-loop poles with PI:", np.roots([1, 5, 10]))

echo |H| at 0, 2, 4, 6 Hz: [1.5 0.5 1.5 0.5]
spectral lines of s(t) at: [ 880  950 1050 1120] Hz
largest error in recovered message: 2.1e-13
Kp = 4, Ki =  0: final value 0.8000, peak 0.800
Kp = 4, Ki = 10: final value 1.0000, peak 1.102
closed-loop poles with PI: [-2.5+1.93649167j -2.5-1.93649167j]

The echo's comb teeth are 4 Hz apart, as predicted. Because every frequency in the test signal falls exactly on a bin, the FFT filter recovers the message to rounding error; with real signals a practical low-pass filter (Chapter 12) is used instead. The simulated loops settle at \(K_p/(1 + K_p) = 0.8\) and at 1, and the PI loop overshoots by 10%.

docs.title: 14.6 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Audio: echoes are FIR combs \(1 + \alpha z^{-D}\), recursive echoes are IIR combs \(1/(1 - \alpha z^{-D})\) with teeth every \(f_s/D\) Hz; equalisers are cascades of biquads; the STFT and spectrogram show how spectra change in time, with window length setting the time-frequency trade-off.
  • Communication: a channel is an LTI system plus noise. DSB-SC shifts the message spectrum to \(\pm\omega_c\) and needs synchronous demodulation; conventional AM adds the carrier so an envelope detector suffices. FDM shares a channel by frequency. Digital links trade symbol rate against bandwidth, fight ISI with equalisers, and (in OFDM) use the FFT with a cyclic prefix to make the channel a per-subcarrier multiplication.
  • Control: the closed loop is \(CG/(1 + CG)\); feedback reduces sensitivity and disturbances and can stabilise. Proportional control leaves a step error \(1/(1 + K_p)\); integral action removes it. Gain and phase margins measure distance from instability; delay erodes phase margin. Digital controllers are difference equations.

docs.title: 14.7 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 14.1

An echo arrives 50 ms after the direct sound, at 0.6 times its amplitude, with \(f_s = 48\) kHz. Write the difference equation and find the spacing of the comb teeth.

Answer

\(D = 0.05 \times 48000 = 2400\): \(y[n] = x[n] + 0.6\,x[n - 2400]\). Teeth every \(48000/2400 = 20\) Hz, with gain between 1.6 and 0.4.

Exercise 14.2

Where are the poles of the recursive comb \(H(z) = 1/(1 - 0.5z^{-4})\), and is it stable?

Answer

\(z^4 = 0.5\), so four poles of radius \(0.5^{1/4} \approx 0.841\) at angles \(0, \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2\). All inside the unit circle: stable.

Exercise 14.3

A spectrogram uses a 512-sample window at \(f_s = 16\) kHz. What are its frequency bin spacing and the duration of each window?

Answer

Bins \(16000/512 = 31.25\) Hz apart; each window lasts \(512/16000 = 32\) ms.

Exercise 14.4

A message band-limited to 5 kHz is sent by DSB-SC on a 100 kHz carrier. What band does it occupy, and how much spectrum does it use?

Answer

95 kHz to 105 kHz: a bandwidth of 10 kHz, twice the message bandwidth.

Exercise 14.5

In synchronous demodulation of \(m(t)\cos\omega_ct\), the receiver's carrier is \(\cos(\omega_ct + \theta)\). Show that the recovered message is \(\frac12 m(t)\cos\theta\).

Answer

\(m\cos\omega_ct\cos(\omega_ct + \theta) = \frac12 m[\cos\theta + \cos(2\omega_ct + \theta)]\). The low-pass filter removes the term at \(2\omega_c\), leaving \(\frac12 m(t)\cos\theta\).

Exercise 14.6

For conventional AM with a sinusoidal message and modulation index \(\mu\), the carrier power is proportional to \(1\) and the sideband power to \(\mu^2/2\). What fraction of the power carries the message when \(\mu = 1\)?

Answer

\(\frac{\mu^2/2}{1 + \mu^2/2} = \frac{0.5}{1.5} = \frac13\).

Exercise 14.7

With \(G(s) = \frac{2}{s + 1}\) and proportional control \(K_p\), find the steady-state error to a unit step and the value of \(K_p\) that makes it 5%.

Answer

\(T(0) = \frac{2K_p}{1 + 2K_p}\), so \(e(\infty) = \frac{1}{1 + 2K_p}\). For 0.05: \(1 + 2K_p = 20\), \(K_p = 9.5\).

Exercise 14.8

For the PI loop of Section 14.4 with \(K_p = 4\), which values of \(K_i > 0\) give a closed loop that is stable? Which give real (non-oscillatory) poles?

Answer

The characteristic polynomial \(s^2 + 5s + K_i\) has both roots in the left half-plane for every \(K_i > 0\). The roots are real when \(25 - 4K_i \ge 0\), that is \(K_i \le 6.25\).

Exercise 14.9

A loop has a phase margin of 50° at a gain crossover frequency of 10 rad/s. How much pure time delay can be added before the loop becomes unstable?

Answer

The delay adds phase \(-\omega T_d\). At 10 rad/s, \(50° = 0.873\) rad, so \(T_d = 0.0873\) s, about 87 ms (assuming the crossover frequency is unchanged, which it is, since a delay does not change the gain).

Exercise 14.10

Write the recursive PI difference equation for \(K_p = 2\), \(K_i = 5\) and \(T = 0.01\) s, and compute \(u[0]\) and \(u[1]\) for \(e[0] = 1\), \(e[1] = 0.8\), starting from \(u[-1] = 0\) and \(e[-1] = 0\).

Answer

\(u[n] = u[n-1] + 2(e[n] - e[n-1]) + 0.05\,e[n]\). Then \(u[0] = 0 + 2(1) + 0.05 = 2.05\) and \(u[1] = 2.05 + 2(-0.2) + 0.04 = 1.69\).

docs.title: Chapter 2: Elementary Signals and Operations on Signals
docs.text:
The building blocks (steps, impulses, exponentials) and how to shift, flip, scale and combine them

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • define the unit step, unit impulse, ramp, rectangular pulse and sinc in continuous and discrete time, and state how they are related;
  • use the sifting property of the impulse to evaluate integrals and sums;
  • describe real and complex exponentials and say how \(\sigma\) and \(\omega\) (or the base \(a\)) shape them;
  • write a piecewise signal as a sum of shifted steps and ramps;
  • carry out time shifting, reversal and scaling, singly and combined, without error, and explain what decimation and expansion do to a sequence.

docs.title: 2.1 The discrete-time unit impulse and unit step
docs.text:
The simplest sequences are the unit impulse (or unit sample) and the unit step:

\[ \delta[n] = \begin{cases} 1, & n = 0 \\ 0, & n \neq 0 \end{cases} \qquad\qquad u[n] = \begin{cases} 1, & n \ge 0 \\ 0, & n < 0 \end{cases} \]

The impulse is a single sample of height one at the origin. The step switches on at \(n = 0\) and stays on. Each can be built from the other. The step is the running sum of the impulse, and the impulse is the first difference of the step:

\[ u[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{n} \delta[k] = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\delta[n - m], \qquad \delta[n] = u[n] - u[n-1]. \]

Multiplying any sequence by a shifted impulse picks out one sample:

\[ x[n]\,\delta[n - n_0] = x[n_0]\,\delta[n - n_0]. \]

The product is zero everywhere except at \(n = n_0\), where it equals \(x[n_0]\). Adding up such products for every \(n_0\) rebuilds the whole sequence:

\[ x[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x[k]\,\delta[n - k]. \]

This equation looks like a trivial restatement, but it is the single most important identity of Chapter 4. It says that any sequence is a weighted sum of shifted impulses, the weights being the samples themselves. If we know what a system does to one impulse, and the system is linear and time-invariant, we will know what it does to every sequence.

Example 2.1 A sequence as a sum of impulses

The finite sequence with \(x[-1] = 2\), \(x[0] = 1\), \(x[1] = -1\), \(x[3] = 4\) and zero elsewhere is

\[ x[n] = 2\delta[n+1] + \delta[n] - \delta[n-1] + 4\delta[n-3]. \]

The pulse \(p[n] = u[n] - u[n-4]\) is 1 for \(n = 0, 1, 2, 3\) and 0 elsewhere: a step switched on at 0 minus a step switched on at 4.

docs.title: 2.2 The continuous-time unit step and unit impulse
docs.text:
The unit step is

\[ u(t) = \begin{cases} 1, & t > 0 \\ 0, & t < 0. \end{cases} \]

Its value exactly at \(t = 0\) does not matter for anything in this book (some authors set it to \(1/2\)), because a single point has no effect on an integral.

The continuous-time unit impulse \(\delta(t)\), also called the Dirac delta, is harder, because no ordinary function does what we want. We want a signal that is zero everywhere except at \(t = 0\) and whose integral is one. Think of a rectangular pulse of width \(\varepsilon\) and height \(1/\varepsilon\), centred on the origin. Its area is always 1. As \(\varepsilon\) shrinks, the pulse becomes narrower and taller (Figure 2.2). The impulse is the idealisation of this pulse in the limit \(\varepsilon \to 0\): it is infinitely narrow, infinitely tall, and has unit area. We draw it as an arrow of height one, with the area written beside it.

Figure 2.1 Elementary signals. The unit step, the unit ramp, the unit rectangular pulse of width one centred on the origin, and the unit impulse, drawn as an arrow labelled with its area (1). Figure 2.2 The impulse as a limit. Rectangular pulses of width ε and height 1/ε for ε = 1, ½ and ¼. Every pulse has unit area; as ε shrinks the pulse approaches the unit impulse.

What matters about \(\delta(t)\) is not its "value" (which is not defined at zero) but what it does inside an integral. The defining property is the sifting property: for any signal \(x(t)\) continuous at \(t_0\),

\[ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)\,\delta(t - t_0)\,dt = x(t_0). \]

To see why, replace the impulse with the narrow pulse. The integral is then the average of \(x(t)\) over a tiny interval around \(t_0\), and as the interval shrinks the average tends to \(x(t_0)\). The impulse "sifts out" the value of \(x\) at the location of the impulse. The properties below all follow from the sifting property or from the pulse picture.

Property Statement Unit area \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(t)\,dt = 1\) Sampling \(x(t)\,\delta(t - t_0) = x(t_0)\,\delta(t - t_0)\) Sifting \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)\,\delta(t - t_0)\,dt = x(t_0)\) Even \(\delta(-t) = \delta(t)\) Scaling \(\delta(at) = \dfrac{1}{\lvert a\rvert}\,\delta(t)\), \(a \neq 0\) Running integral \(\int_{-\infty}^{t}\delta(\tau)\,d\tau = u(t)\) Derivative of the step \(\dfrac{du(t)}{dt} = \delta(t)\)

Table 2.1. Properties of the continuous-time impulse.

The scaling property surprises many students. Compressing time by a factor \(a\) makes the narrow pulse narrower by \(a\) while keeping its height, so its area drops to \(1/|a|\). An impulse is measured by its area, so \(\delta(2t) = \tfrac{1}{2}\delta(t)\).

The last two rows say that the impulse is the derivative of the step: the step jumps by one at the origin, and its slope there is "infinite" in exactly the amount needed to have unit area. More generally, wherever a signal jumps by an amount \(J\), its derivative contains an impulse \(J\delta(t - t_0)\). Engineers use this freely: it is how a sudden switch-on enters the equations of a circuit.

Example 2.2 Using the sifting property

Evaluate (a) \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (t^2 + 3)\,\delta(t - 2)\,dt\); (b) \(\int_{-1}^{1} e^{-t}\delta(t - 3)\,dt\); (c) \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\cos(\pi t)\,\delta(2t - 1)\,dt\).

(a) The impulse sits at \(t = 2\), so the integral is \(2^2 + 3 = 7\).

(b) The impulse sits at \(t = 3\), outside the interval of integration, so the integral is \(0\).

(c) Write \(\delta(2t - 1) = \delta(2(t - \tfrac12)) = \tfrac12\delta(t - \tfrac12)\). The integral is \(\tfrac12\cos(\pi/2) = 0\).

Products of impulses

\(\delta(t)\cdot\delta(t)\) and \(\delta(t)^2\) are not defined. Impulses may be added, scaled, shifted and integrated against ordinary signals, but never multiplied by each other.

docs.title: 2.3 Ramps, pulses, the sign function and sinc
docs.text:
A few more signals appear constantly.

The unit ramp is \(r(t) = t\,u(t)\): zero for negative time and rising with unit slope afterwards. It is the integral of the step, \(r(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{t}u(\tau)\,d\tau\), and the step is its derivative. In discrete time, \(r[n] = n\,u[n]\).

The unit rectangular pulse is \(\mathrm{rect}(t) = 1\) for \(|t| < \tfrac12\) and \(0\) for \(|t| > \tfrac12\). In terms of steps, \(\mathrm{rect}(t) = u(t + \tfrac12) - u(t - \tfrac12)\). A pulse of height \(A\) and width \(\tau\) centred at \(t_0\) is \(A\,\mathrm{rect}\!\left(\frac{t - t_0}{\tau}\right)\).

The sign function is \(\mathrm{sgn}(t) = 1\) for \(t > 0\) and \(-1\) for \(t < 0\), so \(\mathrm{sgn}(t) = 2u(t) - 1\).

The sinc function is

\[ \mathrm{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin(\pi x)}{\pi x}, \qquad \mathrm{sinc}(0) = 1 . \]

It is 1 at the origin and zero at every other integer, and it decays like \(1/x\). This "normalised" sinc is the one used by NumPy (np.sinc). Some books define \(\mathrm{sinc}(x) = \sin(x)/x\) instead; always check which is meant. The sinc is the Fourier transform of the rectangular pulse, as Chapter 6 shows, and it is the interpolating function of the sampling theorem in Chapter 9.

docs.title: Writing a piecewise signal with steps and ramps
docs.text:
A signal made of straight pieces can be written as a sum of shifted steps and ramps, which is convenient both for transforms and for differentiating. The rule is to read the signal from left to right and, at each break point, add whatever change in value (a step) and change in slope (a ramp) occurs there.

Example 2.3 A trapezoid from ramps and steps

Let \(x(t)\) rise linearly from 0 at \(t = -1\) to 1 at \(t = 0\), stay at 1 until \(t = 2\), and then drop suddenly to 0 (the blue signal of Figure 2.4).

  • At \(t = -1\) the slope changes from 0 to 1: add \(r(t + 1)\).
  • At \(t = 0\) the slope changes from 1 to 0: add \(-r(t)\).
  • At \(t = 2\) the value drops by 1: add \(-u(t - 2)\).

So \(x(t) = r(t+1) - r(t) - u(t-2)\). Check at \(t = 1\): \(2 - 1 - 0 = 1\). Check at \(t = 3\): \(4 - 3 - 1 = 0\). Differentiating gives \(x'(t) = u(t+1) - u(t) - \delta(t-2)\): a unit-height pulse on \((-1, 0)\) and a downward impulse of area 1 where the signal jumps.

docs.title: Real exponentials
docs.text: The real exponential \(x(t) = Ce^{at}\), with real \(C\) and \(a\), decays if \(a < 0\), grows if \(a > 0\) and is constant if \(a = 0\). The time it takes to fall by a factor \(e\) is the time constant \(\tau = 1/|a|\). After five time constants a decaying exponential is below 1% of its starting value (\(e^{-5} \approx 0.0067\)). Exponentials describe the charging of capacitors, the cooling of objects, radioactive decay and compound interest.

docs.title: Complex exponentials
docs.text:
Now let the exponent be complex: \(s = \sigma + j\omega\). Then

\[ e^{st} = e^{\sigma t}e^{j\omega t} = e^{\sigma t}\cos\omega t + j\,e^{\sigma t}\sin\omega t . \]

The real part \(\sigma\) sets an exponential envelope, and the imaginary part \(\omega\) sets the frequency of oscillation inside it. With \(\sigma < 0\) we get a damped sinusoid, the response of a struck bell or a plucked string; with \(\sigma > 0\) a growing one, the sign of an unstable system; with \(\sigma = 0\) a pure sinusoid. The whole family \(e^{st}\) is so important that the variable \(s\) gets its own plane, the s-plane, in Chapter 10: the left half of the plane holds decaying signals, the right half growing ones, and the vertical axis pure oscillations.

A general complex exponential \(Ce^{st}\) has a complex amplitude \(C = |C|e^{j\theta}\), so

\[ Ce^{st} = |C|e^{\sigma t}e^{j(\omega t + \theta)}, \qquad \mathrm{Re}\{Ce^{st}\} = |C|e^{\sigma t}\cos(\omega t + \theta). \]

The magnitude of \(C\) sets the size and its angle sets the phase. This is how the "phasor" of circuit theory works.

docs.title: Discrete-time exponentials
docs.text:
In discrete time the exponential is written \(x[n] = Ca^n\), or with a complex base \(z\), \(x[n] = Cz^n\). For real \(a\):

  • \(0 < a < 1\): decays toward zero; \(a > 1\): grows;
  • \(-1 < a < 0\): decays while alternating in sign; \(a < -1\): grows while alternating;
  • \(a = 1\): constant; \(a = -1\): alternates \(\pm1\).

For a complex base \(z = re^{j\Omega_0}\),

\[ z^n = r^n e^{j\Omega_0 n} = r^n\cos(\Omega_0 n) + j\,r^n\sin(\Omega_0 n). \]

The magnitude \(r\) plays the role of \(e^{\sigma}\): \(r < 1\) gives a decaying envelope, \(r > 1\) a growing one, and \(r = 1\) (a point on the unit circle) a pure discrete-time sinusoid. The variable \(z\) gets its own plane in Chapter 11, where the unit circle plays the part of the vertical axis of the s-plane. The two descriptions are linked by sampling: if \(x(t) = e^{st}\) is sampled every \(T_s\) seconds, \(x[n] = e^{snT_s} = (e^{sT_s})^n\), so \(z = e^{sT_s}\).

docs.title: 2.5 Operations on the amplitude
docs.text:
Operations on the dependent variable (the value of the signal) are straightforward:

  • Amplitude scaling: \(y(t) = c\,x(t)\). An amplifier with gain \(c\).
  • Addition: \(y(t) = x_1(t) + x_2(t)\), value by value. A mixer adding two audio tracks.
  • Multiplication: \(y(t) = x_1(t)\,x_2(t)\), value by value. A modulator multiplying a message by a carrier, or a window cutting out part of a signal.
  • Differentiation \(y(t) = dx/dt\) and integration \(y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{t}x(\tau)\,d\tau\). An inductor's voltage is proportional to the derivative of its current; a capacitor's voltage to the integral of its current.

In discrete time, differentiation becomes the first difference \(y[n] = x[n] - x[n-1]\), and integration becomes the running sum (accumulation) \(y[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{n}x[k]\). We already met both: the difference of \(u[n]\) is \(\delta[n]\) and the running sum of \(\delta[n]\) is \(u[n]\).

docs.title: 2.6 Operations on time: shift, reversal and scaling
docs.text:
Operations on the independent variable move or reshape a signal along the time axis. They cause more mistakes than anything else in a first course, so we go slowly.

Time shift. \(y(t) = x(t - t_0)\). If \(t_0 > 0\) the signal is delayed: it moves right by \(t_0\). Whatever \(x\) did at time 0, \(y\) does at time \(t_0\), because \(y(t_0) = x(0)\). If \(t_0 < 0\) the signal is advanced (moved left). An echo is a delayed copy of a sound.

Time reversal. \(y(t) = x(-t)\). The signal is reflected about \(t = 0\): what \(x\) did at time 3, \(y\) does at time \(-3\). A tape played backwards.

Time scaling. \(y(t) = x(at)\) with \(a > 0\). If \(a > 1\) the signal is compressed by the factor \(a\) (played faster); if \(0 < a < 1\) it is expanded (played slower). What \(x\) did at time \(t_1\), \(y\) does at time \(t_1/a\). A recording played at double speed is \(x(2t)\); it lasts half as long and every frequency in it doubles.

In each case the reliable method is the same: ask where the new signal takes a given value. Since \(y(t) = x(\text{something})\), \(y\) takes the value \(x(t_1)\) when the "something" equals \(t_1\). Solve for \(t\).

docs.title: Combined operations
docs.text:
The signal \(y(t) = x(at - b)\) combines a scaling, possibly a reversal (if \(a < 0\)) and a shift. There are two safe orders:

  1. Shift first, then scale. Form \(v(t) = x(t - b)\), then \(y(t) = v(at)\). Check: \(v(at) = x(at - b)\). Correct.
  2. Scale first, then shift by \(b/a\). Form \(w(t) = x(at)\), then \(y(t) = w(t - b/a)\). Check: \(w(t - b/a) = x(a(t - b/a)) = x(at - b)\). Correct.

The tempting mistake is to scale first and then shift by \(b\): that gives \(x(a(t - b)) = x(at - ab)\), which is wrong unless \(a = 1\). The safest method of all is the point-by-point one: take each break point \(t_1\) of \(x\) and solve \(at - b = t_1\) for the new location \(t = (t_1 + b)/a\).

Figure 2.4 Time operations. Top: the signal x(t), a ramp from t = −1 to 0 followed by a level of 1 until t = 2; the delayed signal x(t − 1); the reversed signal x(−t). Bottom: the compressed signal x(2t), occupying −½ to 1; and x(−2t + 3), occupying ½ to 2.

Example 2.4 Sketching x(−2t + 3)

Take \(x(t)\) from Example 2.3: a ramp from \((-1, 0)\) up to \((0, 1)\), a level of 1 until \(t = 2\), then zero. Sketch \(y(t) = x(-2t + 3)\).

Point by point. Solve \(-2t + 3 = t_1\), that is \(t = (3 - t_1)/2\), for each break point \(t_1\):

Point of \(x\) \(t_1\) New time \(t = (3 - t_1)/2\) Value start of ramp \(-1\) \(2\) 0 top of ramp \(0\) \(1.5\) 1 end of level \(2\) \(0.5\) 1 (then 0)

Table 2.2. Break points of \(x(t)\) and where they land in \(x(-2t + 3)\).

So \(y(t)\) jumps from 0 to 1 at \(t = 0.5\), stays at 1 until \(t = 1.5\), then falls linearly to 0 at \(t = 2\). The order has reversed (because of the minus sign) and the duration has halved from 3 to 1.5 (because of the factor 2).

By steps. Shift first: \(v(t) = x(t + 3)\) occupies \([-4, -1]\). Then \(v(-2t)\) reverses and compresses by 2: the interval \([-4, -1]\) maps to \([0.5, 2]\). The same answer.

docs.title: Time operations in discrete time
docs.text:
Shifts and reversals work exactly as in continuous time, with the restriction that a shift \(n_0\) must be an integer. Time scaling is different, because \(x[an]\) is defined only when \(an\) is an integer.

  • Decimation (downsampling) by an integer \(M\): \(y[n] = x[Mn]\). It keeps every \(M\)th sample and discards the rest. Information is lost: two different sequences can have the same decimated version.
  • Expansion (upsampling) by an integer \(L\): \(y[n] = x[n/L]\) when \(n\) is a multiple of \(L\), and \(0\) otherwise. It inserts \(L - 1\) zeros between samples. No information is lost, but the result is not a smooth slower version: the zeros have to be filled in by interpolation, a topic for Chapter 9.

Decimating and then expanding is not the identity

Expanding \(x[2n]\) by 2 gives back the even samples of \(x\) with zeros where the odd samples were. The odd samples are gone for good. Expanding first and then decimating, on the other hand, does return the original sequence.

docs.title: 2.7 Checking operations with NumPy
docs.text:
Writing a signal as a Python function of time makes it easy to check a sketch. The program below evaluates \(x(-2t + 3)\) at a few points, confirms the step-and-ramp formula of Example 2.3, and decimates and expands a sequence.

import numpy as np

def x(t):
    """The signal of Example 2.4: ramp on [-1, 0), 1 on [0, 2), 0 elsewhere."""
    t = np.asarray(t, dtype=float)
    return np.where((t >= -1) & (t < 0), t + 1,
           np.where((t >= 0) & (t < 2), 1.0, 0.0))

t = np.array([0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 1.75, 2.0])
print("t          :", t)
print("x(-2t + 3) :", x(-2 * t + 3))

# The same signal written with steps and ramps
u = lambda t: np.where(np.asarray(t) >= 0, 1.0, 0.0)
r = lambda t: np.asarray(t) * u(t)
x_steps = lambda t: r(t + 1) - r(t) - u(t - 2)
tt = np.linspace(-3, 4, 7001)
print("step form agrees:", np.allclose(x(tt), x_steps(tt)))

# Discrete time: decimation by 2 and expansion by 2
n = np.arange(-4, 5)
xn = np.array([0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 2, 1.5, 1, 0.5])
dec = xn[::2]                      # keeps x[-4], x[-2], x[0], x[2], x[4]
exp = np.zeros(2 * len(xn) - 1)
exp[::2] = xn                      # inserts a zero between samples
print("x[2n]  :", dec)
print("expand :", exp)

t          : [0.25 0.5  1.   1.5  1.75 2.  ]
x(-2t + 3) : [0.  0.  1.  1.  0.5 0. ]
step form agrees: True
x[2n]  : [0.5 1.5 2.5 1.5 0.5]
expand : [0.5 0.  1.  0.  1.5 0.  2.  0.  2.5 0.  2.  0.  1.5 0.  1.  0.  0.5]

The value at \(t = 0.5\) is 0 rather than 1 because the program defines \(x(2) = 0\) (the level ends just before \(t = 2\)); this is the single point where the jump happens, and it does not affect the sketch. At \(t = 1.75\), halfway down the ramp, the value is 0.5 as expected.

A habit worth forming

After every time operation, check one easy point. For \(x(-2t + 3)\), ask: where does \(y\) equal \(x(0)\)? When \(-2t + 3 = 0\), so at \(t = 1.5\). If your sketch does not have the top of the ramp at \(t = 1.5\), something went wrong.

docs.title: 2.8 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • \(\delta[n]\) and \(u[n]\) are related by \(u[n] = \sum_{k\le n}\delta[k]\) and \(\delta[n] = u[n] - u[n-1]\). Every sequence is a sum of shifted, scaled impulses: \(x[n] = \sum_k x[k]\delta[n-k]\).
  • The CT impulse \(\delta(t)\) is the limit of unit-area pulses. It is defined by the sifting property \(\int x(t)\delta(t - t_0)dt = x(t_0)\). It is the derivative of the step, and \(\delta(at) = \delta(t)/|a|\).
  • Ramps, rectangular pulses, the sign function and \(\mathrm{sinc}(x) = \sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)\) complete the toolkit. Piecewise-linear signals are sums of shifted steps and ramps.
  • \(e^{st}\) with \(s = \sigma + j\omega\) is an oscillation at \(\omega\) inside an envelope \(e^{\sigma t}\). In discrete time \(z^n\) with \(z = re^{j\Omega_0}\) plays the same part, \(r\) setting the envelope; sampling links them by \(z = e^{sT_s}\).
  • \(x(t - t_0)\) delays by \(t_0\); \(x(-t)\) reflects; \(x(at)\) compresses for \(a > 1\). For \(x(at - b)\) shift first and then scale, or scale and then shift by \(b/a\); when in doubt, map the break points.
  • Decimation \(x[Mn]\) discards samples; expansion inserts zeros.

docs.title: 2.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 2.1

Evaluate \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-2t}\,\delta(t + 1)\,dt\).

Answer

\(e^{2}\), about 7.389. The impulse is at \(t = -1\), so the integral is \(e^{-2(-1)} = e^2\).

Exercise 2.2

Simplify \((t^3 + 1)\,\delta(t - 1)\) and \(\sin(t)\,\delta(t)\).

Answer

\((t^3 + 1)\delta(t - 1) = 2\delta(t - 1)\), by the sampling property. \(\sin(t)\delta(t) = \sin(0)\delta(t) = 0\).

Exercise 2.3

Evaluate \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} t^2\,\delta(3t - 6)\,dt\).

Answer

\(\delta(3t - 6) = \delta(3(t - 2)) = \tfrac13\delta(t - 2)\), so the integral is \(\tfrac13 \cdot 4 = 4/3\).

Exercise 2.4

Write the triangular pulse that rises from 0 at \(t = 0\) to 1 at \(t = 1\) and falls back to 0 at \(t = 2\) as a sum of ramps.

Answer

\(x(t) = r(t) - 2r(t - 1) + r(t - 2)\). The slope changes by \(+1\) at 0, by \(-2\) at 1 (from \(+1\) to \(-1\)) and by \(+1\) at 2 (from \(-1\) to 0).

Exercise 2.5

For the triangular pulse of Exercise 2.4, where does \(x(3 - t)\) reach its peak, and what interval does it occupy?

Answer

The peak of \(x\) is at \(t_1 = 1\); solve \(3 - t = 1\), so \(t = 2\). The interval \([0, 2]\) maps to \(t = 3 - t_1\), giving \([1, 3]\). (The triangle is symmetric, so reversal does not change its shape.)

Exercise 2.6

A student writes \(x(2t - 4)\) as "compress by 2, then delay by 4". Which correct description should replace it?

Answer

Compress by 2, then delay by \(4/2 = 2\); or delay by 4 first, then compress by 2. Either gives \(x(2(t - 2)) = x(2t - 4)\).

Exercise 2.7

Describe \(x(t) = e^{-t}\cos(10\pi t)\): what is its envelope, and how many oscillations occur per second?

Answer

It is \(\mathrm{Re}\{e^{st}\}\) with \(s = -1 + j10\pi\). The envelope is \(e^{-t}\), with a time constant of 1 second, and the frequency is \(10\pi\) rad/s, which is 5 oscillations per second.

Exercise 2.8

For which values of \(a\) does \(a^n u[n]\) have finite energy?

Answer

For \(|a| < 1\). The energy is \(\sum_{n\ge0}|a|^{2n} = 1/(1 - |a|^2)\), which is finite only when \(|a| < 1\).

Exercise 2.9

Let \(x[n] = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\) for \(n = 0, \ldots, 5\). Write out \(x[2n]\) and \(x[n - 2]\).

Answer

\(x[2n]\) takes \(x[0], x[2], x[4]\): the values \(1, 3, 5\) at \(n = 0, 1, 2\). \(x[n - 2]\) is the same list moved right by two: \(1, \ldots, 6\) at \(n = 2, \ldots, 7\).

Exercise 2.10

Show that \(\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n]\,\delta[n - 3] = x[3]\), and use it to evaluate \(\sum_n (n^2 + 1)\,\delta[n + 2]\).

Answer

Every term is zero except \(n = 3\), where \(\delta[0] = 1\), leaving \(x[3]\). For the second sum the only non-zero term is at \(n = -2\), giving \((-2)^2 + 1 = 5\).

docs.title: 2.10 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 2

Exercise 1

Evaluate the integral of (t² + 1) δ(t − 2) over all t.

Answer

5

Sifting picks out the value at t = 2: 4 + 1 = 5.

Exercise 2

δ(4t) equals

  1. 4δ(t)
  2. δ(t)/4
  3. δ(t)
  4. δ(t − 4)
Answer

δ(t)/4

Compressing by 4 divides the area by 4.

Exercise 3

Relative to x(t), the signal x(t + 3) is

  1. delayed by 3
  2. advanced by 3
  3. compressed by 3
  4. reversed
Answer

advanced by 3

y(−3) = x(0): what x did at 0 now happens at −3, earlier.

Exercise 4

In e^(σt)cos(ωt), which quantity decides whether the signal grows or decays?

  1. σ
  2. ω
  3. the phase
  4. the amplitude
Answer

σ

Exercise 5

In discrete time, the unit impulse is the first ___ of the unit step.

Answer

difference

Exercise 6

x(2t − 6) is obtained from x(t) by compressing by 2 and then delaying by

  1. 6
  2. 3
  3. 12
  4. 2
Answer

3

x(2t − 6) = x(2(t − 3)).

Exercise 7

Match each operation on a sequence with its effect.

ABx[2n]delays by two samplesx[n − 2]reflects about n = 0x[−n]discards every other sample Answer

x[2n] — discards every other sample; x[n − 2] — delays by two samples; x[−n] — reflects about n = 0

docs.title: Chapter 5: Fourier Series
docs.text:
Periodic signals as sums of harmonics, and what an LTI system does to each harmonic

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • write the synthesis and analysis equations of the exponential Fourier series and derive the analysis equation from orthogonality;
  • convert between the exponential and trigonometric forms, and use the symmetry of real signals;
  • compute the Fourier coefficients of square waves, pulse trains and other standard periodic signals;
  • state the Dirichlet conditions, explain the Gibbs phenomenon, and apply Parseval's relation;
  • find the steady-state output of an LTI system for a periodic input;
  • compute the discrete-time Fourier series of a periodic sequence.

docs.title: 5.1 Why build signals from sinusoids?
docs.text:
Chapter 4 ended with a striking fact: a complex exponential \(e^{j\omega t}\) passes through any LTI system unchanged in shape, only multiplied by a complex number \(H(j\omega)\). If an input can be written as a sum of complex exponentials, the output is the same sum with each term multiplied by its own \(H\). The hard operation of convolution is replaced by multiplications, one per frequency.

The question is which signals can be written this way. In 1807 Joseph Fourier claimed, in a study of heat flow, that any periodic function could be written as a sum of sinusoids whose frequencies are whole multiples of the fundamental. The claim was disputed for decades, and the precise conditions were worked out later by Dirichlet and others, but in the form used by engineers it is true for every periodic signal we are likely to meet. This chapter develops it.

A signal with period \(T_0\) and fundamental frequency \(\omega_0 = 2\pi/T_0\) can only be built from exponentials that also repeat every \(T_0\). Those are the harmonically related exponentials

\[ \phi_k(t) = e^{jk\omega_0 t}, \qquad k = 0, \pm1, \pm2, \ldots \]

The term \(k = 0\) is a constant (the DC component). The terms \(k = \pm1\) have the fundamental frequency and together form the fundamental or first harmonic. The terms \(k = \pm N\) form the \(N\)th harmonic. Musical instruments give a vivid example: a violin and a flute playing the same note have the same fundamental, but different strengths of the higher harmonics, which is why they sound different.

docs.title: 5.2 The exponential Fourier series
docs.text:
A periodic signal \(x(t)\) with period \(T_0\) is represented by its Fourier series

\[ x(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} a_k\,e^{jk\omega_0 t} \qquad\text{(synthesis equation)}, \]

with Fourier coefficients

\[ a_k = \frac{1}{T_0}\int_{T_0} x(t)\,e^{-jk\omega_0 t}\,dt \qquad\text{(analysis equation)}. \]

The integral is over any interval of length \(T_0\), for example from \(0\) to \(T_0\) or from \(-T_0/2\) to \(T_0/2\); choose whichever makes the integration easiest. The coefficients \(a_k\) are in general complex. The coefficient \(a_0 = \frac{1}{T_0}\int_{T_0}x(t)\,dt\) is the average value of the signal over one period.

docs.title: Where the analysis equation comes from
docs.text:
The key is that the harmonics are orthogonal over a period:

\[ rac{1}{T_0}\int_{T_0} e^{jk\omega_0 t}\,e^{-jm\omega_0 t}\,dt = rac{1}{T_0}\int_{T_0}e^{j(k - m)\omega_0 t}\,dt = egin{cases} 1, & k = m \ 0, & k eq m. \end{cases} \]

When \(k = m\) the integrand is 1. When \(k e m\) the integrand is a complex exponential that makes exactly \(k - m\) whole turns around the unit circle in one period, so its real and imaginary parts both integrate to zero.

Now multiply the synthesis equation by \(e^{-jm\omega_0 t}\) and integrate over a period. Every term with \(k e m\) integrates to zero, and the term \(k = m\) gives \(T_0\,a_m\). Dividing by \(T_0\) gives the analysis equation. The idea is the same as finding the components of a vector by taking dot products with orthogonal unit vectors: the harmonics are the "axes" of the space of periodic signals, and \(a_k\) is the component of \(x\) along the \(k\)th axis.

Key idea

The analysis equation measures how much of each harmonic a periodic signal contains. The synthesis equation adds the harmonics back together. The set \(\{a_k\}\) is the spectrum of the signal: a list of strengths and phases at the frequencies \(k\omega_0\).

docs.title: A first example: sinusoids by inspection
docs.text:
For signals that are already sums of sinusoids, there is no need to integrate: use Euler's formula and read off the coefficients.

Example 5.1 Coefficients by inspection

Find the Fourier coefficients of \(x(t) = 1 + 2\cos(2t) + \sin(4t + \pi/4)\).

The fundamental is \(\omega_0 = 2\) (period \(\pi\)). Expand:

\[ x(t) = 1 + e^{j2t} + e^{-j2t} + \frac{1}{2j}\left(e^{j\pi/4}e^{j4t} - e^{-j\pi/4}e^{-j4t}\right). \]

So \(a_0 = 1\), \(a_{\pm1} = 1\), \(a_2 = \frac{1}{2j}e^{j\pi/4} = \frac12 e^{-j\pi/4}\), \(a_{-2} = -\frac{1}{2j}e^{-j\pi/4} = \frac12 e^{j\pi/4}\), and all other \(a_k = 0\). Notice \(a_{-2} = a_2^*\), as the next section explains.

docs.title: 5.3 Real signals and the trigonometric form
docs.text:
For a real signal, taking the conjugate of the analysis equation gives

\[ a_{-k} = a_k^* . \]

This is conjugate symmetry: \(|a_{-k}| = |a_k|\) (the magnitude spectrum is even) and \(\angle a_{-k} = -\angle a_k\) (the phase spectrum is odd). The pair of terms at \(\pm k\) then combines into one real sinusoid. Writing \(a_k = |a_k|e^{j\theta_k}\),

\[ a_k e^{jk\omega_0 t} + a_{-k}e^{-jk\omega_0 t} = 2\,\mathrm{Re}\{a_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}\} = 2|a_k|\cos(k\omega_0 t + \theta_k). \]

So every real periodic signal has the compact trigonometric form

\[ x(t) = a_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 2|a_k|\cos(k\omega_0 t + \theta_k). \]

Writing \(a_k = \frac12(A_k - jB_k)\) gives the trigonometric form found in many books:

\[ x(t) = a_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\left[A_k\cos(k\omega_0 t) + B_k\sin(k\omega_0 t)\right], \qquad A_k = \frac{2}{T_0}\int_{T_0}x(t)\cos(k\omega_0 t)\,dt, \quad B_k = \frac{2}{T_0}\int_{T_0}x(t)\sin(k\omega_0 t)\,dt. \]

The three forms carry the same information. The exponential form is the most convenient for the algebra of systems; the trigonometric forms are convenient for real signals with symmetry. If \(x\) is real and even, the sine terms vanish (\(B_k = 0\)) and the \(a_k\) are real. If \(x\) is real and odd, the cosine terms and \(a_0\) vanish (\(A_k = 0\)) and the \(a_k\) are purely imaginary. The rules of Section 1.5 about integrals of even and odd functions are what make this work.

docs.title: The square wave
docs.text:
Example 5.2 A symmetric square wave

Let \(x(t) = 1\) for \(0 < t < T_0/2\) and \(x(t) = -1\) for \(-T_0/2 < t < 0\), repeated with period \(T_0\). Find its Fourier series.

The signal is real and odd, so \(a_0 = 0\) and the coefficients are imaginary. For \(k \ne 0\):

\[ a_k = \frac{1}{T_0}\left[\int_0^{T_0/2}e^{-jk\omega_0 t}dt - \int_{-T_0/2}^{0}e^{-jk\omega_0 t}dt\right] = \frac{1}{T_0}\cdot\frac{(1 - e^{-jk\pi}) - (e^{jk\pi} - 1)}{jk\omega_0}. \]

Since \(e^{\pm jk\pi} = (-1)^k\) and \(\omega_0T_0 = 2\pi\),

\[ a_k = \frac{2\left(1 - (-1)^k\right)}{j2\pi k} = \begin{cases} \dfrac{2}{j\pi k}, & k \text{ odd}, \\[2mm] 0, & k \text{ even}. \end{cases} \]

In trigonometric form, \(B_k = 2j\,a_k = \frac{4}{\pi k}\) for odd \(k\), so

\[ x(t) = \frac{4}{\pi}\left(\sin\omega_0 t + \frac13\sin 3\omega_0 t + \frac15\sin 5\omega_0 t + \cdots\right). \]

Only odd harmonics appear, and their amplitudes fall off as \(1/k\).

The absence of even harmonics is no accident. This square wave has half-wave symmetry: \(x(t + T_0/2) = -x(t)\), the second half of each period is the negative of the first. Every signal with half-wave symmetry has only odd harmonics.

docs.title: The rectangular pulse train
docs.text:
Example 5.3 A pulse train and the sinc envelope

Let \(x(t) = 1\) for \(|t| < T_1\) and \(0\) for \(T_1 < |t| < T_0/2\), repeated with period \(T_0\). Find its Fourier coefficients.

\[ a_0 = \frac{2T_1}{T_0}, \qquad a_k = \frac{1}{T_0}\int_{-T_1}^{T_1}e^{-jk\omega_0 t}dt = \frac{1}{T_0}\cdot\frac{e^{jk\omega_0T_1} - e^{-jk\omega_0T_1}}{jk\omega_0} = \frac{2\sin(k\omega_0T_1)}{k\omega_0T_0} = \frac{\sin(k\omega_0T_1)}{\pi k}. \]

The signal is real and even, so the coefficients are real. In terms of the normalised sinc, \(a_k = \dfrac{2T_1}{T_0}\,\mathrm{sinc}\!\left(\dfrac{2kT_1}{T_0}\right)\). For a 50% duty cycle (\(T_1 = T_0/4\)) this gives \(a_0 = \frac12\), \(a_k = \frac{\sin(k\pi/2)}{\pi k}\): \(a_1 = 1/\pi\), \(a_2 = 0\), \(a_3 = -1/(3\pi)\), and so on.

Figure 5.1 Spectrum of a pulse train. Fourier coefficients a_k of a rectangular pulse train, drawn as stems, with the sinc envelope dashed. Left: duty cycle one half, where every even harmonic is zero. Right: duty cycle one quarter; the envelope is twice as wide and the coefficients are smaller, falling to zero at every fourth harmonic.

Figure 5.1 shows a pattern that will recur in Chapter 6. The coefficients are samples of a fixed envelope, \(\frac{2T_1}{T_0}\mathrm{sinc}(2T_1 f)\) evaluated at \(f = k/T_0\). Making the pulses narrower (smaller \(T_1\)) makes the envelope wider: short events need many frequencies. Making the period longer (larger \(T_0\)) packs the samples closer together. In the limit \(T_0 \to \infty\) only a single pulse remains, the samples merge into a continuous curve, and the Fourier series becomes the Fourier transform.

docs.title: 5.5 Convergence and the Gibbs phenomenon
docs.text:
Does the infinite sum really add up to \(x(t)\)? Two facts settle it for engineering purposes.

Energy convergence. If \(x\) has finite energy over one period, \(\int_{T_0}|x(t)|^2dt < \infty\), then the partial sums \(x_N(t) = \sum_{k=-N}^{N}a_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}\) converge to \(x\) in the sense that the energy of the error over a period tends to zero as \(N \to \infty\). Moreover \(x_N\) is the best approximation to \(x\), in this energy sense, that can be made from the harmonics up to \(N\).

Pointwise convergence (Dirichlet conditions). If over one period \(x\) is absolutely integrable, has a finite number of maxima and minima, and has a finite number of finite discontinuities, then the series converges to \(x(t)\) at every point where \(x\) is continuous, and to the midpoint of the jump, \(\frac12[x(t^-) + x(t^+)]\), at every discontinuity. Every periodic signal you can generate in a laboratory satisfies these conditions.

Near a discontinuity something curious happens. Figure 5.2 shows partial sums of the square wave. As \(N\) grows, the ripples crowd closer to the jump, but the first overshoot does not get smaller: it stays at about 9% of the size of the jump. For the square wave, which jumps by 2, the partial sums peak at about 1.179 instead of 1, however many terms are taken. This is the Gibbs phenomenon. It does not contradict convergence: at any fixed point away from the jump the ripple eventually dies out, and the region of overshoot becomes ever narrower, so the error energy tends to zero. But the maximum error does not tend to zero.

Figure 5.2 The Gibbs phenomenon. Partial sums of the ±1 square wave with harmonics up to N = 1, 3 and 19. The higher the N, the closer the sum hugs the square wave, but the overshoot next to each jump stays at about 9% of the jump.

Gibbs in practice

The same overshoot appears whenever a signal with sharp edges is passed through a filter that cuts off abruptly in frequency: ringing next to sharp edges in compressed images and audio, for instance. Chapter 12 shows how windows trade a slightly gentler cut-off for much smaller ripple.

docs.title: 5.6 Properties of the Fourier series
docs.text:
Let \(x(t) \leftrightarrow a_k\) and \(y(t) \leftrightarrow b_k\), both with period \(T_0\). The properties in Table 5.1 follow from the analysis equation with simple substitutions. They save a great deal of integration.

Property Signal Coefficients Linearity \(Ax(t) + By(t)\) \(Aa_k + Bb_k\) Time shift \(x(t - t_0)\) \(a_k\,e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}\) Frequency shift \(e^{jM\omega_0 t}x(t)\) \(a_{k - M}\) Time reversal \(x(-t)\) \(a_{-k}\) Time scaling \(x(\alpha t)\), period \(T_0/\alpha\) \(a_k\) (at the new fundamental \(\alpha\omega_0\)) Conjugation \(x^*(t)\) \(a_{-k}^*\) Differentiation \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}\) \(jk\omega_0\,a_k\) Periodic convolution \(\int_{T_0}x(\tau)y(t - \tau)\,d\tau\) \(T_0\,a_k b_k\) Multiplication \(x(t)\,y(t)\) \(\sum_{m} a_m b_{k-m}\) Real signal \(x\) real \(a_{-k} = a_k^*\) Parseval \(\dfrac{1}{T_0}\displaystyle\int_{T_0}\lvert x(t)\rvert^2dt\) \(\displaystyle\sum_k \lvert a_k\rvert^2\)

Table 5.1. Properties of the continuous-time Fourier series.

The time-shift property says that delaying a signal leaves the magnitudes \(|a_k|\) unchanged and adds a phase \(-k\omega_0t_0\) that grows linearly with frequency. The differentiation property says that differentiating multiplies each harmonic by \(jk\omega_0\), which emphasises high harmonics; integration (of a signal with \(a_0 = 0\)) divides by \(jk\omega_0\) and smooths. So the coefficients of a signal with jumps fall as \(1/k\), those of a continuous signal with kinks (like a triangle wave) fall as \(1/k^2\), and smoother signals fall faster still.

Parseval's relation says that the average power of a periodic signal is the sum of the powers of its harmonics. Each pair \(\pm k\) contributes \(2|a_k|^2\), which is the power \(\frac12(2|a_k|)^2\) of the sinusoid \(2|a_k|\cos(k\omega_0 t + \theta_k)\), as Example 1.6 requires.

Example 5.4 Using Parseval

For the square wave of Example 5.2, the power is 1 (since \(|x| = 1\) always). Parseval gives

\[ 1 = \sum_{k \text{ odd}}\left|\frac{2}{j\pi k}\right|^2 = 2\sum_{k = 1, 3, 5, \ldots}\frac{4}{\pi^2k^2}, \]

so \(\sum_{k \text{ odd}}\frac{1}{k^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{8}\). A signals result gives a classical sum for free. The fundamental alone carries \(2\cdot\frac{4}{\pi^2} = 0.811\) of the power, or 81%.

Example 5.5 A triangle wave from a square wave

Let \(v(t) = 1 - 4|t|/T_0\) for \(|t| \le T_0/2\), repeated with period \(T_0\): an even triangle wave that peaks at 1 at \(t = 0\) and falls to \(-1\) at \(t = \pm T_0/2\). Find its coefficients without integrating \(v\) directly.

Its average is 0, so \(d_0 = 0\). Its derivative is \(-4/T_0\) for \(0 < t < T_0/2\) and \(+4/T_0\) for \(-T_0/2 < t < 0\), which is \(-\frac{4}{T_0}\) times the square wave of Example 5.2. So \(dv/dt\) has coefficients \(c_k = -\frac{4}{T_0}\cdot\frac{2}{j\pi k}\) for odd \(k\) and 0 for even \(k\). By the differentiation property, \(c_k = jk\omega_0 d_k\), hence for odd \(k\)

\[ d_k = \frac{c_k}{jk\omega_0} = -\frac{4}{T_0}\cdot\frac{2}{j\pi k}\cdot\frac{T_0}{j2\pi k} = \frac{4}{\pi^2k^2}. \]

The coefficients are real (the signal is even), present only for odd \(k\) (half-wave symmetry), and fall as \(1/k^2\), faster than the square wave's \(1/k\). Check at \(t = 0\): \(v(0) = \sum_k d_k = 2\cdot\frac{4}{\pi^2}\sum_{k\text{ odd}}\frac{1}{k^2} = \frac{8}{\pi^2}\cdot\frac{\pi^2}{8} = 1\), using Example 5.4.

docs.title: 5.7 LTI systems with periodic inputs
docs.text:
Here is the payoff. Let a periodic signal \(x(t) = \sum_k a_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}\) drive a stable LTI system with frequency response

\[ H(j\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t)\,e^{-j\omega t}\,dt . \]

Each harmonic is an eigenfunction, so it emerges multiplied by \(H(jk\omega_0)\):

\[ y(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} a_k\,H(jk\omega_0)\,e^{jk\omega_0 t}. \]

The output is periodic with the same period, and its coefficients are \(b_k = a_k H(jk\omega_0)\). The system reshapes the spectrum: harmonics where \(|H|\) is large are emphasised, those where \(|H|\) is small are suppressed. This is filtering. (Strictly, this is the steady-state response, after any transient caused by switching the input on has died away; for a periodic input defined for all time there is no transient.)

Example 5.6 A square wave through an RC low-pass filter

An RC circuit with \(RC = 1/(2\pi\cdot 100)\) s has \(H(j\omega) = \dfrac{1}{1 + j\omega RC}\) and a cut-off frequency of 100 Hz. The input is the ±1 square wave of Example 5.2 with fundamental 100 Hz, so \(\omega_0RC = 1\). Find the amplitudes of the first three non-zero harmonics at the output.

At harmonic \(k\), \(H(jk\omega_0) = \dfrac{1}{1 + jk}\), with magnitude \(1/\sqrt{1 + k^2}\). The input sinusoid at harmonic \(k\) (odd) has amplitude \(2|a_k| = \frac{4}{\pi k}\).

\(k\) Input amplitude \(\frac{4}{\pi k}\) \(\lvert H\rvert = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+k^2}}\) Output amplitude 1 1.273 0.707 0.900 3 0.424 0.316 0.134 5 0.255 0.196 0.050

Table 5.2. Harmonic amplitudes before and after the filter.

The third harmonic falls from 33% to 15% of the fundamental, and the fifth from 20% to 6%. The output looks much more like a sinusoid: the corners of the square wave are rounded off, as anyone who has looked at a square wave through a slow amplifier on an oscilloscope has seen.

docs.title: 5.8 The discrete-time Fourier series
docs.text:
A periodic sequence \(x[n]\) with fundamental period \(N\) can also be written as a sum of harmonically related exponentials \(e^{jk(2\pi/N)n}\). There is one big difference from continuous time: because \(e^{j(k + N)(2\pi/N)n} = e^{jk(2\pi/N)n}\), there are only \(N\) distinct harmonics. The series is a finite sum:

\[ x[n] = \sum_{k=\langle N\rangle} a_k\,e^{jk(2\pi/N)n}, \qquad a_k = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=\langle N\rangle} x[n]\,e^{-jk(2\pi/N)n}, \]

where \(\langle N\rangle\) means any \(N\) consecutive integers, such as \(0, 1, \ldots, N-1\). The coefficients are themselves periodic: \(a_{k+N} = a_k\). There are no convergence questions, because nothing is infinite; the \(N\) equations of the synthesis formula are simply solved exactly by the analysis formula. The orthogonality that makes it work is \(\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}e^{j(k-m)(2\pi/N)n} = N\) if \(k - m\) is a multiple of \(N\) and \(0\) otherwise, which is the finite geometric series with ratio \(e^{j(k-m)2\pi/N}\).

Example 5.7 DTFS of a short periodic sequence

Let \(x[n]\) have period 4 with \(x[0] = 1\), \(x[1] = 1\), \(x[2] = 0\), \(x[3] = 0\). With \(e^{-j2\pi/4} = -j\):

\[ a_k = \frac14\left(1 + (-j)^k\right). \]

So \(a_0 = \frac12\), \(a_1 = \frac{1 - j}{4}\), \(a_2 = 0\), \(a_3 = \frac{1 + j}{4}\). Since \(x\) is real, \(a_3 = a_{-1} = a_1^*\), as conjugate symmetry requires. Check by synthesis at \(n = 0\): \(\frac12 + \frac{1 - j}{4} + 0 + \frac{1 + j}{4} = 1\). Correct.

Up to the factor \(\frac1N\), the DTFS coefficients over one period are exactly what is computed by the discrete Fourier transform of Chapter 8, the most widely used algorithm in signal processing.

docs.title: 5.9 Fourier coefficients numerically
docs.text:
Computing \(a_k\) by numerical integration is a good check on algebra. The program below approximates the analysis integral for the pulse train of Example 5.3 with \(T_0 = 1\) and \(T_1 = 0.25\), checks Parseval's relation, and measures the Gibbs overshoot of the square wave.

import numpy as np

T0, T1 = 1.0, 0.25                 # period and half-width of the pulse
w0 = 2 * np.pi / T0
M = 100_000                        # samples per period for the numerical integral
t = (np.arange(M) + 0.5) / M * T0 - T0 / 2      # midpoints over one period
x = (np.abs(t) < T1).astype(float)

def coeff(k):
    """a_k = (1/T0) * integral over one period of x(t) e^{-j k w0 t} dt (midpoint rule)."""
    return np.mean(x * np.exp(-1j * k * w0 * t))

for k in range(0, 6):
    exact = 2 * T1 / T0 if k == 0 else np.sin(k * w0 * T1) / (np.pi * k)
    print(f"a_{k}: numerical {coeff(k).real:+.5f}   formula {exact:+.5f}")

# Parseval: power from time samples versus sum of |a_k|^2
K = np.arange(-2000, 2001)
ak = np.where(K == 0, 2 * T1 / T0, np.sin(K * w0 * T1) / (np.pi * np.where(K == 0, 1, K)))
print("power in time      :", np.mean(x ** 2))
print("sum |a_k|^2 (|k|<=2000):", round(float(np.sum(ak ** 2)), 5))

# Gibbs: peak of the partial sum of the +/-1 square wave, (4/pi) sum sin(k w0 t)/k, k odd
tt = np.linspace(0, 0.1, 20001)
for N in (9, 49, 199):
    s = sum(4 / np.pi * np.sin(k * w0 * tt) / k for k in range(1, N + 1, 2))
    print(f"N = {N:3d}: peak of partial sum = {s.max():.4f}")

a_0: numerical +0.50000   formula +0.50000
a_1: numerical +0.31831   formula +0.31831
a_2: numerical +0.00000   formula +0.00000
a_3: numerical -0.10610   formula -0.10610
a_4: numerical -0.00000   formula -0.00000
a_5: numerical +0.06366   formula +0.06366
power in time      : 0.5
sum |a_k|^2 (|k|<=2000): 0.49995
N =   9: peak of partial sum = 1.1823
N =  49: peak of partial sum = 1.1791
N = 199: peak of partial sum = 1.1790

The coefficients match the formula to five decimal places, and Parseval's sum approaches the power 0.5 as more harmonics are included (the coefficients fall only as \(1/k\), so convergence is slow). The Gibbs peak settles near 1.179 and does not fall as \(N\) grows.

docs.title: 5.10 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • A periodic signal is a sum of harmonics: \(x(t) = \sum_k a_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}\) with \(a_k = \frac{1}{T_0}\int_{T_0}x(t)e^{-jk\omega_0 t}dt\). Orthogonality of the harmonics gives the analysis equation.
  • For real signals \(a_{-k} = a_k^*\), and the series can be written with cosines and sines. Even signals give real \(a_k\); odd signals give imaginary \(a_k\); half-wave symmetry gives only odd harmonics.
  • The square wave has \(a_k = 2/(j\pi k)\) for odd \(k\); the pulse train has a sinc-shaped spectrum whose width is inversely proportional to the pulse width.
  • Under the Dirichlet conditions the series converges to \(x\) where \(x\) is continuous and to the midpoint at jumps. Near a jump the partial sums overshoot by about 9% of the jump (Gibbs).
  • Delay adds linear phase; differentiation multiplies by \(jk\omega_0\); Parseval equates power with \(\sum|a_k|^2\).
  • An LTI system multiplies the \(k\)th harmonic by \(H(jk\omega_0)\).
  • A periodic sequence of period \(N\) has exactly \(N\) distinct DTFS coefficients, found by a finite sum.

docs.title: 5.11 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 5.1

Find the Fourier coefficients of \(x(t) = 3\cos(5t) - 4\sin(10t)\).

Answer

\(\omega_0 = 5\). \(a_{\pm1} = \frac32\); \(-4\sin 10t = -\frac{4}{2j}(e^{j10t} - e^{-j10t})\) gives \(a_2 = -\frac{2}{j} = 2j\) and \(a_{-2} = -2j\). All others are zero.

Exercise 5.2

What is \(a_0\) for the pulse train of Example 5.3 with \(T_0 = 5\) ms and \(T_1 = 0.5\) ms?

Answer

0.2. \(a_0 = 2T_1/T_0 = 1/5\): the fraction of each period during which the signal is on.

Exercise 5.3

The square wave of Example 5.2 is delayed by \(T_0/4\). Find the new coefficients and show that they are real.

Answer

By the time-shift property, \(b_k = a_k e^{-jk\omega_0 T_0/4} = \frac{2}{j\pi k}e^{-jk\pi/2}\) for odd \(k\) (and 0 for even \(k\)). For \(k = 1\), \(e^{-j\pi/2} = -j\) gives \(b_1 = -\frac{2}{\pi}\); for \(k = 3\), \(e^{-j3\pi/2} = j\) gives \(b_3 = \frac{2}{3\pi}\). In general \(b_k = (-1)^{(k+1)/2}\frac{2}{\pi k}\), which is real. This is expected: the delayed wave is \(-1\) on \((-T_0/4, T_0/4)\) and \(+1\) on the rest of the period, an even signal.

Exercise 5.4

A periodic signal has \(a_0 = 2\), \(a_{\pm1} = 1\), \(a_{\pm3} = j\) and \(a_{\mp3}\) such that the signal is real. Is \(a_3 = j\) and \(a_{-3} = j\) consistent with a real signal?

Answer

No. A real signal needs \(a_{-3} = a_3^* = -j\). With \(a_3 = j\) and \(a_{-3} = -j\), the pair gives \(2\,\mathrm{Re}\{je^{j3\omega_0t}\} = -2\sin 3\omega_0t\).

Exercise 5.5

Use Parseval to find the power of \(x(t) = 1 + \cos(t) + \frac12\sin(2t)\).

Answer

\(|a_0|^2 = 1\); \(a_{\pm1} = \frac12\) contribute \(2\cdot\frac14 = \frac12\); \(a_{\pm2}\) have magnitude \(\frac14\) and contribute \(2\cdot\frac{1}{16} = \frac18\). Power \(= 1.625\).

Exercise 5.6

Without integrating, say which harmonics are present in a periodic signal that is real, even and has half-wave symmetry.

Answer

Only odd harmonics (half-wave symmetry), and only cosines with real coefficients (even). For example the even square wave and the triangle wave.

Exercise 5.7

A system has \(H(j\omega) = \dfrac{1}{1 + j\omega}\). Find the steady-state output for \(x(t) = 2 + \cos t\).

Answer

DC: \(H(0) = 1\), so 2 passes unchanged. At \(\omega = 1\): \(H = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}e^{-j\pi/4}\). Output \(y(t) = 2 + \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cos(t - \pi/4)\).

Exercise 5.8

Find the DTFS coefficients of \(x[n] = \cos(\pi n/3)\).

Answer

\(N = 6\). \(\cos(\pi n/3) = \frac12 e^{j(2\pi/6)n} + \frac12 e^{-j(2\pi/6)n}\), so \(a_1 = a_{-1} = a_5 = \frac12\) and the other coefficients in a period are zero.

Exercise 5.9

Compute the DTFS of the period-3 sequence \(x[0] = 3\), \(x[1] = 0\), \(x[2] = 0\).

Answer

\(a_k = \frac13\cdot 3 = 1\) for every \(k\). A single impulse per period contains all harmonics equally.

Exercise 5.10

Explain why the Fourier coefficients of a triangle wave fall off faster than those of a square wave.

Answer

The triangle is the integral of a square wave (minus its mean). Integration divides the \(k\)th coefficient by \(jk\omega_0\), turning \(1/k\) decay into \(1/k^2\). In general, the smoother the signal, the faster its coefficients decay.

docs.title: 5.12 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 5

Exercise 1

For a real periodic signal, a₋ₖ equals

  1. aₖ
  2. −aₖ
  3. the conjugate of aₖ
  4. zero
Answer

Exercise 2

A real, odd periodic signal has Fourier coefficients that are

  1. real
  2. purely imaginary
  3. all zero for odd k
  4. equal to 1
Answer

Exercise 3

What is the average value a₀ of a pulse train that is 1 for 20% of each period and 0 otherwise?

Answer

Exercise 4

  1. shrinks to zero
  2. stays near 9% of the jump
  3. grows without limit
  4. moves away from the jump

Exercise 5

Delaying a periodic signal by t₀ multiplies aₖ by

  2. e^(jkω₀t₀)
  3. t₀
  4. jkω₀

docs.title: Chapter 12: Frequency Response and Filters
docs.text:
Bode plots, filter specifications, Butterworth designs, and digital IIR and FIR filters

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • interpret magnitude and phase responses, decibels, group delay and the condition for distortionless transmission;
  • sketch Bode plots of first- and second-order factors and combine them;
  • write a filter specification in terms of passband, stopband, transition band and tolerances;
  • find the order of a Butterworth filter that meets a specification;
  • design a digital IIR filter by the bilinear transform with prewarping, and a notch filter by placing poles and zeros;
  • design a linear-phase FIR filter by the window method and choose a window;
  • compare FIR and IIR filters for a given task.

docs.title: 12.1 What the frequency response tells us
docs.text:
A stable LTI system multiplies the complex exponential \(e^{j\omega t}\) by \(H(j\omega)\), and so, for a real system, it turns the sinusoid \(A\cos(\omega t + \phi)\) into

\[ A\,|H(j\omega)|\cos\!\big(\omega t + \phi + \angle H(j\omega)\big). \]

The magnitude response \(|H(j\omega)|\) is the gain at each frequency; the phase response \(\angle H(j\omega)\) is the phase shift. (For DT systems replace \(H(j\omega)\) by \(H(e^{j\Omega})\).) Shaping the magnitude response is called filtering: passing some frequencies and suppressing others.

docs.title: Decibels
docs.text:
Gains are usually quoted in decibels: \(|H|_{\text{dB}} = 20\log_{10}|H|\). The logarithm turns products into sums, so the gain of a cascade in dB is the sum of the gains. Some values are worth knowing by heart:

\(\lvert H\rvert\) 10 2 \(\sqrt2\) 1 \(1/\sqrt2\) \(1/2\) \(0.1\) \(0.01\) \(0.001\) dB 20 6.0 3.0 0 \(-3.0\) \(-6.0\) \(-20\) \(-40\) \(-60\)

Table 12.1. Gains in decibels.

The frequency at which the gain falls to \(1/\sqrt2\) of its passband value is the 3 dB or half-power frequency, because the power, proportional to \(|H|^2\), has halved.

docs.title: Phase, delay and distortion
docs.text:
A system transmits without distortion if its output is a scaled, delayed copy of the input, \(y(t) = Kx(t - t_0)\). Taking transforms, \(H(j\omega) = Ke^{-j\omega t_0}\): constant magnitude and linear phase. Within the band occupied by a signal, a filter must therefore have flat magnitude and a phase that is a straight line through the origin if the waveform is to be preserved. The slope of the phase measures the delay; for a general system we define the group delay

\[ \tau_g(\omega) = -\frac{d\angle H(j\omega)}{d\omega}, \]

the delay experienced by a narrow band of frequencies around \(\omega\). A linear-phase system has constant group delay; a system whose group delay varies across the band smears the waveform, an effect called phase distortion. The ear is fairly tolerant of phase distortion; data transmission and image processing are not.

docs.title: 12.2 Bode plots
docs.text: A Bode plot draws \(|H(j\omega)|\) in dB and \(\angle H(j\omega)\) in degrees against a logarithmic frequency axis. The logarithmic axes turn the factors of a rational transfer function into straight-line pieces that simply add.

docs.title: A first-order low-pass factor
docs.text:
Take \(H(j\omega) = \dfrac{1}{1 + j\omega/\omega_c}\). Then

\[ |H|_{\text{dB}} = -10\log_{10}\!\left(1 + \frac{\omega^2}{\omega_c^2}\right), \qquad \angle H = -\arctan\frac{\omega}{\omega_c}. \]
  • For \(\omega \ll \omega_c\): \(|H| \approx 1\), so 0 dB, and the phase is about \(0°\).
  • For \(\omega \gg \omega_c\): \(|H| \approx \omega_c/\omega\), so \(|H|_{\text{dB}} \approx -20\log_{10}(\omega/\omega_c)\): a straight line falling at 20 dB per decade (a decade is a factor of 10 in frequency), and the phase approaches \(-90°\).
  • At the corner frequency \(\omega = \omega_c\): \(|H| = 1/\sqrt2\) (\(-3\) dB) and the phase is \(-45°\).

The two straight-line asymptotes meeting at \(\omega_c\) approximate the magnitude within 3 dB everywhere. The phase is approximated by a line from \(0°\) at \(0.1\omega_c\) to \(-90°\) at \(10\omega_c\).

Figure 12.1 A first-order Bode plot. Bode plot of 1/(1 + jω/ω_c). Left: the magnitude is flat at 0 dB below ω_c and falls at 20 dB per decade above it; the dashed asymptotes meet at the corner frequency, where the true curve is 3 dB down. Right: the phase falls from 0° to −90°, passing −45° at ω_c; the dashed straight-line approximation runs from 0.1ω_c to 10ω_c.

A zero factor \(1 + j\omega/\omega_z\) gives the mirror image: \(+20\) dB per decade and \(+90°\) of phase. A pole at the origin, \(1/(j\omega)\), gives a line falling at 20 dB per decade through 0 dB at \(\omega = 1\), with a constant phase of \(-90°\). A constant gain \(K\) shifts the magnitude by \(20\log_{10}|K|\).

docs.title: Second-order factors
docs.text:
The factor \(\dfrac{\omega_n^2}{(j\omega)^2 + 2\zeta\omega_n(j\omega) + \omega_n^2}\) of Section 10.7 has asymptotes at 0 dB below \(\omega_n\) and \(-40\) dB per decade above it, with the phase going from \(0°\) to \(-180°\). Near \(\omega_n\) the true curve depends on \(\zeta\): at \(\omega = \omega_n\) the magnitude is \(\frac{1}{2\zeta}\). For \(\zeta < 1/\sqrt2\) there is a resonant peak of height \(\frac{1}{2\zeta\sqrt{1 - \zeta^2}}\) near \(\omega_n\); for \(\zeta = 0.1\) it is about 5, or 14 dB. Lightly damped poles mean a sharp resonance, the frequency-domain image of the ringing step response.

Example 12.1 A Bode sketch

Sketch the magnitude of \(H(s) = \dfrac{100(s + 10)}{(s + 1)(s + 100)}\).

Write it in Bode form: \(H(j\omega) = \dfrac{100\cdot10\,(1 + j\omega/10)}{1\cdot100\,(1 + j\omega)(1 + j\omega/100)} = \dfrac{10(1 + j\omega/10)}{(1 + j\omega)(1 + j\omega/100)}\).

The DC gain is 10, or 20 dB. Reading the corners in order: at \(\omega = 1\) a pole starts a slope of \(-20\) dB/decade; at \(\omega = 10\) the zero cancels it, so the magnitude is flat again, at \(20 - 20 = 0\) dB; at \(\omega = 100\) the second pole resumes the fall at \(-20\) dB/decade. So the gain is 20 dB up to 1 rad/s, falls to 0 dB at 10 rad/s, stays near 0 dB to 100 rad/s, and then falls. (Exact value at \(\omega = 30\): \(|H| = \frac{10\sqrt{1 + 9}}{\sqrt{1 + 900}\sqrt{1 + 0.09}} = 1.01\), about 0 dB, as the sketch says.)

docs.title: 12.3 Filter types and specifications
docs.text:
The ideal filters of Chapters 6 and 7 pass a band of frequencies with gain 1 and reject everything else completely:

  • low-pass: passes \(|\omega| < \omega_c\);
  • high-pass: passes \(|\omega| > \omega_c\);
  • band-pass: passes \(\omega_1 < |\omega| < \omega_2\);
  • band-stop (or notch, when narrow): rejects \(\omega_1 < |\omega| < \omega_2\).

They cannot be built: their impulse responses are non-causal and infinitely long (Example 6.5). A practical design therefore starts from a specification with tolerances (Figure 12.2):

  • a passband \(0 \le \omega \le \omega_p\) in which the gain stays within \(1 \pm \delta_p\) (or a ripple of so many dB);
  • a stopband \(\omega \ge \omega_s\) in which the gain stays below \(\delta_s\) (an attenuation of \(-20\log_{10}\delta_s\) dB);
  • a transition band \(\omega_p < \omega < \omega_s\) in which anything is allowed.
Figure 12.2 A low-pass specification. The tolerance scheme for a low-pass filter. In the passband (green), up to ω_p, the gain must stay between 1 − δ_p and 1 + δ_p. In the stopband (red), beyond ω_s, it must stay below δ_s. Between them is the transition band. The blue curve meets the specification.

The tighter the tolerances and the narrower the transition band, the higher the order of filter required, and the more it costs in components or computation. Filter design is the art of meeting the specification with the lowest order.

docs.title: 12.4 Analog Butterworth filters
docs.text:
The Butterworth low-pass filter of order \(N\) has
