\[ |H(j\omega)|^2 = \frac{1}{1 + (\omega/\omega_c)^{2N}} . \]

Its magnitude is \(1\) at \(\omega = 0\), exactly \(1/\sqrt2\) (\(-3\) dB) at \(\omega = \omega_c\) for every \(N\), and falls at \(20N\) dB per decade far above \(\omega_c\). The first \(2N - 1\) derivatives of \(|H|^2\) are zero at \(\omega = 0\), so the passband is as flat as possible: it is called maximally flat. Higher order gives a sharper edge (Figure 12.3).

Figure 12.3 Butterworth filters. Butterworth magnitude responses for N = 1, 2, 4 and 8. All pass through 0.707 at ω = ω_c. Higher orders are flatter in the passband and fall more steeply beyond the cut-off.

The poles of \(H(s)H(-s) = 1/(1 + (s/j\omega_c)^{2N})\) lie equally spaced on a circle of radius \(\omega_c\); the causal, stable filter takes the \(N\) of them in the left half-plane. For \(N = 2\) these are \(\omega_c e^{\pm j3\pi/4}\), giving \(H(s) = \dfrac{\omega_c^2}{s^2 + \sqrt2\,\omega_cs + \omega_c^2}\), a second-order system with \(\zeta = 1/\sqrt2\).

docs.title: Choosing the order
docs.text:
With the cut-off \(\omega_c\) at the passband edge (3 dB passband loss), the attenuation at the stopband edge \(\omega_s\) must be at least \(A_s\) dB:

\[ 10\log_{10}\!\left(1 + (\omega_s/\omega_c)^{2N}\right) \ge A_s \quad\Longrightarrow\quad N \ge \frac{\log_{10}\!\left(10^{A_s/10} - 1\right)}{2\log_{10}(\omega_s/\omega_c)} . \]

Example 12.2 Order of a Butterworth filter

A low-pass filter must be 3 dB down at 1 kHz and at least 40 dB down at 3 kHz. Then \(N \ge \dfrac{\log_{10}(10^4 - 1)}{2\log_{10}3} = \dfrac{4.000}{0.954} = 4.19\), so \(N = 5\).

Other classical families trade flatness for steepness. Chebyshev filters allow ripple in the passband (type I) or stopband (type II) and achieve a sharper transition for the same order; elliptic filters allow ripple in both and are sharper still; Bessel filters give up sharpness to obtain a nearly linear phase. All are available in libraries such as scipy.signal.

docs.title: 12.5 Digital IIR filters
docs.text: An IIR filter is a recursive difference equation whose system function has poles away from the origin. There are two common ways to design one.

docs.title: The bilinear transform
docs.text:
Start from a good analog design and convert it. The bilinear transform replaces \(s\) by

\[ s = \frac{2}{T}\cdot\frac{1 - z^{-1}}{1 + z^{-1}} . \]

It maps the left half of the s-plane exactly onto the inside of the unit circle, so a stable analog filter always gives a stable digital filter, and it maps the whole \(j\omega\) axis once around the unit circle, so there is no aliasing. The price is a nonlinear compression of frequency, called warping: the analog frequency \(\omega\) and the digital frequency \(\Omega\) are related by

\[ \omega = \frac{2}{T}\tan\frac{\Omega}{2} . \]

To place a critical frequency correctly, prewarp it: design the analog prototype with cut-off \(\omega_a = \frac{2}{T}\tan(\Omega_c/2)\), then transform.

Example 12.3 A first-order digital low-pass filter

Design a first-order low-pass filter with a 3 dB cut-off of 1 kHz for a sampling rate of 8 kHz.

\(\Omega_c = 2\pi\cdot1000/8000 = \pi/4\). Prewarp: \(\omega_a = \frac{2}{T}\tan(\pi/8)\). The analog prototype is \(H(s) = \frac{\omega_a}{s + \omega_a}\). Substituting \(s = \frac{2}{T}\frac{1 - z^{-1}}{1 + z^{-1}}\) and writing \(c = \omega_aT/2 = \tan(\pi/8) = 0.41421\):

\[ H(z) = \frac{c(1 + z^{-1})}{(1 + c) - (1 - c)z^{-1}} = \frac{0.29289\,(1 + z^{-1})}{1 - 0.41421\,z^{-1}} . \]

The difference equation is \(y[n] = 0.41421\,y[n-1] + 0.29289\,(x[n] + x[n-1])\). Its gain is 1 at DC, \(1/\sqrt2\) at exactly 1 kHz (thanks to prewarping), and 0 at 4 kHz (the zero at \(z = -1\)), as the program in Section 12.8 confirms.

docs.title: Placing poles and zeros directly
docs.text:
Simple filters can be designed straight from the geometric picture of Section 11.7. A notch filter that removes one frequency \(\Omega_0\) puts zeros on the unit circle at \(e^{\pm j\Omega_0}\) and poles just inside, at \(re^{\pm j\Omega_0}\) with \(r\) slightly less than 1:

\[ H(z) = \frac{1 - 2\cos\Omega_0\,z^{-1} + z^{-2}}{1 - 2r\cos\Omega_0\,z^{-1} + r^2z^{-2}} . \]

Away from \(\Omega_0\), each pole is almost as far from the point \(e^{j\Omega}\) as its neighbouring zero, so the gain is close to 1; at \(\Omega_0\) the zero makes it exactly 0. The width of the notch is roughly \(2(1 - r)\) rad/sample: the closer the poles to the circle, the narrower the notch.

Example 12.4 Removing mains hum

For 50 Hz hum in audio sampled at 8 kHz (Example 9.3), \(\Omega_0 = \pi/80\). With \(r = 0.99\) the notch width is about \(0.02\) rad/sample, or \(0.02 \times 8000/(2\pi) \approx 25\) Hz. The program in Section 12.8 measures a 3 dB band from 37 Hz to 63 Hz.

docs.title: 12.6 Digital FIR filters and the window method
docs.text: An FIR filter \(y[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{M}h[k]\,x[n-k]\) has a finite impulse response of \(M + 1\) taps. FIR filters are always stable, and they can have exactly linear phase: if the coefficients are symmetric, \(h[k] = h[M - k]\), the frequency response is \(H(e^{j\Omega}) = A(\Omega)e^{-j\Omega M/2}\) with \(A\) real, a pure delay of \(M/2\) samples times a real gain. This is impossible for a causal IIR filter, and it is the main reason FIR filters are used in audio, communications and image processing.

docs.title: The window method
docs.text:
1. Start from the ideal frequency response, for a low-pass filter \(H_d = 1\) for \(|\Omega| < \Omega_c\), with linear phase \(e^{-j\Omega M/2}\). Its impulse response is the shifted sinc

    \[ h_d[n] = \frac{\sin\!\big(\Omega_c(n - M/2)\big)}{\pi(n - M/2)} , \]

    which is infinitely long.

  2. Keep only \(n = 0, \ldots, M\) and multiply by a window \(w[n]\): \(h[n] = h_d[n]\,w[n]\).

Truncation with the plain rectangular window gives the Gibbs phenomenon of Section 5.5: ripples near the band edge, with a first stopband side lobe only about 21 dB down, whatever the length. A tapered window trades a wider transition band for much smaller ripples. Table 12.2 lists the common windows; the attenuation is a property of the window shape, while the transition width shrinks in proportion to \(1/M\).

Window \(w[n]\), \(0 \le n \le M\) Peak side lobe of window Approx. stopband attenuation of filter Rectangular \(1\) \(-13\) dB 21 dB Hann \(0.5 - 0.5\cos(2\pi n/M)\) \(-31\) dB 44 dB Hamming \(0.54 - 0.46\cos(2\pi n/M)\) \(-41\) dB 53 dB Blackman \(0.42 - 0.5\cos(2\pi n/M) + 0.08\cos(4\pi n/M)\) \(-57\) dB 74 dB

Table 12.2. Windows for FIR design (approximate values from standard tables).

Figure 12.4 Window design of an FIR filter. Magnitude response in dB of a 51-tap low-pass filter with cut-off π/4, designed with a rectangular window (blue) and a Hamming window (orange). The rectangular design has a sharper edge but stopband ripples only 20 to 40 dB down; the Hamming design has a wider transition and ripples more than 50 dB down.

More refined methods (frequency sampling, and the optimal equiripple design of Parks and McClellan) give lower orders for the same specification; libraries provide them, but the window method remains the clearest introduction and is often good enough.

docs.title: 12.7 FIR or IIR?
docs.text:
FIR IIR Stability always stable must check that poles are inside the unit circle Phase exactly linear possible nonlinear (approximately linear only near DC, or with extra stages) Order for a sharp edge high (tens to hundreds of taps) low (a few poles) Computation per sample more less Sensitivity to coefficient rounding low can be high for poles near the circle Design windows, equiripple; direct in DT from analog prototypes (bilinear transform), pole placement

Table 12.3. FIR and IIR filters compared.

Choose FIR when phase linearity or guaranteed stability matters, or when the filter must adapt; choose IIR when computation is scarce and phase does not matter, or when an analog design is to be copied.

docs.title: 12.8 Designing filters in NumPy
docs.text:
The program below computes a Butterworth order, designs the IIR filter of Example 12.3 and checks its gain at four frequencies, designs 51-tap FIR filters with two windows and measures their stopband levels, and measures the width of the notch of Example 12.4. The helper freqz evaluates \(H(e^{j\Omega})\) from the coefficients in powers of \(z^{-1}\).

import numpy as np

def freqz(b, a, W):
    """H(e^{jW}) for H(z) = B(z^-1) / A(z^-1)."""
    zinv = np.exp(-1j * np.asarray(W))
    return np.polyval(b[::-1], zinv) / np.polyval(a[::-1], zinv)

# 1. Butterworth order: at most 3 dB loss at 1 kHz, at least 40 dB attenuation at 3 kHz
N = np.log10(10 ** (40 / 10) - 1) / (2 * np.log10(3000 / 1000))
print(f"Butterworth order needed: {N:.2f} -> N = {int(np.ceil(N))}")

# 2. Bilinear transform of H(s) = wa / (s + wa), cut-off 1 kHz at fs = 8 kHz (with prewarping)
fs, fc = 8000, 1000
c = np.tan(np.pi * fc / fs)                 # = wa / (2 fs) after prewarping
b = np.array([c, c]) / (1 + c)
a = np.array([1, -(1 - c) / (1 + c)])
print("IIR b =", np.round(b, 5), " a =", np.round(a, 5))
for f in (0, 1000, 2000, 3000):
    H = freqz(b, a, 2 * np.pi * f / fs)
    print(f"  {f:4d} Hz: |H| = {abs(H):.4f} ({20 * np.log10(abs(H)):7.2f} dB)")

# 3. Windowed-sinc FIR low-pass: cut-off pi/4, 51 taps, rectangular versus Hamming window
M = 50                                       # order; 51 taps, symmetric about n = 25
n = np.arange(M + 1)
Wc = np.pi / 4
hd = Wc / np.pi * np.sinc(Wc / np.pi * (n - M / 2))      # sin(Wc m)/(pi m), m = n - M/2
W = np.linspace(0, np.pi, 4001)
for name, w in (("rectangular", np.ones(M + 1)), ("Hamming", np.hamming(M + 1))):
    h = hd * w
    H = np.abs(freqz(h, np.array([1.0]), W))
    stop = W >= Wc + 0.15 * np.pi            # stopband from 0.4 pi
    print(f"  {name:11s}: DC gain {H[0]:.4f}, worst stopband level {20 * np.log10(H[stop].max()):6.1f} dB,"
          f" symmetric (linear phase): {np.allclose(h, h[::-1])}")

# 4. Notch at 50 Hz for fs = 8 kHz: zeros on the circle, poles at radius 0.99
W0 = 2 * np.pi * 50 / 8000
bn = np.array([1, -2 * np.cos(W0), 1])
an = np.array([1, -2 * 0.99 * np.cos(W0), 0.99 ** 2])
f = np.linspace(0, 200, 20001)
Hn = np.abs(freqz(bn, an, 2 * np.pi * f / 8000))
band = f[Hn < 1 / np.sqrt(2)]
print(f"notch: |H| at 50 Hz = {Hn[np.argmin(abs(f - 50))]:.1e}, at 0 Hz = {Hn[0]:.3f},"
      f" -3 dB band {band.min():.1f} to {band.max():.1f} Hz")

Butterworth order needed: 4.19 -> N = 5
IIR b = [0.29289 0.29289]  a = [ 1.      -0.41421]
     0 Hz: |H| = 1.0000 (   0.00 dB)
  1000 Hz: |H| = 0.7071 (  -3.01 dB)
  2000 Hz: |H| = 0.3827 (  -8.34 dB)
  3000 Hz: |H| = 0.1691 ( -15.44 dB)
  rectangular: DC gain 0.9862, worst stopband level  -30.2 dB, symmetric (linear phase): True
  Hamming    : DC gain 0.9992, worst stopband level  -55.2 dB, symmetric (linear phase): True
notch: |H| at 50 Hz = 1.4e-13, at 0 Hz = 0.948, -3 dB band 37.2 to 62.7 Hz

The IIR filter is exactly 3 dB down at 1 kHz. The stopband here starts at \(0.4\pi\), past the transition band of both FIR designs; the rectangular design's worst ripple beyond that point is \(-30\) dB, while its first side lobe, just after the edge, is near \(-21\) dB, as Figure 12.4 shows. The Hamming design stays below \(-55\) dB. The notch removes 50 Hz completely; because it sits so close to DC, it also lowers the gain at 0 Hz slightly (to 0.948), which could be corrected by a constant gain if it mattered.

docs.title: 12.9 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • A sinusoid is scaled by \(|H|\) and shifted by \(\angle H\). Gains are quoted in dB, \(20\log_{10}|H|\); the 3 dB frequency is where the power halves.
  • Distortionless transmission needs constant magnitude and linear phase; group delay \(-d\angle H/d\omega\) measures delay versus frequency.
  • Bode plots add straight-line asymptotes: each pole bends the magnitude down by 20 dB/decade and adds up to \(-90°\); each zero does the opposite. Lightly damped second-order poles give a resonant peak \(\approx 1/(2\zeta)\).
  • Practical filters meet a tolerance scheme of passband ripple, stopband attenuation and transition width.
  • Butterworth filters are maximally flat, \(-3\) dB at \(\omega_c\), falling \(20N\) dB/decade; the order follows from the specification.
  • The bilinear transform \(s = \frac2T\frac{1 - z^{-1}}{1 + z^{-1}}\) turns stable analog filters into stable digital ones; prewarp with \(\omega = \frac2T\tan\frac\Omega2\). Notches come from zeros on the unit circle with poles just inside.
  • FIR filters by the window method: truncate the ideal sinc and taper it. Symmetric taps give exact linear phase; the window sets the stopband attenuation, the length sets the transition width.

docs.title: 12.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 12.1

A filter has gain 0.05 at some frequency. Express it in dB.

Answer

−26 dB. \(20\log_{10}0.05 = 20(-1.301) = -26.0\) dB.

Exercise 12.2

Find the corner frequency and the gain at \(\omega = 1000\) rad/s of \(H(s) = \dfrac{1}{1 + s/100}\), both exactly and from the asymptote.

Answer

Corner at 100 rad/s. Exact: \(|H| = 1/\sqrt{1 + 100} = 0.0995\), or \(-20.04\) dB. Asymptote: one decade above the corner, \(-20\) dB.

Exercise 12.3

What is the group delay of the FIR filter \(y[n] = \frac14(x[n] + 2x[n-1] + x[n-2])\)?

Answer

The coefficients are symmetric about \(n = 1\), so the phase is \(-\Omega\) (where the real amplitude \(\frac12(1 + \cos\Omega)\) is non-negative, which is everywhere): a constant group delay of 1 sample.

Exercise 12.4

Find the Butterworth order needed for at most 3 dB loss at 2 kHz and at least 60 dB attenuation at 8 kHz.

Answer

\(N \ge \dfrac{\log_{10}(10^6 - 1)}{2\log_{10}4} = \dfrac{6.0}{1.204} = 4.98\), so \(N = 5\).

Exercise 12.5

At what height is the resonant peak of a second-order low-pass factor with \(\zeta = 0.25\)? Express it in dB.

Answer

\(\frac{1}{2\cdot0.25\sqrt{1 - 0.0625}} = \frac{1}{0.5\cdot0.968} = 2.07\), or about 6.3 dB.

Exercise 12.6

With \(f_s = 10\) kHz, a digital filter is to have its cut-off at 2.5 kHz. What analog cut-off must the prototype have before the bilinear transform? Express it in hertz.

Answer

\(\Omega_c = \pi/2\); \(\omega_a = 2f_s\tan(\pi/4) = 20000\) rad/s, which is \(20000/2\pi \approx 3183\) Hz, higher than 2.5 kHz because of warping.

Exercise 12.7

Write the system function of a notch filter that removes \(\Omega_0 = \pi/2\), with poles at radius 0.9.

Answer

\(\cos(\pi/2) = 0\), so \(H(z) = \dfrac{1 + z^{-2}}{1 + 0.81z^{-2}}\).

Exercise 12.8

An FIR filter has coefficients \(h = [1, -2, 3, -2, 1]\). Does it have linear phase? What is its delay?

Answer

Yes: the coefficients are symmetric about \(n = 2\). The delay is 2 samples.

Exercise 12.9

An FIR low-pass filter needs at least 50 dB of stopband attenuation. Which windows in Table 12.2 are suitable?

Answer

Hamming (about 53 dB) and Blackman (about 74 dB). Rectangular and Hann fall short.

Exercise 12.10

Compute the first three coefficients \(h[0], h[1], h[2]\) of the ideal low-pass impulse response with \(\Omega_c = \pi/2\) and \(M = 4\) (before windowing).

Answer

\(h_d[n] = \frac{\sin(\pi(n - 2)/2)}{\pi(n - 2)}\). \(h[0] = \frac{\sin(-\pi)}{-2\pi} = 0\); \(h[1] = \frac{\sin(-\pi/2)}{-\pi} = \frac{1}{\pi} \approx 0.318\); \(h[2] = \frac{\Omega_c}{\pi} = 0.5\). By symmetry \(h[3] = 0.318\) and \(h[4] = 0\).

docs.title: 12.11 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 12

Exercise 1

How many dB does a first-order low-pass response fall per decade well above its corner?

Answer

20 / 20 dB

Exercise 2

At the corner frequency of a first-order low-pass filter, the phase is

  1. −45°
  2. −90°
  3. 0°
  4. −180°
Answer

−45°

Exercise 3

A system transmits a signal without distortion if, in the signal's band, it has

  1. constant magnitude and linear phase
  2. constant phase
  3. a resonant peak
  4. zero group delay only
Answer

constant magnitude and linear phase

Exercise 4

A Butterworth filter of any order has, at ω = ωc, a gain of

  1. 1/√2
  2. 1/2
  3. 1
  4. 0
Answer

1/√2

Exercise 5

Which filters can have exactly linear phase?

  1. FIR filters with symmetric coefficients
  2. all IIR filters
  3. Butterworth filters
  4. notch filters
Answer

FIR filters with symmetric coefficients

Exercise 6

The bilinear transform maps the left half of the s-plane to

  1. the inside of the unit circle
  2. the outside of the unit circle
  3. the real axis
  4. the unit circle
Answer

the inside of the unit circle

Exercise 7

In window design, a tapered window reduces ripple at the cost of a wider ___ band.

Answer

transition

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Standard books and sources for going deeper

docs.title: Textbooks on signals and systems
docs.text:
• A. V. Oppenheim and A. S. Willsky, with S. H. Nawab, Signals and Systems, 2nd edition, Prentice Hall, 1997. The classic text on the subject, treating continuous and discrete time in parallel, with many problems.
  • S. Haykin and B. Van Veen, Signals and Systems, 2nd edition, Wiley, 2003. A thorough treatment with applications to communication and control.
  • B. P. Lathi, Linear Systems and Signals, 2nd edition, Oxford University Press, 2005. A readable development with an emphasis on system analysis and many worked examples.

docs.title: Digital signal processing
docs.text:
• A. V. Oppenheim and R. W. Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, 3rd edition, Pearson, 2010. The standard advanced text on DT systems, the DFT, the FFT and filter design.
  • J. G. Proakis and D. G. Manolakis, Digital Signal Processing: Principles, Algorithms, and Applications, 4th edition, Pearson Prentice Hall, 2007. A comprehensive text with detailed coverage of filter design and multirate processing.
  • S. W. Smith, The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing, California Technical Publishing, 1997. A practical, lightly mathematical introduction.

docs.title: Fourier analysis
docs.text: • R. N. Bracewell, The Fourier Transform and Its Applications, 3rd edition, McGraw-Hill, 2000. A broad and intuitive account of the Fourier transform across science and engineering.

docs.title: Communication and control
docs.text:
• S. Haykin, Communication Systems, 4th edition, Wiley, 2001. Modulation, noise and digital transmission, building on the material of Chapters 6, 9 and 14.
  • G. F. Franklin, J. D. Powell and A. Emami-Naeini, Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems, Pearson (several editions). A standard introduction to classical and state-space control design.

docs.title: Original papers
docs.text:
• C. E. Shannon, "Communication in the presence of noise", Proceedings of the IRE, vol. 37, pp. 10–21, 1949. Includes a clear statement and proof of the sampling theorem.
  • J. W. Cooley and J. W. Tukey, "An algorithm for the machine calculation of complex Fourier series", Mathematics of Computation, vol. 19, pp. 297–301, 1965. The paper that brought the FFT into wide use.

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
• The NumPy documentation (numpy.org), especially the sections on numpy.fft and on polynomials, covers the functions used in this book.
  • The SciPy documentation (scipy.org), module scipy.signal, describes ready-made routines for filter design (butter, firwin), frequency responses (freqz, freqs), filtering (lfilter), spectral analysis (spectrogram) and system simulation (lsim, step), which go beyond the short programs printed here.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Terms used in the book, with the chapter where each is developed

docs.title: A
docs.text: Aliasing The appearance of a frequency above half the sampling rate as a lower frequency after sampling; it cannot be undone after sampling (Chapter 9). Amplitude modulation (AM) Multiplying a message by a sinusoidal carrier, which moves the message spectrum to the carrier frequency; conventional AM also transmits the carrier (Chapters 6, 14). Analog signal A signal whose amplitude can take any value in a continuous range (Chapter 1). Anti-aliasing filter An analog low-pass filter placed before a sampler to remove frequencies above half the sampling rate (Chapter 9).

docs.title: B
docs.text: Bandwidth The width of the band of frequencies that holds most of a signal's energy, or that a system passes; several definitions exist, such as the 3 dB bandwidth (Chapters 6, 12). BIBO stability Bounded-input, bounded-output stability: every bounded input gives a bounded output. For an LTI system it holds if and only if the impulse response is absolutely summable or integrable (Chapters 3, 4). Bilinear transform The substitution \(s = \frac{2}{T}\frac{1 - z^{-1}}{1 + z^{-1}}\), which turns a stable analog filter into a stable digital filter with warped frequency axis (Chapter 12). Bode plot Magnitude in decibels and phase in degrees plotted against frequency on a logarithmic axis (Chapter 12). Butterfly The basic FFT operation \(E[k] \pm W_N^kO[k]\), which forms two outputs from two inputs with one multiplication (Chapter 8). Butterworth filter A filter with maximally flat passband, \(|H|^2 = 1/(1 + (\omega/\omega_c)^{2N})\) (Chapter 12).

docs.title: C
docs.text: Causal system A system whose output never depends on future inputs; for an LTI system, \(h = 0\) for negative time (Chapters 3, 4). Circular convolution Convolution of two length-\(N\) sequences in which shifts wrap around modulo \(N\); it corresponds to multiplying DFTs (Chapter 8). Comb filter A filter whose magnitude response has regularly spaced peaks and dips, produced by adding a delayed copy of a signal (Chapter 14). Complex exponential The signal \(e^{st}\) or \(z^n\); an eigenfunction of every LTI system (Chapters 2, 4). Conjugate symmetry The property \(X(-j\omega) = X^*(j\omega)\) (or \(a_{-k} = a_k^*\)) of the spectrum of every real signal (Chapters 5 to 8). Convolution The operation \(y = x * h\), \(y[n] = \sum_k x[k]h[n-k]\) or \(y(t) = \int x(\tau)h(t - \tau)d\tau\), that gives the output of an LTI system (Chapter 4). Corner frequency The frequency at which the straight-line asymptotes of a first-order Bode plot meet, 3 dB from the true curve (Chapter 12).

docs.title: D
docs.text: Decibel (dB) A logarithmic measure of gain, \(20\log_{10}|H|\) (Chapter 12). Decimation Keeping every \(M\)th sample of a sequence, \(x[Mn]\); it must be preceded by low-pass filtering to avoid aliasing (Chapters 2, 9). Difference equation An equation relating the present output of a DT system to past outputs and present and past inputs (Chapters 3, 11). Dirichlet conditions Conditions on a periodic signal under which its Fourier series converges to it at points of continuity and to the midpoint at jumps (Chapter 5). Discrete Fourier transform (DFT) The transform \(X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-j2\pi kn/N}\) of a finite sequence; it samples the DTFT at \(N\) frequencies (Chapter 8). Discrete-time Fourier transform (DTFT) The transform \(X(e^{j\Omega}) = \sum_n x[n]e^{-j\Omega n}\); always periodic with period \(2\pi\) (Chapter 7). Discrete-time signal A signal defined only at integer values of its index, \(x[n]\) (Chapter 1).

docs.title: E
docs.text: Eigenfunction A signal that passes through a system unchanged in shape, only scaled; complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems (Chapter 4). Energy signal A signal with finite, non-zero energy \(\int|x|^2dt\); its average power is zero (Chapter 1). Envelope detector A simple AM receiver that follows the peaks of the modulated carrier (Chapter 14). Even signal A signal with \(x(-t) = x(t)\) (Chapter 1).

docs.title: F
docs.text: Fast Fourier transform (FFT) An algorithm that computes the DFT in about \(\frac{N}{2}\log_2N\) multiplications instead of \(N^2\) (Chapter 8). FIR filter A filter with a finite impulse response; non-recursive, always stable, and able to have exactly linear phase (Chapters 11, 12). Fourier series The representation of a periodic signal as a sum of harmonically related complex exponentials (Chapter 5). Fourier transform The representation of an aperiodic signal as a continuous superposition of complex exponentials, \(X(j\omega) = \int x(t)e^{-j\omega t}dt\) (Chapter 6). Frequency response The factor \(H(j\omega)\) or \(H(e^{j\Omega})\) by which an LTI system multiplies a complex exponential; the Fourier transform of the impulse response (Chapters 5 to 7).

docs.title: G
docs.text: Gibbs phenomenon The overshoot of about 9% of the jump that persists near a discontinuity in partial Fourier sums (Chapter 5). Group delay The negative derivative of phase with respect to frequency; the delay of a narrow band of frequencies (Chapter 12).

docs.title: I
docs.text: IIR filter A filter with an infinite impulse response, implemented recursively, with poles away from the origin (Chapters 11, 12). Impulse response The output of a system when the input is a unit impulse; it characterises an LTI system completely (Chapter 4). Initial rest The condition that a system's output is zero until its input becomes non-zero (Chapter 3). Intersymbol interference (ISI) Overlap of successive symbols in a digital link caused by the spreading effect of the channel (Chapter 14). Invertible system A system whose input can be recovered from its output (Chapters 3, 4).

docs.title: L
docs.text: Laplace transform The transform \(X(s) = \int x(t)e^{-st}dt\), which generalises the Fourier transform to growing signals and unstable systems (Chapter 10). Leakage The spreading of a sinusoid's energy across many DFT bins when the record does not hold a whole number of its cycles (Chapter 8). Linear phase A phase response that is a straight line through the origin, corresponding to a pure delay (Chapters 6, 12). Linear system A system that obeys superposition: a weighted sum of inputs gives the same weighted sum of outputs (Chapter 3). LTI system A system that is both linear and time-invariant (Chapters 3, 4).

docs.title: M
docs.text: Matrix exponential \(e^{At} = I + At + (At)^2/2! + \cdots\), which gives the free response of a state-space model (Chapter 13). Memoryless system A system whose output at each time depends only on the input at that time (Chapter 3). Modulation Multiplying a signal by a carrier to move its spectrum (Chapters 6, 14).

docs.title: N
docs.text: Notch filter A filter that removes a narrow band around one frequency, made with zeros on the unit circle and poles just inside (Chapter 12). Nyquist frequency Half the sampling rate; the highest frequency a sampled signal can represent (Chapter 9). Nyquist rate Twice the highest frequency in a band-limited signal; sampling must be faster than this (Chapter 9).

docs.title: O
docs.text: Odd signal A signal with \(x(-t) = -x(t)\) (Chapter 1). OFDM Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing, which carries data on many subcarriers generated and separated by the FFT (Chapter 14). Orthogonality The property that harmonically related exponentials integrate (or sum) to zero against each other over a period; it gives the Fourier analysis formulas (Chapter 5).

docs.title: P
docs.text: Parseval's relation The equality of energy (or power) computed in the time domain and in the frequency domain (Chapters 5 to 8). Partial fractions The expansion of a rational transform into simple terms that can be inverted from a table (Chapters 10, 11). Periodic signal A signal that repeats: \(x(t + T) = x(t)\) for all \(t\); the smallest such \(T > 0\) is the fundamental period (Chapter 1). Phase margin The extra phase lag a feedback loop can tolerate, at the frequency where the loop gain is 1, before becoming unstable (Chapter 14). PID controller A controller whose output is a weighted sum of the error, its integral and its derivative (Chapter 14). Pole A value of \(s\) or \(z\) at which a transfer function becomes infinite; poles govern stability and the natural modes of a system (Chapters 10, 11). Power signal A signal with finite, non-zero average power; its energy is infinite (Chapter 1).

docs.title: Q
docs.text: Quantization Rounding signal values to a finite set of levels; with \(B\) bits the SNR for a full-scale sinusoid is about \(6.02B + 1.76\) dB (Chapter 9).

docs.title: R
docs.text: Region of convergence (ROC) The set of \(s\) or \(z\) for which a Laplace or z-transform converges; it is part of the transform and distinguishes signals with the same formula (Chapters 10, 11). Residue The coefficient of a simple pole term in a partial-fraction expansion (Chapters 10, 11).

docs.title: S
docs.text: Sampling theorem A signal band-limited to \(\omega_M\) is determined by samples taken at a rate \(\omega_s > 2\omega_M\) (Chapter 9). Sifting property \(\int x(t)\delta(t - t_0)dt = x(t_0)\) (Chapter 2). Sinc function \(\mathrm{sinc}(x) = \sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)\); the Fourier transform of a rectangular pulse and the interpolating function of ideal reconstruction (Chapters 2, 6, 9). Spectrogram A picture of the magnitude of the short-time Fourier transform against time and frequency (Chapter 14). Spectrum The description of a signal by the amplitudes and phases of its frequency components (Chapters 5, 6). State The smallest set of variables that, with future inputs, determines a system's future behaviour (Chapter 13). Step response The output of a system when the input is a unit step; for an LTI system, the running integral of the impulse response (Chapter 4). System function The transfer function of a DT system, \(H(z)\) (Chapter 11).

docs.title: T
docs.text: Time-invariant system A system for which delaying the input delays the output by the same amount and changes nothing else (Chapter 3). Transfer function The Laplace (or z-) transform of the impulse response; the ratio of output to input transforms (Chapters 10, 11).

docs.title: U
docs.text: Unit impulse \(\delta[n]\), equal to 1 at \(n = 0\) and 0 elsewhere; or \(\delta(t)\), the unit-area limit of ever-narrower pulses (Chapter 2). Unit step \(u(t)\) or \(u[n]\): zero before the origin and one after it (Chapter 2).

docs.title: W
docs.text: Window A tapering sequence applied before a DFT to reduce leakage, or to an ideal impulse response in FIR design (Chapters 8, 12).

docs.title: Z
docs.text: Zero A value of \(s\) or \(z\) at which a transfer function is zero (Chapters 10, 11). z-transform The transform \(X(z) = \sum x[n]z^{-n}\); on the unit circle it equals the DTFT (Chapter 11). Zero-order hold A reconstruction method that holds each sample value until the next one (Chapter 9).

docs.title: Chapter 4: LTI Systems and Convolution
docs.text:
How the impulse response determines everything, in discrete and continuous time

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • derive the convolution sum and the convolution integral from linearity and time invariance;
  • compute convolutions of finite sequences by table, of closed-form signals by direct summation or integration, and of any signals by the flip-and-slide method;
  • use the commutative, associative and distributive properties to simplify interconnections of LTI systems;
  • read memory, causality, stability and invertibility of an LTI system directly from its impulse response;
  • relate the step response to the impulse response, and explain why complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems.

docs.title: 4.1 The idea: one response tells all
docs.text:
Chapter 3 introduced linearity and time invariance separately. Together they have a remarkable consequence: if we know how an LTI system responds to a single impulse, we can compute its response to any input. The response to the unit impulse is called the impulse response, written \(h[n]\) in discrete time and \(h(t)\) in continuous time:

\[ h[n] = T\{\delta[n]\}, \qquad h(t) = T\{\delta(t)\}. \]

The argument has three steps, and it is the same in both domains. First, write the input as a sum of shifted, scaled impulses. Second, use time invariance: each shifted impulse produces a shifted copy of \(h\). Third, use linearity: the scaled sum of impulses produces the same scaled sum of shifted impulse responses. The result is an operation called convolution. This chapter derives it, shows how to compute it, and draws out its consequences.

docs.title: 4.2 The convolution sum
docs.text:
Chapter 2 showed that every sequence is a weighted sum of shifted impulses:

\[ x[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x[k]\,\delta[n - k]. \]

Read this as a recipe: at each position \(k\) there is an impulse \(\delta[n-k]\) with weight \(x[k]\). Now pass it through an LTI system.

  • By time invariance, the input \(\delta[n - k]\) produces \(h[n - k]\).
  • By homogeneity, the input \(x[k]\,\delta[n - k]\) produces \(x[k]\,h[n - k]\) (the weight \(x[k]\) is just a number).
  • By additivity, the sum of all these inputs produces the sum of all these outputs.

Therefore

\[ \boxed{\,y[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x[k]\,h[n - k] = x[n] * h[n]\,} \]

This is the convolution sum, and the star denotes convolution (not multiplication). The output at time \(n\) is a weighted sum of input samples, and the weight given to the input at time \(k\) is \(h[n - k]\): the impulse response evaluated at the time elapsed since \(k\). A system with a long impulse response "remembers" inputs from long ago.

Key idea

An LTI system is completely characterised by its impulse response. Once \(h\) is known, the output for any input is \(y = x * h\).

docs.title: 4.3 Computing the convolution sum
docs.text: There are three practical methods. Choose by the form of the signals.

docs.title: Method 1: a table for finite sequences
docs.text:
When \(x\) and \(h\) are short lists, write the output as a sum of shifted copies of \(h\), one for each input sample, and add the columns. Let \(x[n] = \{1, 2, 3\}\) and \(h[n] = \{1, 1, 1\}\), both starting at \(n = 0\).

\(n = 0\) 1 2 3 4 \(x[0]\,h[n] = 1\cdot h[n]\) 1 1 1 \(x[1]\,h[n-1] = 2\cdot h[n-1]\) 2 2 2 \(x[2]\,h[n-2] = 3\cdot h[n-2]\) 3 3 3 \(y[n]\) 1 3 6 5 3

Table 4.1. Convolution of two finite sequences by adding shifted copies of h.

The procedure is exactly the multiplication of polynomials: \((1 + 2z + 3z^2)(1 + z + z^2) = 1 + 3z + 6z^2 + 5z^3 + 3z^4\). Two facts follow. If \(x\) has \(N_x\) samples starting at \(n_1\) and \(h\) has \(N_h\) samples starting at \(n_2\), then \(y\) has \(N_x + N_h - 1\) samples starting at \(n_1 + n_2\). And the sum of the output samples is the product of the input sums: here \(18 = 6 \times 3\).

docs.title: Method 2: flip and slide
docs.text:
To compute one output sample \(y[n]\) directly from the formula, think of \(h[n - k]\) as a function of \(k\). It is \(h[k]\) flipped (reflected to \(h[-k]\)) and then slid to the right by \(n\). Multiply it, sample by sample, with \(x[k]\) and add up the products. Then increase \(n\) by one, slide the flipped sequence one step further, and repeat. The step-through figure below does this for the sequences of Table 4.1.

1n = 0. Only x[0] overlaps the flipped h, so y[0] = 1.

2n = 1. Two samples overlap: y[1] = 1 + 2 = 3.

3n = 2. Full overlap: y[2] = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.

4n = 3. The flipped h starts to leave x: y[3] = 2 + 3 = 5.

5n = 4. Only x[2] overlaps: y[4] = 3. For n ≥ 5 there is no overlap and y[n] = 0.

Figure 4.1 Flip and slide. The flipped impulse response h[n − k] slides past x[k]; at each n the overlapping products are added to give y[n].

Flip and slide is the method to use when the signals are given by sketches or when you need to know where the output is non-zero. The overlap picture also explains the length rule: the output is non-zero from the first moment of overlap to the last.

docs.title: Method 3: direct summation for closed forms
docs.text:
When the signals are given by formulas, substitute them into the sum, use the steps to fix the limits, and sum a geometric series.

Example 4.1 Exponential convolved with a step

Find \(y[n] = a^n u[n] * u[n]\) for \(|a| \ne 1\).

\[ y[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} a^k u[k]\,u[n - k]. \]

The factor \(u[k]\) is zero for \(k < 0\); the factor \(u[n - k]\) is zero for \(k > n\). So for \(n < 0\) every term vanishes and \(y[n] = 0\). For \(n \ge 0\) the sum runs from \(k = 0\) to \(k = n\):

\[ y[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a^k = \frac{1 - a^{n+1}}{1 - a}, \qquad n \ge 0 . \]

So \(y[n] = \dfrac{1 - a^{n+1}}{1 - a}\,u[n]\). With \(a = 0.5\) the output climbs \(1, 1.5, 1.75, 1.875, \ldots\) towards 2, which is the step response found by iteration in Exercise 3.8. That is no coincidence: \((0.5)^n u[n]\) is the impulse response of \(y[n] = x[n] + 0.5y[n-1]\), and convolving it with \(u[n]\) gives the response to a step.

Example 4.2 Two exponentials

Find \(y[n] = a^n u[n] * b^n u[n]\) with \(a \ne b\).

For \(n \ge 0\),

\[ y[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a^k b^{n-k} = b^n\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^k = b^n\,\frac{1 - (a/b)^{n+1}}{1 - a/b} = \frac{a^{n+1} - b^{n+1}}{a - b}. \]

So \(y[n] = \dfrac{a^{n+1} - b^{n+1}}{a - b}\,u[n]\). Check \(n = 0\): \(y[0] = 1\), which is \(a^0b^0\). Check \(n = 1\): \(y[1] = a + b\), which is \(x[0]h[1] + x[1]h[0]\).

docs.title: 4.4 The convolution integral
docs.text:
The continuous-time argument mirrors the discrete one. The sifting property of Chapter 2 lets us write any signal as a "sum" (an integral) of shifted impulses:

\[ x(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)\,\delta(t - \tau)\,d\tau . \]

An impulse at time \(\tau\) produces \(h(t - \tau)\) by time invariance. Its weight is \(x(\tau)\,d\tau\). Linearity lets us add (integrate) the responses:

\[ \boxed{\,y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)\,h(t - \tau)\,d\tau = x(t) * h(t)\,} \]

This is the convolution integral. The graphical meaning is the same as before: flip \(h(\tau)\) to \(h(-\tau)\), slide it right by \(t\) to get \(h(t - \tau)\), multiply by \(x(\tau)\), and take the area of the product. The area depends on \(t\), and it is the output \(y(t)\).

docs.title: Working an integral step by step
docs.text:
The skill is in finding the limits. Because the signals usually switch on and off, the product \(x(\tau)h(t - \tau)\) is non-zero only on an interval whose ends depend on \(t\), and the form of the integral changes as \(t\) crosses certain values. Sketch first, then integrate on each range.

Figure 4.2 A continuous-time convolution. Top: a unit pulse x(t) on 0 ≤ t < 1, the impulse response h(t) = e^(−t)u(t), and the overlap of x(τ) with the flipped and shifted h(t − τ) at t = 0.6 (shaded). Bottom: the output y(t), which rises as 1 − e^(−t) while the pulse is on and decays as (e − 1)e^(−t) afterwards.

Example 4.3 A pulse into a first-order system

Let \(x(t) = u(t) - u(t - 1)\) (a unit pulse lasting one second) and \(h(t) = e^{-t}u(t)\) (the impulse response of an RC circuit with \(RC = 1\)). Find \(y = x * h\).

As a function of \(\tau\), \(x(\tau)\) is 1 on \([0, 1)\). The flipped, shifted response \(h(t - \tau) = e^{-(t - \tau)}\) is non-zero for \(\tau < t\): it ends at \(\tau = t\) and trails off to the left. There are three cases.

\(t < 0\). The flipped response lies entirely left of the pulse. No overlap: \(y(t) = 0\).

\(0 \le t < 1\). Overlap on \(0 \le \tau \le t\) (shaded in Figure 4.2):

\[ y(t) = \int_0^t e^{-(t - \tau)}\,d\tau = e^{-t}\left[e^{\tau}\right]_0^t = 1 - e^{-t}. \]

\(t \ge 1\). Overlap on the whole pulse, \(0 \le \tau < 1\):

\[ y(t) = \int_0^1 e^{-(t - \tau)}\,d\tau = e^{-t}(e - 1). \]

The two pieces agree at \(t = 1\), where both equal \(1 - e^{-1} \approx 0.632\), as they must for a continuous output. Physically, the capacitor charges towards 1 while the pulse is on, reaching 63% of the way, and then discharges.

Five checks for a convolution

(1) The output starts at the sum of the start times and ends at the sum of the end times. (2) The pieces join continuously unless one signal contains an impulse. (3) The area of \(y\) is the product of the areas of \(x\) and \(h\). (4) For a causal \(h\), \(y\) cannot start before \(x\). (5) The answer has the right units: an integral over \(\tau\) adds a factor of time.

Check (3) on Example 4.3: the area of \(x\) is 1, the area of \(h\) is \(\int_0^\infty e^{-t}dt = 1\), and the area of \(y\) is \(\int_0^1(1 - e^{-t})dt + \int_1^\infty(e - 1)e^{-t}dt = e^{-1} + (e - 1)e^{-1} = 1\). It agrees.

docs.title: 4.5 Properties of convolution
docs.text:
Convolution behaves like multiplication in several ways. Each property below holds in both domains; we write them for continuous time.

Property Statement Meaning for systems Commutative \(x * h = h * x\) input and impulse response are interchangeable Associative \((x * h_1) * h_2 = x * (h_1 * h_2)\) a cascade has impulse response \(h_1 * h_2\) Distributive \(x * (h_1 + h_2) = x * h_1 + x * h_2\) a parallel connection has impulse response \(h_1 + h_2\) Identity \(x * \delta = x\) the identity system has \(h = \delta\) Shift \(x(t) * \delta(t - t_0) = x(t - t_0)\) the ideal delay has \(h = \delta(t - t_0)\) Shift of both if \(y = x * h\) then \(x(t - t_1) * h(t - t_2) = y(t - t_1 - t_2)\) delays add Derivative \(\frac{d}{dt}(x * h) = \frac{dx}{dt} * h = x * \frac{dh}{dt}\)

Table 4.2. Properties of convolution.

The commutative property follows from the substitution \(\sigma = t - \tau\) in the integral. Its practical meaning is surprising: the order of LTI systems in a cascade does not matter, because \(h_1 * h_2 = h_2 * h_1\). An equaliser followed by an amplifier gives the same output as the amplifier followed by the equaliser, provided both are linear and time-invariant. (Real amplifiers clip, which is nonlinear; then the order does matter.)

The associative and distributive properties let us reduce any network of LTI systems without feedback to a single equivalent impulse response. Feedback networks are easier to reduce in the transform domain, as Chapter 10 shows.

Example 4.4 Reducing an interconnection

A system consists of \(h_1[n] = \delta[n] - \delta[n-1]\) in cascade with \(h_2[n] = u[n]\). What is the overall impulse response?

\(h[n] = h_1 * h_2 = u[n] - u[n-1] = \delta[n]\). The cascade is the identity: the first difference undoes the accumulator. This confirms that the two are inverse systems.

docs.title: 4.6 Reading system properties from the impulse response
docs.text:
For an LTI system, every property of Chapter 3 becomes a simple condition on \(h\).

Memory. An LTI system is memoryless if and only if \(h[n] = K\delta[n]\) (or \(h(t) = K\delta(t)\)). Then \(y = Kx\). Any other impulse response mixes in inputs from other times.

Causality. An LTI system is causal if and only if

\[ h[n] = 0 \text{ for } n < 0, \qquad h(t) = 0 \text{ for } t < 0 . \]

The reason: \(y[n] = \sum_k h[k]x[n-k]\), and a non-zero \(h[k]\) with \(k < 0\) would make \(y[n]\) depend on the future input \(x[n - k]\). For a causal system the sum runs only over \(k \ge 0\): \(y[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}h[k]\,x[n-k]\).

Stability. An LTI system is BIBO stable if and only if its impulse response is absolutely summable (or absolutely integrable):

\[ \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} |h[n]| < \infty, \qquad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|h(t)|\,dt < \infty . \]

Proof of sufficiency. If \(|x[n]| \le B\) for all \(n\), then

\[ |y[n]| = \Big|\sum_k h[k]\,x[n-k]\Big| \le \sum_k |h[k]|\,|x[n-k]| \le B\sum_k|h[k]| , \]

which is finite. Proof of necessity. If \(\sum|h[k]|\) is infinite, choose the bounded input \(x[n] = \mathrm{sgn}(h[-n])\) (that is, \(\pm1\) with the sign of \(h[-n]\), and 0 where \(h[-n] = 0\)). Then \(y[0] = \sum_k h[k]\,\mathrm{sgn}(h[k]) = \sum_k|h[k]|\), which is infinite. So the system is unstable.

Invertibility. An LTI system with impulse response \(h\) has an LTI inverse with impulse response \(h_{\text{inv}}\) if and only if

\[ h * h_{\text{inv}} = \delta . \]

Example 4.5 Properties from h

(a) \(h[n] = (0.9)^n u[n]\): causal (\(h = 0\) for \(n < 0\)); stable (\(\sum 0.9^n = 10\)); has memory.

(b) \(h[n] = 2^n u[-n]\): not causal (non-zero for negative \(n\)); stable, because \(\sum_{n=-\infty}^{0}2^n = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty}2^{-m} = 2\).

(c) \(h(t) = u(t)\), the integrator: causal, but \(\int_0^\infty 1\,dt\) is infinite, so unstable (as Example 3.1 found by another route).

(d) \(h(t) = e^{-2|t|}\): not causal; stable, with \(\int|h| = 1\).

(e) \(h(t) = \delta(t - 3)\): a pure delay; causal, stable, has memory, and invertible (the inverse \(\delta(t + 3)\) is an advance, which is not causal).

docs.title: 4.7 The step response
docs.text:
The response of an LTI system to a unit step is its step response \(s\). Since \(u = u * \delta\), the step response is the convolution of \(u\) with \(h\):

\[ s[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{n} h[k], \qquad s(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{t} h(\tau)\,d\tau . \]

The step response is the running sum (or integral) of the impulse response; conversely

\[ h[n] = s[n] - s[n-1], \qquad h(t) = \frac{ds(t)}{dt}. \]

The step response is often easier to measure in the laboratory than the impulse response, because a step (switching something on) is easier to produce than a very short, very strong pulse. Differentiating the measured step response then gives \(h\). For the RC circuit with \(h(t) = \frac{1}{RC}e^{-t/RC}u(t)\), the step response is \(s(t) = (1 - e^{-t/RC})u(t)\), the familiar charging curve.

docs.title: 4.8 Complex exponentials are eigenfunctions
docs.text:
One more consequence of convolution sets up the second half of the book. Feed the complex exponential \(x(t) = e^{st}\) into an LTI system:

\[ y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(\tau)\,e^{s(t - \tau)}\,d\tau = e^{st}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}h(\tau)\,e^{-s\tau}\,d\tau = H(s)\,e^{st}, \]

where \(H(s) = \int h(\tau)e^{-s\tau}d\tau\), provided the integral converges. The output is the same exponential, multiplied by a complex constant. A signal that passes through a system unchanged in shape, merely scaled, is called an eigenfunction of the system, and the scale factor \(H(s)\) is its eigenvalue. In discrete time the same calculation with \(x[n] = z^n\) gives \(y[n] = H(z)\,z^n\) with \(H(z) = \sum_k h[k]z^{-k}\).

This is the reason complex exponentials dominate the theory. If we can write an input as a sum of complex exponentials, each passes through the system multiplied by its own \(H\), and the output is the sum of the scaled exponentials. Convolution, a hard operation, becomes multiplication, an easy one. With \(s = j\omega\) the factor \(H(j\omega)\) is the frequency response; writing signals as sums of \(e^{j\omega t}\) is Fourier analysis (Chapters 5 to 8); allowing general \(s\) and \(z\) gives the Laplace and z-transforms (Chapters 10 and 11).

Example 4.6 An eigenvalue

For \(h(t) = e^{-t}u(t)\), find the output for \(x(t) = e^{j t}\).

\(H(s) = \int_0^\infty e^{-\tau}e^{-s\tau}d\tau = \dfrac{1}{s + 1}\) for \(\mathrm{Re}\{s\} > -1\). At \(s = j\), \(H(j) = \dfrac{1}{1 + j} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}e^{-j\pi/4}\). So \(y(t) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}e^{j(t - \pi/4)}\): the same frequency, amplitude reduced by \(\sqrt{2}\), phase delayed by \(45°\). Taking real parts, the input \(\cos t\) produces \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cos(t - \pi/4)\).

docs.title: 4.9 Convolution in NumPy
docs.text:
np.convolve computes the convolution of two finite arrays. It does not know where the sequences start, so you must keep track of the starting index yourself: the output starts at the sum of the two starting indices. For continuous-time signals, sampling both at a small step \(\Delta t\) and multiplying the discrete convolution by \(\Delta t\) approximates the integral by a Riemann sum.

import numpy as np

# Finite sequences: the convolution sum is polynomial multiplication
x = np.array([1, 2, 3])          # x[0], x[1], x[2]
h = np.array([1, 1, 1])          # h[0], h[1], h[2]
print("x * h        =", np.convolve(x, h))

# a^n u[n] convolved with u[n]: compare with the closed form
a = 0.5
n = np.arange(8)
y = np.convolve(a ** n, np.ones(8))[:8]      # first 8 samples are exact
closed = (1 - a ** (n + 1)) / (1 - a)
print("numerical    =", np.round(y, 4))
print("closed form  =", np.round(closed, 4))

# Continuous time: pulse of width 1 convolved with exp(-t)u(t), by a Riemann sum
dt = 1e-3
t = np.arange(0, 5, dt)
xc = ((t >= 0) & (t < 1)).astype(float)
hc = np.exp(-t)
yc = np.convolve(xc, hc)[:len(t)] * dt
exact = np.where(t < 1, 1 - np.exp(-t), (np.e - 1) * np.exp(-t))
print("y(0.5), y(2) =", np.round(yc[[500, 2000]], 4), " exact:", np.round(exact[[500, 2000]], 4))
print("largest error:", f"{np.max(np.abs(yc - exact)):.1e}")

x * h        = [1 3 6 5 3]
numerical    = [1.     1.5    1.75   1.875  1.9375 1.9688 1.9844 1.9922]
closed form  = [1.     1.5    1.75   1.875  1.9375 1.9688 1.9844 1.9922]
y(0.5), y(2) = [0.3943 0.2324]  exact: [0.3935 0.2325]
largest error: 1.0e-03

Two details deserve comment. Truncating \(a^n u[n]\) and \(u[n]\) to 8 samples does not spoil the first 8 output samples, because \(y[n]\) for \(n < 8\) uses only \(x[k]\) and \(h[k]\) with \(k \le n\). And the Riemann-sum error of about \(10^{-3}\) is of the order of the step \(\Delta t\), as expected for a rectangle rule; a smaller step gives a smaller error.

docs.title: 4.10 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • An LTI system is characterised by its impulse response. The output is the convolution of the input with it: \(y[n] = \sum_k x[k]h[n-k]\) and \(y(t) = \int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau\).
  • Compute convolutions by a table of shifted copies (finite sequences), by direct summation with geometric series (closed forms), or by flipping and sliding (sketches). Fix the limits of the integral case by case.
  • Convolution is commutative, associative and distributive, with \(\delta\) as identity. Cascades convolve impulse responses, parallel connections add them, and the order of a cascade of LTI systems does not matter.
  • An LTI system is memoryless iff \(h = K\delta\); causal iff \(h = 0\) for negative time; BIBO stable iff \(h\) is absolutely summable or integrable; invertible iff some \(h_{\text{inv}}\) gives \(h * h_{\text{inv}} = \delta\).
  • The step response is the running integral of the impulse response.
  • Complex exponentials \(e^{st}\) and \(z^n\) are eigenfunctions of LTI systems: they come out scaled by \(H(s)\) or \(H(z)\). This is the doorway to the frequency domain.

docs.title: 4.11 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 4.1

Convolve \(x[n] = \{2, -1, 1\}\) (starting at \(n = 0\)) with \(h[n] = \{1, 3\}\) (starting at \(n = -1\)).

Answer

Polynomial product: \((2 - z + z^2)(1 + 3z) = 2 + 5z - 2z^2 + 3z^3\). The output starts at \(0 + (-1) = -1\), so \(y[-1] = 2\), \(y[0] = 5\), \(y[1] = -2\), \(y[2] = 3\).

Exercise 4.2

Find \(y[n] = u[n] * u[n]\).

Answer

For \(n \ge 0\), \(y[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{n}1 = n + 1\). So \(y[n] = (n+1)u[n]\), a ramp starting at 1.

Exercise 4.3

Find \(y[n] = (0.5)^n u[n] * (0.25)^n u[n]\) and give \(y[2]\).

Answer

By Example 4.2, \(y[n] = \dfrac{0.5^{n+1} - 0.25^{n+1}}{0.25}u[n] = (2\cdot0.5^{n} - 0.25^{n})u[n]\). Then \(y[2] = 0.5 - 0.0625 = 0.4375\). Directly: \(1\cdot0.0625 + 0.5\cdot0.25 + 0.25\cdot1 = 0.4375\).

Exercise 4.4

Show that \(\mathrm{rect}(t) * \mathrm{rect}(t)\) is the triangle \(\Lambda(t)\), equal to \(1 - |t|\) for \(|t| \le 1\) and 0 otherwise.

Answer

The two unit-width pulses overlap only for \(|t| < 1\). For \(-1 \le t \le 0\) the overlap runs from \(-\tfrac12\) to \(t + \tfrac12\), length \(1 + t\). For \(0 \le t \le 1\) it runs from \(t - \tfrac12\) to \(\tfrac12\), length \(1 - t\). So \(y(t) = 1 - |t|\) on \([-1, 1]\).

Exercise 4.5

Find \(y(t) = e^{-2t}u(t) * u(t)\).

Answer

For \(t > 0\), \(y(t) = \int_0^t e^{-2\tau}\,d\tau = \tfrac12(1 - e^{-2t})\). So \(y(t) = \tfrac12(1 - e^{-2t})u(t)\). (This is the step response of the system with \(h(t) = e^{-2t}u(t)\).)

Exercise 4.6

Find \(y(t) = e^{-t}u(t) * e^{-3t}u(t)\).

Answer

For \(t > 0\), \(y(t) = \int_0^t e^{-\tau}e^{-3(t-\tau)}d\tau = e^{-3t}\int_0^t e^{2\tau}d\tau = \tfrac12(e^{-t} - e^{-3t})\). So \(y(t) = \tfrac12(e^{-t} - e^{-3t})u(t)\).

Exercise 4.7

Is the system with \(h[n] = (1.1)^n u[n]\) stable? Is \(h[n] = (-0.5)^n u[n] + \delta[n+2]\) causal? stable?

Answer

The first is unstable: \(\sum 1.1^n\) diverges. The second is not causal (the impulse at \(n = -2\)) but is stable: \(\sum|h| = \sum 0.5^n + 1 = 3\).

Exercise 4.8

The step response of an LTI system is \(s(t) = (1 - e^{-5t})u(t)\). Find its impulse response.

Answer

\(h(t) = ds/dt = 5e^{-5t}u(t)\). (The derivative of \(u(t)\) multiplies \(1 - e^{-5t}\), which is zero at \(t = 0\), so no impulse appears.)

Exercise 4.9

Two LTI systems with \(h_1(t) = \delta(t - 1)\) and \(h_2(t) = e^{-t}u(t)\) are connected in parallel, and the combination is followed by \(h_3(t) = 2\delta(t)\). Find the overall impulse response.

Answer

\(h = (h_1 + h_2) * h_3 = 2\delta(t - 1) + 2e^{-t}u(t)\).

Exercise 4.10

For \(h[n] = \delta[n] + \delta[n-1]\), find the output for \(x[n] = e^{j\pi n/2}\), using the eigenfunction property.

Answer

\(H(z) = 1 + z^{-1}\); with \(z = e^{j\pi/2} = j\), \(H = 1 - j = \sqrt2 e^{-j\pi/4}\). So \(y[n] = \sqrt2\,e^{j(\pi n/2 - \pi/4)}\). Direct check: \(y[n] = e^{j\pi n/2} + e^{j\pi(n-1)/2} = e^{j\pi n/2}(1 - j)\).

docs.title: 4.12 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 4

Exercise 1

x[n] has 5 non-zero samples and h[n] has 4. How many samples (at most) does x * h have?

Answer

8

N_x + N_h − 1 = 5 + 4 − 1 = 8.

Exercise 2

An LTI system is causal if and only if

  1. h(t) = 0 for t < 0
  2. h(t) is absolutely integrable
  3. h(t) = Kδ(t)
  4. h(t) is even
Answer

h(t) = 0 for t < 0

Exercise 3

The impulse response of a cascade of two LTI systems is

  1. h1 + h2
  2. h1 · h2
  3. h1 * h2
  4. h1 − h2
Answer

h1 * h2

Cascades convolve impulse responses; parallel connections add them.

Exercise 4

Which impulse response gives a BIBO stable system?

  1. u[n]
  2. 1.2ⁿ u[n]
  3. 0.7ⁿ u[n]
  4. n u[n]
Answer

0.7ⁿ u[n]

Only 0.7ⁿ u[n] is absolutely summable (sum = 1/0.3).

Exercise 5

The impulse response is the ___ of the step response with respect to time.

Answer

derivative

Exercise 6

Compute y[2] for {1, 2, 3} * {1, 1, 1}, both starting at n = 0.

Answer

6

Exercise 7

When e^(st) is the input to an LTI system, the output is

  1. H(s) e^(st)
  2. e^(st) * e^(st)
  3. a different exponential e^(−st)
  4. zero
Answer

H(s) e^(st)

Complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems.

docs.title: Preface
docs.text: About this book: who it is for, how it is organised and how to use it

docs.title: About this book
docs.text:
Signals and systems is the subject that gives engineers a common language for everything that varies in time: the voltage from a microphone, the position of a robot arm, the samples of a digital photograph, the radio waves of a mobile phone. Its central ideas (convolution, the frequency domain, poles and zeros, sampling) appear again in electronics, communication, control, audio, image processing, instrumentation and machine learning. A student who understands them well will meet them as old friends in every later course.

This book is a complete first course in the subject. It treats continuous-time and discrete-time signals side by side, because modern engineering uses both: physical systems are continuous, while the computers that measure and control them are discrete. Each idea is built up from intuition to a precise statement, illustrated with worked numerical examples, and checked with a short Python program whose output is printed beside it.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
The book is written for students in a first university course on signals and systems, typically in electrical, electronic, communication, computer, instrumentation or mechanical engineering, and for practising engineers who want a clear refresher. It assumes:

  • calculus of one variable, including integration by parts, and the idea of an infinite series;
  • complex numbers (reviewed in Chapter 1, since everything depends on them);
  • a little linear algebra (matrices, determinants, eigenvalues) for Chapter 13;
  • for the programs, some familiarity with Python. The programs use only NumPy (version 2 or later), and were run as printed.

No previous course in circuits is needed, although readers who have taken one will recognise many of the examples.

docs.title: How the book is organised
docs.text:
The fourteen chapters fall into four parts.

Part Chapters Topics Foundations 1 to 4 classification of signals; elementary signals and operations on them; properties of systems; LTI systems and convolution Fourier analysis 5 to 9 Fourier series; the continuous-time and discrete-time Fourier transforms; the DFT and FFT; sampling and aliasing Transforms for systems 10 to 13 the Laplace transform; the z-transform; frequency response and filter design; state-space models Applications 14 audio, communication and control

Table P.1. The structure of the book.

The parts depend on one another in order, but within them there is some freedom. A course that concentrates on continuous time can take Chapters 1 to 6, 9 (sampling), 10 and 12, with the discrete-time sections as optional reading. A course centred on digital signal processing can move quickly through Chapter 5 and spend more time on Chapters 7, 8, 11 and 12. Chapter 13 can be read at any time after Chapter 10. Reference tables of transform pairs and properties are collected at the end of the book, followed by a glossary and a list of further reading.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
Every chapter has the same structure:

  • learning outcomes at the start, so that you know what to look for;
  • numbered sections that move from motivation to definitions, properties and methods;
  • worked examples in shaded boxes, each solved step by step; try them yourself before reading the solution;
  • boxes for key ideas, notes and common mistakes;
  • figures of signals, spectra, block diagrams and pole-zero plots, and at least one short NumPy program with its output;
  • a summary of the chapter;
  • exercises with answers that stay folded until you open them;
  • a short quiz to check your understanding.

The best way to learn the subject is to do it. Work the examples on paper, then run the programs and change them: alter a pole, lengthen a window, sample more slowly, and see what happens. A result that you have predicted, computed and then seen on the screen is a result you will remember.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
The book follows the conventions that are most common in engineering texts.

Symbol Meaning \(x(t)\), \(x[n]\) continuous-time signal; discrete-time signal (sequence) \(u(t)\), \(u[n]\); \(\delta(t)\), \(\delta[n]\) unit step; unit impulse \(j\) the imaginary unit, \(j^2 = -1\) \(\omega\) continuous-time frequency, in radians per second (\(\omega = 2\pi f\), with \(f\) in hertz) \(\Omega\) discrete-time frequency, in radians per sample \(T\) or \(T_s\), \(f_s\), \(\omega_s\) sampling interval; sampling rate in hertz; sampling rate in rad/s \(h(t)\), \(h[n]\) impulse response \(X(j\omega)\), \(X(e^{j\Omega})\) Fourier transform; discrete-time Fourier transform \(X(s)\), \(X(z)\) Laplace transform; z-transform \(X[k]\) discrete Fourier transform (DFT) \(a_k\) Fourier series coefficients \(*\) convolution \(\mathrm{sinc}(x)\) \(\sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)\), the normalised sinc, as in NumPy

Table P.2. Notation used in the book.

Square brackets always mean a discrete variable and round brackets a continuous one. Sections are numbered within chapters (Section 6.4 is the fourth section of Chapter 6), and examples, figures, tables and exercises are numbered in the same way.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Sampling and Aliasing
docs.text:
When samples capture everything, how to rebuild the signal, and what goes wrong when they do not

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • model sampling as multiplication by an impulse train and derive the spectrum of the sampled signal;
  • state and apply the sampling theorem, and compute the Nyquist rate of a band-limited signal;
  • reconstruct a signal from its samples with the ideal low-pass filter and explain the sinc interpolation formula and the zero-order hold;
  • predict the apparent frequency of an aliased tone and specify an anti-aliasing filter;
  • relate the DTFT of the samples to the CTFT of the original, and find the effective frequency response of a digital system that processes analog signals;
  • estimate the signal-to-noise ratio set by quantization.

docs.title: 9.1 The question
docs.text:
A continuous-time signal has a value at every instant; a sampled signal keeps only the values at \(t = nT\). Something must be lost, surely? The surprising answer is: not necessarily. If the signal contains no frequencies above a certain limit, and the samples are taken often enough, the samples determine the signal completely, and it can be rebuilt exactly. This fact, the sampling theorem, is what makes digital audio, digital video and digital communication possible. This chapter proves it with the tools of Chapters 6 and 7, and studies what happens when its conditions are broken.

Throughout, \(T\) is the sampling interval, \(f_s = 1/T\) the sampling rate in hertz, and \(\omega_s = 2\pi/T\) the sampling rate in radians per second.

docs.title: 9.2 Sampling as multiplication by an impulse train
docs.text:
To analyse sampling with the CT Fourier transform, we represent the samples by a CT signal: a train of impulses whose areas are the sample values.

\[ x_p(t) = x(t)\,p(t), \qquad p(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(t - nT), \]

so that, by the sampling property of the impulse,

\[ x_p(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}x(nT)\,\delta(t - nT). \]

This is called impulse-train sampling. It is an idealisation (no circuit produces impulses), but it carries exactly the information of the samples \(x(nT)\) and it lets us use the multiplication property of the Fourier transform.

The impulse train is periodic, and its transform (Table 6.1) is another impulse train:

\[ P(j\omega) = \frac{2\pi}{T}\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(\omega - k\omega_s). \]

Multiplication in time is convolution in frequency, divided by \(2\pi\), and convolving with a shifted impulse shifts. Therefore

\[ \boxed{\,X_p(j\omega) = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}X\big(j(\omega - k\omega_s)\big)\,} \]

The spectrum of the sampled signal is the original spectrum, scaled by \(1/T\), plus copies of it shifted to every multiple of the sampling frequency. Sampling in time has made the spectrum periodic, exactly as the duality of Section 7.6 predicted.

docs.title: 9.3 The sampling theorem
docs.text:
Suppose \(x(t)\) is band-limited: \(X(j\omega) = 0\) for \(|\omega| > \omega_M\). The copy centred at 0 occupies \([-\omega_M, \omega_M]\); the copy centred at \(\omega_s\) occupies \([\omega_s - \omega_M, \omega_s + \omega_M]\). They do not overlap provided \(\omega_M < \omega_s - \omega_M\), that is,

\[ \omega_s > 2\omega_M \qquad\text{or}\qquad f_s > 2f_M . \]

When the copies do not overlap (Figure 9.1, middle), the original spectrum sits untouched in the band \(|\omega| < \omega_s/2\), and it can be recovered by a low-pass filter. When they do overlap (Figure 9.1, bottom), the tails of neighbouring copies add onto the original, and no filter can separate them again.

Figure 9.1 Spectrum of a sampled signal. Top: a band-limited spectrum occupying −ω_M to ω_M. Middle: after sampling with ω_s > 2ω_M, copies of height 1/T appear at multiples of ω_s, separated by gaps; an ideal low-pass filter (dashed box) can pick out the central copy. Bottom: with ω_s < 2ω_M the copies overlap and add (red), and the original spectrum is lost.

The sampling theorem

Let \(x(t)\) be band-limited with \(X(j\omega) = 0\) for \(|\omega| > \omega_M\). Then \(x(t)\) is uniquely determined by its samples \(x(nT)\) if

\[ \omega_s = \frac{2\pi}{T} > 2\omega_M . \]

The frequency \(2\omega_M\) (or \(2f_M\) in hertz) is the Nyquist rate; half the sampling rate, \(\omega_s/2\) (or \(f_s/2\)), is the Nyquist frequency.

The theorem is associated with the names of Nyquist, Shannon, Whittaker and Kotelnikov, who arrived at it, in various forms, in the first half of the twentieth century.

Example 9.1 Nyquist rates

(a) Speech for a telephone channel is filtered to about 3.4 kHz. The Nyquist rate is 6.8 kHz; telephone systems sample at 8 kHz, leaving room for a practical filter.

(b) Human hearing extends to roughly 20 kHz. The compact disc samples at 44.1 kHz, a little above the Nyquist rate of 40 kHz.

(c) \(x(t) = \cos(200\pi t) + 3\sin(500\pi t)\) contains 100 Hz and 250 Hz. The Nyquist rate is \(2 \times 250 = 500\) samples per second.

(d) \(x(t) = \cos^2(100\pi t) = \frac12 + \frac12\cos(200\pi t)\) contains 0 and 100 Hz, so the Nyquist rate is 200 samples per second, not 100. Multiplying signals widens their spectra, so check the highest frequency after expanding.

Sampling exactly at the Nyquist rate

The theorem needs \(\omega_s > 2\omega_M\), strictly. At exactly twice the frequency of a sinusoid, the samples may all fall on its zero crossings: \(\sin(2\pi f_0 t)\) sampled at \(2f_0\) gives \(\sin(\pi n) = 0\) for every \(n\). In practice one samples comfortably above the Nyquist rate.

docs.title: The ideal reconstruction filter
docs.text:
If the sampling theorem holds, pass \(x_p(t)\) through an ideal low-pass filter with gain \(T\) and cut-off \(\omega_c\) anywhere between \(\omega_M\) and \(\omega_s - \omega_M\), usually \(\omega_c = \omega_s/2\). The filter keeps the central copy, restores its height from \(1/T\) to 1, and removes all the others. The output is \(x(t)\) exactly.

The impulse response of this filter is (Example 6.5, with gain \(T\) and \(W = \omega_s/2 = \pi/T\))

\[ h_r(t) = T\,\frac{\sin(\pi t/T)}{\pi t} = \mathrm{sinc}\!\left(\frac{t}{T}\right). \]

Passing the impulse train through it replaces each impulse \(x(nT)\delta(t - nT)\) by a sinc pulse \(x(nT)\,\mathrm{sinc}((t - nT)/T)\). So

\[ \boxed{\,x(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}x(nT)\,\mathrm{sinc}\!\left(\frac{t - nT}{T}\right)\,} \]

This is the sinc interpolation formula. Each sinc pulse equals 1 at its own sample instant and 0 at every other sample instant, so the sum passes through every sample; between samples, the pulses combine to fill in exactly the band-limited signal (Figure 9.2).

Figure 9.2 Sinc interpolation. Samples (orange stems) and the sinc pulse belonging to each (dashed grey). Each pulse is 1 at its own sample time and 0 at all others. Their sum (blue) passes through every sample and is the band-limited signal.

docs.title: Practical reconstruction: the hold
docs.text:
The ideal filter is not causal, and the sinc pulses extend forever. A practical digital-to-analog converter (DAC) holds each sample value constant until the next one arrives, producing a staircase. This zero-order hold (ZOH) is a filter with impulse response \(h_0(t) = 1\) for \(0 \le t < T\) and 0 otherwise, whose frequency response is

\[ H_0(j\omega) = T\,\mathrm{sinc}\!\left(\frac{\omega T}{2\pi}\right)e^{-j\omega T/2}. \]

It passes the central copy, but with a gentle droop (at \(\omega = \omega_s/2\) the gain has fallen to \(2/\pi\) of its DC value, about \(-3.9\) dB), and it only partly suppresses the copies at \(\pm\omega_s, \pm2\omega_s, \ldots\), which appear as the steps of the staircase. A smoothing reconstruction filter after the DAC removes the remaining copies, and the droop can be corrected digitally before the DAC. Sampling well above the Nyquist rate (oversampling) makes both tasks easier, because it leaves wide gaps between the copies.

docs.title: 9.5 Aliasing
docs.text:
When a signal is sampled too slowly, a frequency above the Nyquist frequency reappears in the samples as a lower frequency. The high frequency is said to take on an alias.

The simplest case shows it clearly. Sample \(\cos(2\pi\cdot7t)\) at \(f_s = 8\) Hz:

\[ \cos\!\left(2\pi\cdot\frac{7n}{8}\right) = \cos\!\left(2\pi n - \frac{2\pi n}{8}\right) = \cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi n}{8}\right) = \cos\!\left(2\pi\cdot\frac{1\cdot n}{8}\right). \]

The samples are identical to those of a 1 Hz cosine (Figure 9.3). After sampling, nothing can tell them apart, and an ideal reconstruction filter (which keeps only frequencies below 4 Hz) produces the 1 Hz cosine.

Figure 9.3 Aliasing in time. A 7 Hz cosine (grey) sampled at 8 Hz (blue dots). The samples lie exactly on a 1 Hz cosine (orange), which is what reconstruction produces.

In general, a tone at frequency \(f\) sampled at \(f_s\) is indistinguishable from tones at \(f + mf_s\) and \(-f + mf_s\) for every integer \(m\). The apparent frequency, the one in the range \(0 \le f_a \le f_s/2\) that reconstruction produces, is found by "folding": subtract the nearest multiple of \(f_s\) and take the absolute value,

\[ f_a = \left|f - f_s\cdot\mathrm{round}(f/f_s)\right| . \]

Example 9.2 Apparent frequencies

With \(f_s = 8\) Hz: 7 Hz appears at 1 Hz; 9 Hz at 1 Hz; 12 Hz at 4 Hz; 25 Hz at 1 Hz (since \(25 - 3\cdot8 = 1\)). With \(f_s = 1000\) Hz, a 1400 Hz tone appears at 400 Hz, and a 1900 Hz tone at 100 Hz.

The phase may change too: a tone folded from just above \(f_s/2\) appears with its phase reversed, because the alias is at a negative frequency \(f - f_s\). For a real cosine that only flips the sign of the phase; for a sine it flips the sign of the whole signal.

Aliasing is familiar from films, where the spokes of a fast wheel seem to turn slowly or backwards: the camera samples the rotation 24 times a second, and the true rotation rate is folded into a slow apparent one. A stroboscope uses the same effect deliberately to "freeze" a rotating machine.

docs.title: Anti-aliasing filters
docs.text: Real signals are never perfectly band-limited: there is always some noise or some harmonic above the Nyquist frequency, and once sampled it folds down onto the wanted band, where it can never be removed. The only cure is prevention: an analog low-pass anti-aliasing filter before the sampler, which removes everything above \(f_s/2\) (or reduces it below the noise level) while the signal is still continuous. Figure 9.4 shows the complete chain for processing an analog signal digitally.

docs.title: 9.6 Discrete-time processing of continuous-time signals
docs.text:
The sampled sequence \(x[n] = x(nT)\) has a DTFT, and the impulse-train signal \(x_p(t)\) has a CTFT. They are the same function with the frequency axis relabelled: comparing \(X_p(j\omega) = \sum_n x(nT)e^{-j\omega nT}\) with \(X(e^{j\Omega}) = \sum_n x[n]e^{-j\Omega n}\) gives \(X(e^{j\Omega}) = X_p(j\Omega/T)\). Combined with the result of Section 9.2,

\[ X(e^{j\Omega}) = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}X_c\!\left(j\,\frac{\Omega - 2\pi k}{T}\right), \]

where \(X_c\) is the CTFT of the original. The continuous frequency \(\omega\) maps to \(\Omega = \omega T\), and the Nyquist frequency \(\omega_s/2 = \pi/T\) maps to \(\Omega = \pi\). The periodicity of the DTFT is the periodicity created by sampling.

Now suppose a band-limited signal, sampled above the Nyquist rate, is processed by a DT system \(H(e^{j\Omega})\) and then ideally reconstructed. The overall system from \(x(t)\) to \(y(t)\) behaves like a CT LTI system with frequency response

\[ H_{\text{eff}}(j\omega) = \begin{cases} H(e^{j\omega T}), & |\omega| < \pi/T, \\ 0, & |\omega| > \pi/T. \end{cases} \]

This is the justification for "digital filtering" of analog signals.

Example 9.3 A digital notch for mains hum

Audio sampled at 8 kHz is contaminated by 50 Hz hum. Which DT frequency must a notch filter remove?

\(\Omega_0 = 2\pi\cdot50/8000 = \pi/80 \approx 0.0393\) rad/sample. A filter with zeros at \(e^{\pm j\pi/80}\) on the unit circle does it; Chapter 12 shows how to place poles near those zeros to keep the notch narrow.

docs.title: Changing the sampling rate
docs.text:
Two operations of Chapter 2 change the rate of a sequence directly.

  • Decimation by \(M\) keeps every \(M\)th sample: the new rate is \(f_s/M\). In frequency, the spectrum is stretched by \(M\), and any content above \(\pi/M\) aliases. So the sequence must first be low-pass filtered to \(|\Omega| < \pi/M\).
  • Interpolation by \(L\) inserts \(L - 1\) zeros between samples (expansion), which compresses the spectrum by \(L\) and creates \(L - 1\) unwanted images in each period (Section 7.3), and then removes them with a low-pass filter of cut-off \(\pi/L\) and gain \(L\).

Combining the two changes the rate by any rational factor \(L/M\): converting 44.1 kHz audio to 48 kHz uses \(L/M = 160/147\).

docs.title: 9.7 Quantization
docs.text:
An analog-to-digital converter also rounds each sample to one of a finite number of levels. With \(B\) bits, a full-scale range from \(-1\) to \(1\) is divided into \(2^B\) steps of size \(\Delta = 2/2^B\). The rounding error lies between \(-\Delta/2\) and \(\Delta/2\). For a busy signal it behaves like a random noise, uniformly distributed over that interval, with power

\[ \sigma_e^2 = \frac{\Delta^2}{12}. \]

For a full-scale sinusoid (power \(\frac12\)), the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio is

\[ \mathrm{SNR} = 10\log_{10}\frac{1/2}{\Delta^2/12} \approx 6.02B + 1.76\ \text{dB}. \]

Each extra bit adds about 6 dB. Sixteen-bit audio gives about 98 dB; eight bits give about 50 dB, which is audibly noisy. Signals below full scale give proportionally less: a signal 20 dB below full scale loses 20 dB of SNR.

docs.title: 9.8 Sampling experiments in NumPy
docs.text:
The program below demonstrates aliasing numerically, reconstructs a band-limited signal from samples with the sinc formula, and measures the SNR of quantized sine waves.

import numpy as np

# 1. Aliasing: a 7 Hz cosine sampled at 8 Hz gives the same samples as a 1 Hz cosine
fs = 8
n = np.arange(16)
x7 = np.cos(2 * np.pi * 7 * n / fs)
x1 = np.cos(2 * np.pi * 1 * n / fs)
print("samples identical:", np.allclose(x7, x1))

def alias(f, fs):
    """Apparent frequency (0 .. fs/2) of a tone at f Hz sampled at fs Hz."""
    r = f % fs
    return min(r, fs - r)
for f in (7, 9, 12, 25, 1000):
    print(f"{f:5d} Hz sampled at {fs} Hz looks like {alias(f, fs):g} Hz")

# 2. Ideal (sinc) reconstruction of a band-limited signal from its samples
fs, T = 10.0, 0.1
nn = np.arange(-400, 401)                  # many samples, so truncation error is small
xs = np.cos(2 * np.pi * 1.3 * nn * T) + 0.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 3.1 * nn * T)
t = np.linspace(-1, 1, 9)
xr = np.array([np.sum(xs * np.sinc((tk - nn * T) / T)) for tk in t])
xtrue = np.cos(2 * np.pi * 1.3 * t) + 0.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 3.1 * t)
print("largest reconstruction error:", f"{np.max(np.abs(xr - xtrue)):.1e}")

# 3. Quantization noise: B-bit rounding of a full-scale sine
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
s = np.sin(2 * np.pi * rng.random() + 2 * np.pi * 0.01234 * np.arange(200_000))
for B in (8, 12, 16):
    step = 2 / 2 ** B                       # full scale is -1 .. 1
    q = np.round(s / step) * step
    snr = 10 * np.log10(np.mean(s ** 2) / np.mean((s - q) ** 2))
    print(f"B = {B:2d}: measured SNR {snr:5.1f} dB, formula 6.02B + 1.76 = {6.02 * B + 1.76:5.1f} dB")

samples identical: True
    7 Hz sampled at 8 Hz looks like 1 Hz
    9 Hz sampled at 8 Hz looks like 1 Hz
   12 Hz sampled at 8 Hz looks like 4 Hz
   25 Hz sampled at 8 Hz looks like 1 Hz
 1000 Hz sampled at 8 Hz looks like 0 Hz
largest reconstruction error: 6.0e-04
B =  8: measured SNR  50.0 dB, formula 6.02B + 1.76 =  49.9 dB
B = 12: measured SNR  74.0 dB, formula 6.02B + 1.76 =  74.0 dB
B = 16: measured SNR  98.1 dB, formula 6.02B + 1.76 =  98.1 dB

The 1000 Hz tone, an exact multiple of the 8 Hz sampling rate, is sampled at the same point of every cycle and looks like a constant (0 Hz). The reconstruction error of \(6\times10^{-4}\) comes only from using 801 samples instead of infinitely many; the sinc pulses decay slowly, so the sum must be long. The quantization measurements match \(6.02B + 1.76\) dB closely.

docs.title: 9.9 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Impulse-train sampling gives \(X_p(j\omega) = \frac1T\sum_k X(j(\omega - k\omega_s))\): copies of the spectrum at every multiple of \(\omega_s\).
  • Sampling theorem: a signal band-limited to \(\omega_M\) is determined by samples taken at \(\omega_s > 2\omega_M\) (the Nyquist rate is \(2\omega_M\)).
  • Ideal reconstruction uses a low-pass filter of gain \(T\) and cut-off \(\omega_s/2\), which amounts to the sinc interpolation formula \(x(t) = \sum x(nT)\,\mathrm{sinc}((t - nT)/T)\). Practical DACs use a zero-order hold followed by a smoothing filter.
  • Undersampling folds a frequency \(f\) to \(|f - f_s\,\mathrm{round}(f/f_s)|\). An analog anti-aliasing filter before the sampler is the only cure.
  • The DTFT of the samples is the periodised CTFT with \(\Omega = \omega T\). A DT system inside an ideal sampler and reconstructor acts as \(H(e^{j\omega T})\) for \(|\omega| < \pi/T\).
  • Decimation needs a low-pass filter first; interpolation needs one afterwards.
  • \(B\)-bit quantization of a full-scale sine gives an SNR of about \(6.02B + 1.76\) dB.

docs.title: 9.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 9.1

Find the Nyquist rate of \(x(t) = 4\cos(1000\pi t)\cos(3000\pi t)\).

Answer

The product is \(2\cos(2000\pi t) + 2\cos(4000\pi t)\): 1000 Hz and 2000 Hz. The Nyquist rate is 4000 samples per second.

Exercise 9.2

A 3 kHz tone is sampled at 5 kHz and ideally reconstructed. What frequency comes out?

Answer

2 kHz. \(|3 - 5| = 2\) kHz, which is below the Nyquist frequency of 2.5 kHz.

Exercise 9.3

The signal \(x(t) = \cos(2\pi\cdot 30t) + \cos(2\pi\cdot 70t)\) is sampled at 100 Hz. Write the sampled sequence and describe what reconstruction gives.

Answer

\(x[n] = \cos(0.6\pi n) + \cos(1.4\pi n)\), and \(\cos(1.4\pi n) = \cos(2\pi n - 0.6\pi n) = \cos(0.6\pi n)\). So \(x[n] = 2\cos(0.6\pi n)\), and reconstruction gives \(2\cos(2\pi\cdot30t)\): the 70 Hz tone has aliased onto the 30 Hz tone.

Exercise 9.4

A signal band-limited to 4 kHz is sampled at 10 kHz. Between which frequencies can the cut-off of the ideal reconstruction filter lie?

Answer

Between 4 kHz (the top of the signal band) and \(10 - 4 = 6\) kHz (the bottom of the first copy).

Exercise 9.5

At what sampling rate must an ECG with useful content up to 150 Hz be sampled, at minimum? Why do instruments use a higher rate?

Answer

Above 300 samples per second. Higher rates (500 or 1000 per second are common) leave room for a practical anti-aliasing filter with a gradual roll-off and capture sharp features more faithfully.

Exercise 9.6

A DT filter \(H(e^{j\Omega})\) is an ideal low-pass filter with cut-off \(\pi/4\). It is used between an ideal sampler and reconstructor at \(f_s = 16\) kHz. What is the cut-off of the equivalent analog filter?

Answer

\(\omega = \Omega/T\), so \(f = \frac{\pi/4}{2\pi}\cdot16\,\text{kHz} = 2\) kHz.

Exercise 9.7

How many bits are needed for a quantization SNR of at least 80 dB with a full-scale sinusoid?

Answer

\(6.02B + 1.76 \ge 80\) gives \(B \ge 13.0\), so 13 bits (\(6.02\times13 + 1.76 = 80.0\) dB); 14 bits for a margin.

Exercise 9.8

A sequence sampled at 48 kHz is to be decimated by 3. What must be done first, and what is the new rate?

Answer

Low-pass filter to \(|\Omega| < \pi/3\) (8 kHz in analog terms) to avoid aliasing, then keep every third sample. The new rate is 16 kHz.

Exercise 9.9

Show that the sinc interpolation formula returns \(x(mT)\) at \(t = mT\).

Answer

At \(t = mT\), \(\mathrm{sinc}((mT - nT)/T) = \mathrm{sinc}(m - n)\), which is 1 for \(n = m\) and 0 for every other integer. Only the term \(n = m\) survives.

Exercise 9.10

A wheel with 12 identical spokes turns at 2.5 revolutions per second and is filmed at 24 frames per second. How fast does it appear to turn?

Answer

The spoke pattern repeats 30 times per second (12 spokes × 2.5 rev/s). Sampled at 24 Hz, 30 Hz aliases to \(30 - 24 = 6\) Hz, below the Nyquist frequency of 12 Hz. The pattern appears to repeat 6 times per second, so the wheel seems to turn forwards at \(6/12 = 0.5\) revolutions per second. (Had the folded frequency come out negative, the wheel would seem to turn backwards.)

docs.title: 9.11 Quiz
