docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 9

Exercise 1

A signal contains frequencies up to 5 kHz. What is its Nyquist rate in kHz?

Answer

10 / 10 kHz

Exercise 2

A 900 Hz tone is sampled at 1000 Hz. At what frequency (Hz) does it appear?

Answer

100 / 100 Hz

Exercise 3

Sampling in time makes the spectrum

  1. periodic
  2. discrete
  3. zero above the Nyquist frequency
  4. real
Answer

periodic

Exercise 4

Aliasing can be prevented by

  1. an analog low-pass filter before sampling
  2. a digital filter after sampling
  3. zero-padding the DFT
  4. a reconstruction filter after the DAC
Answer

an analog low-pass filter before sampling

Once a high frequency has folded onto the signal band, no later filter can separate it.

Exercise 5

The ideal reconstruction filter has impulse response

  1. sinc(t/T)
  2. a rectangular pulse of width T
  3. δ(t)
  4. e^(−t/T)u(t)
Answer

sinc(t/T)

Exercise 6

Roughly how many dB of SNR does each extra bit of quantization add?

Answer

6 / 6 dB / 6.02

Exercise 7

Half the sampling rate is called the ___ frequency.

Answer

Nyquist

docs.title: Chapter 1: Signals and Their Classification
docs.text:
What a signal is, and the handful of questions that sort every signal into families

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • describe a signal as a function of an independent variable and tell continuous-time from discrete-time signals;
  • use complex numbers and Euler's formula confidently, because every later chapter depends on them;
  • split any signal into its even and odd parts;
  • decide whether a continuous-time or discrete-time signal is periodic and find its fundamental period;
  • compute the energy and the average power of a signal and say whether it is an energy signal, a power signal or neither.

docs.title: 1.1 Signals and systems in everyday engineering
docs.text:
A signal is a quantity that varies and carries information. The voltage from a microphone rises and falls with the pressure of the air in front of it; the reading of a thermometer changes through the day; the brightness of a pixel changes from one point of an image to the next; the closing price of a share changes from one trading day to the next. In each case there is something we can measure, and it changes with something else: with time, with position, with the day number.

Mathematically, a signal is simply a function. The thing it depends on is called the independent variable, and the value it takes is the amplitude or the value of the signal. Most of this book uses time as the independent variable, so we write \(x(t)\) for a signal that depends on a continuous time \(t\), and \(x[n]\) for one that is defined only at whole numbers \(n\). Nothing in the mathematics requires the variable to be time: an image is a signal of two spatial variables, and the same ideas of filtering and frequency apply to it.

A system is anything that takes a signal in and produces a signal out. An amplifier takes a weak microphone voltage and produces a stronger copy of it. A car's suspension takes the bumps of the road as its input and produces the motion of the cabin as its output. A program that averages the last five daily share prices is a system whose input and output are both sequences of numbers. We draw a system as a box with an arrow going in and an arrow coming out, and we write \(y(t) = T\{x(t)\}\) to say that the system \(T\) turns the input \(x\) into the output \(y\).

The subject of this book is the relationship between signals and the systems that process them. Three questions recur in every chapter:

  1. Description. How do we describe a signal compactly and usefully? Sometimes as a formula in time, often as a sum of sinusoids of different frequencies.
  2. Analysis. Given a system and an input, what is the output? For the important class of linear time-invariant systems there is a complete answer, called convolution, and a simpler one in the frequency domain.
  3. Design. Given what we want the output to look like, how do we build the system? This is the problem of filter and controller design.

This first chapter is about the vocabulary of signals: the families they fall into and the numbers (period, energy, power) that summarise them. The next chapter adds the basic signals from which all others are built and the operations we perform on them.

docs.title: 1.2 Continuous-time and discrete-time signals
docs.text:
A continuous-time (CT) signal is defined for every real value of time. The voltage across a capacitor, the position of a pendulum and the pressure of a sound wave are continuous-time signals. We write the time variable in round brackets, \(x(t)\), with \(t \in \mathbb{R}\).

A discrete-time (DT) signal is defined only at separate instants, which we number with integers. We write the index in square brackets, \(x[n]\), with \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\), and call the signal a sequence. The values \(x[n]\) are called samples. A discrete-time signal is not zero between the integers: it is simply not defined there. Asking for \(x[2.5]\) is as meaningless as asking for the 2.5th day of the week.

Figure 1.1 Continuous and discrete time. Left: a continuous-time signal, a decaying cosine defined for every instant t. Right: a discrete-time signal, the same shape known only at the integers n, drawn as stems.

Discrete-time signals arise in two ways. Some are discrete by nature: the number of passengers on each day's train, the balance of a bank account at the end of each month. Most of the discrete-time signals in engineering, however, come from sampling a continuous-time signal every \(T_s\) seconds:

\[ x[n] = x_c(nT_s), \qquad n = \ldots, -1, 0, 1, 2, \ldots \]

Here \(x_c\) is the continuous-time signal, \(T_s\) is the sampling interval and \(f_s = 1/T_s\) is the sampling rate in samples per second. Audio on a compact disc, for example, is sampled 44,100 times a second. Chapter 9 asks the central question of sampling: when do the samples hold all the information of the original signal?

docs.title: Analog and digital
docs.text:
Two further words are often confused with continuous and discrete. An analog signal is one whose amplitude can take any value in a continuous range; a digital signal is one whose amplitude is restricted to a finite set of levels, so that each value can be stored as a binary number. Sampling makes time discrete; quantization makes amplitude discrete. A signal in a computer is both: discrete in time and quantized in amplitude. In this book we treat discrete-time signals as having real (or complex) amplitudes and set quantization aside, except for a short look at its effect in Chapter 9; the theory of discrete-time systems does not depend on the number of bits.

Continuous amplitude Discrete amplitude Continuous time analog signal, \(x(t)\) quantized continuous-time signal (rare) Discrete time sampled sequence, \(x[n]\) digital signal

Table 1.1. Time and amplitude can each be continuous or discrete.

docs.title: 1.3 Real and complex signals
docs.text:
A signal whose values are real numbers is a real signal. Physical measurements are real. Even so, we shall work constantly with complex signals, whose values are complex numbers, because they make the mathematics of sinusoids far simpler. A short review is worth the time now.

A complex number \(z = a + jb\) has a real part \(a\) and an imaginary part \(b\), where \(j = \sqrt{-1}\). (Electrical engineers write \(j\) because \(i\) is taken by current.) The same number can be written in polar form:

\[ z = r e^{j\theta}, \qquad r = |z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}, \qquad \theta = \angle z, \]

where \(r\) is the magnitude and \(\theta\) the angle or phase, chosen so that \(a = r\cos\theta\) and \(b = r\sin\theta\). The bridge between the two forms is Euler's formula:

\[ e^{j\theta} = \cos\theta + j\sin\theta . \]

Two consequences are used on almost every page of this book:

\[ \cos\theta = \frac{e^{j\theta} + e^{-j\theta}}{2}, \qquad \sin\theta = \frac{e^{j\theta} - e^{-j\theta}}{2j}. \]

The complex conjugate of \(z = a + jb = re^{j\theta}\) is \(z^* = a - jb = re^{-j\theta}\), and \(zz^* = |z|^2\). Multiplying complex numbers multiplies their magnitudes and adds their angles: \((r_1e^{j\theta_1})(r_2e^{j\theta_2}) = r_1r_2e^{j(\theta_1+\theta_2)}\). This is why the polar form suits systems that scale and delay sinusoids: scaling changes the magnitude, delaying changes the angle.

The most important complex signal is the complex exponential \(x(t) = e^{j\omega_0 t}\). Its magnitude is always 1, and its angle grows steadily with time at \(\omega_0\) radians per second: it is a point going round the unit circle. Its real part is \(\cos\omega_0 t\) and its imaginary part is \(\sin\omega_0 t\). A real sinusoid is the sum of two such points rotating in opposite directions, which is the first formula above with \(\theta = \omega_0 t\).

Example 1.1 Polar form of a complex number

Write \(z = -1 + j\sqrt{3}\) in polar form and find \(z^3\).

Magnitude. \(r = \sqrt{1 + 3} = 2\).

Angle. The point lies in the second quadrant, so \(\theta = \pi - \arctan(\sqrt{3}/1) = \pi - \pi/3 = 2\pi/3\). (A calculator's \(\arctan(b/a)\) gives \(-\pi/3\) here; always check the quadrant.)

Power. \(z^3 = 2^3 e^{j3 \cdot 2\pi/3} = 8e^{j2\pi} = 8\). Multiplying in polar form is far easier than expanding \((-1 + j\sqrt{3})^3\), though the expansion gives the same answer.

The quadrant of the angle

The angle of \(a + jb\) is not always \(\arctan(b/a)\). That formula is right only when \(a > 0\). For \(a < 0\) add or subtract \(\pi\). In NumPy use np.angle(z) or np.arctan2(b, a), which check the quadrant for you.

docs.title: 1.4 Deterministic and random signals, and other descriptions
docs.text:
A deterministic signal is one whose value at every instant is fixed by a formula, a table or a rule: \(x(t) = 3\cos(100\pi t)\) is deterministic. A random signal is one whose future values cannot be predicted exactly, only described by probabilities: the hiss of a radio between stations, the noise in a measurement, the fluctuation of a share price. Random signals are studied with probability theory and are outside the scope of this book, except that we shall often add noise to a deterministic signal in an example to see how a filter copes with it. Everything we prove about systems applies to random inputs as well, because a system does not know whether its input was predictable.

Several other words describe where a signal is non-zero:

  • A signal is causal (or right-sided starting at zero) if \(x(t) = 0\) for \(t < 0\). The name comes from systems: the response of a physical system to a kick at \(t = 0\) cannot start before the kick.
  • A signal is anticausal if \(x(t) = 0\) for \(t > 0\).
  • A signal is right-sided if it is zero before some time \(t_1\), left-sided if it is zero after some time \(t_2\), and two-sided if it is neither.
  • A signal is of finite duration if it is zero outside some interval \(t_1 \le t \le t_2\). A finite-duration sequence can be listed in full, and we often do so with an arrow under the sample at \(n = 0\); in this book we say in words which sample is at \(n = 0\).

These descriptions matter later, when the region of convergence of a Laplace or z-transform turns out to depend on whether a signal is right-sided, left-sided or two-sided.

docs.title: 1.5 Even and odd signals
docs.text:
A signal is even if it is unchanged when time is reversed, and odd if reversing time changes its sign:

\[ \text{even: } x(-t) = x(t), \qquad \text{odd: } x(-t) = -x(t). \]

The same definitions hold for sequences with \(n\) in place of \(t\). The cosine is even, the sine is odd, \(t^2\) is even and \(t^3\) is odd. Geometrically, an even signal is a mirror image of itself about the vertical axis, and an odd signal is unchanged by a half-turn about the origin. An odd signal must be zero at the origin, because \(x(0) = -x(0)\).

The useful fact is that every signal is the sum of an even part and an odd part, and the parts are unique:

\[ x_e(t) = \frac{x(t) + x(-t)}{2}, \qquad x_o(t) = \frac{x(t) - x(-t)}{2}, \qquad x(t) = x_e(t) + x_o(t). \]

To check: \(x_e(-t) = \frac{x(-t) + x(t)}{2} = x_e(t)\), so \(x_e\) is even; \(x_o(-t) = \frac{x(-t) - x(t)}{2} = -x_o(t)\), so \(x_o\) is odd; and adding the two gives \(x(t)\).

Figure 1.2 Even and odd parts. A causal decaying exponential (left) is the sum of an even part, half the exponential reflected about t = 0 (centre), and an odd part, half the exponential with its left half turned upside down (right).

Example 1.2 Even and odd parts of a causal exponential

Find the even and odd parts of \(x(t) = e^{-t}u(t)\), where \(u(t)\) is 1 for \(t > 0\) and 0 for \(t < 0\).

For \(t > 0\): \(x(t) = e^{-t}\) and \(x(-t) = 0\), so \(x_e(t) = \tfrac{1}{2}e^{-t}\) and \(x_o(t) = \tfrac{1}{2}e^{-t}\).

For \(t < 0\): \(x(t) = 0\) and \(x(-t) = e^{t}\), so \(x_e(t) = \tfrac{1}{2}e^{t}\) and \(x_o(t) = -\tfrac{1}{2}e^{t}\).

Together, \(x_e(t) = \tfrac{1}{2}e^{-|t|}\) and \(x_o(t) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{sgn}(t)\,e^{-|t|}\), where \(\mathrm{sgn}(t)\) is \(+1\) for \(t > 0\) and \(-1\) for \(t < 0\). Figure 1.2 shows the three signals. For \(t > 0\) the two parts add to \(e^{-t}\); for \(t < 0\) they cancel.

A few rules save work. The product of two even signals or of two odd signals is even; the product of an even and an odd signal is odd. The integral of an odd signal over a symmetric interval is zero, and the integral of an even signal over \([-a, a]\) is twice its integral over \([0, a]\). These rules will halve the work of computing Fourier series in Chapter 5.

For complex signals the corresponding idea is conjugate symmetry: \(x(-t) = x^*(t)\). A real even signal is conjugate symmetric; we meet the idea again when we find that the spectrum of every real signal is conjugate symmetric.

docs.title: 1.6 Periodic and aperiodic signals
docs.text:
A continuous-time signal is periodic if there is a positive number \(T\) such that

\[ x(t + T) = x(t) \quad \text{for all } t . \]

If \(x\) repeats every \(T\) seconds it also repeats every \(2T\), \(3T\) and so on. The smallest such positive \(T\) is the fundamental period \(T_0\), and \(f_0 = 1/T_0\) (in hertz) and \(\omega_0 = 2\pi/T_0\) (in radians per second) are the fundamental frequency. A signal that is not periodic is aperiodic. A constant is periodic with every period and has no fundamental period; we treat it as a special case.

Figure 1.3 A periodic signal. A periodic signal: the same shape, a falling ramp followed by a flat stretch, repeats every T = 2 time units for all time.

The sinusoid \(x(t) = A\cos(\omega_0 t + \phi)\) is periodic with fundamental period \(T_0 = 2\pi/\omega_0\), for any amplitude \(A\) and phase \(\phi\). The complex exponential \(e^{j\omega_0 t}\) has the same period.

docs.title: Sums of periodic signals
docs.text:
If \(x_1\) has period \(T_1\) and \(x_2\) has period \(T_2\), their sum repeats when both have completed a whole number of cycles, that is at a time \(T\) with \(T = mT_1 = kT_2\) for some positive integers \(m\) and \(k\). Such a time exists exactly when the ratio \(T_1/T_2 = k/m\) is a rational number. The fundamental period of the sum is then the least common multiple of \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) (unless terms cancel, which happens rarely).

Example 1.3 Periods of sums

(a) \(x(t) = \cos 2t + \sin 3t\). The periods are \(T_1 = 2\pi/2 = \pi\) and \(T_2 = 2\pi/3\). The ratio is \(T_1/T_2 = 3/2\), rational. The least common multiple is \(2\pi\) (two periods of the first, three of the second), so \(T_0 = 2\pi\).

(b) \(x(t) = \cos t + \cos(\sqrt{2}\,t)\). The ratio of periods is \(\sqrt{2}\), which is irrational, so no common period exists and the sum is aperiodic, even though each term is periodic.

docs.title: Discrete-time periodicity is different
docs.text:
A sequence is periodic with period \(N\) (a positive integer) if \(x[n + N] = x[n]\) for all \(n\); the smallest such \(N\) is the fundamental period \(N_0\). Because \(N\) must be an integer, a discrete-time sinusoid behaves differently from a continuous one. Consider \(x[n] = \cos(\Omega_0 n)\), where \(\Omega_0\) is in radians per sample. It is periodic with period \(N\) only if \(\Omega_0 N\) is a whole multiple of \(2\pi\):

\[ \Omega_0 N = 2\pi m \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{\Omega_0}{2\pi} = \frac{m}{N}. \]

So a discrete-time sinusoid is periodic only if \(\Omega_0/2\pi\) is a rational number. When it is, write \(\Omega_0/2\pi = m/N\) in lowest terms; then the fundamental period is \(N_0 = N\).

Example 1.4 Periodic or not?

(a) \(x[n] = \cos(3\pi n/8)\). Here \(\Omega_0/2\pi = 3/16\), already in lowest terms, so \(N_0 = 16\). In 16 samples the cosine completes 3 full cycles.

(b) \(x[n] = \cos(n)\). Here \(\Omega_0/2\pi = 1/(2\pi)\), which is irrational. The sequence never repeats exactly, although its samples lie on a cosine curve of period \(2\pi\) seconds.

(c) \(x[n] = e^{j2\pi n/5} + e^{j3\pi n/4}\). The periods are 5 and 8, so \(N_0 = \operatorname{lcm}(5, 8) = 40\).

A second surprise of discrete time is that frequencies wrap around. Because \(n\) is an integer, \(e^{j(\Omega_0 + 2\pi)n} = e^{j\Omega_0 n}e^{j2\pi n} = e^{j\Omega_0 n}\). A discrete-time complex exponential at frequency \(\Omega_0 + 2\pi\) is the same sequence as one at \(\Omega_0\). Discrete-time frequencies therefore need only be considered over an interval of length \(2\pi\), usually \(-\pi < \Omega \le \pi\), and the "highest" frequency a sequence can have is \(\Omega = \pi\), which is \((-1)^n\), a sequence that flips sign at every sample. This fact is the root of aliasing in Chapter 9.

A common mistake

Students often say that \(\cos(\Omega_0 n)\) oscillates faster as \(\Omega_0\) increases. That is true only from \(0\) to \(\pi\). From \(\pi\) to \(2\pi\) the oscillation becomes slower again, because \(\cos((2\pi - \Omega)n) = \cos(\Omega n)\).

docs.title: 1.7 Energy and power
docs.text:
Two numbers measure the "size" of a signal. If \(x(t)\) is a voltage across a 1-ohm resistor, the instantaneous power is \(|x(t)|^2\), and the total energy delivered is its integral. By analogy, for any signal we define the energy

\[ E_x = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x(t)|^2\,dt, \qquad E_x = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} |x[n]|^2, \]

and the average power

\[ P_x = \lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{2T}\int_{-T}^{T}|x(t)|^2\,dt, \qquad P_x = \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{2N+1}\sum_{n=-N}^{N}|x[n]|^2 . \]

The magnitude bars let the definitions cover complex signals. Three cases arise:

  • An energy signal has \(0 < E_x < \infty\). Its average power is then zero, because a finite energy spread over an infinitely long time averages to nothing. Pulses and decaying signals are energy signals.
  • A power signal has \(0 < P_x < \infty\). Its energy is then infinite. Periodic signals and the unit step are power signals.
  • Some signals are neither: \(x(t) = t\) has infinite energy and infinite power, and \(x(t) = e^{t}\) grows too fast to have finite power.

For a periodic signal the limit in the power formula is just the average over one period: \(P_x = \frac{1}{T_0}\int_{T_0}|x(t)|^2\,dt\), where the integral is over any interval of length \(T_0\).

Example 1.5 Energy of a decaying exponential

Find the energy of \(x(t) = Ae^{-at}u(t)\) with \(a > 0\).

\[ E_x = \int_0^{\infty} A^2 e^{-2at}\,dt = A^2\left[\frac{-e^{-2at}}{2a}\right]_0^{\infty} = \frac{A^2}{2a}. \]

With \(A = 1\) and \(a = 2\) the energy is \(1/4\). The signal is an energy signal, so its power is zero.

Example 1.6 Power of a sinusoid

Find the power of \(x(t) = A\cos(\omega_0 t + \phi)\).

Over one period \(T_0 = 2\pi/\omega_0\), use \(\cos^2\theta = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + \cos 2\theta)\):

\[ P_x = \frac{1}{T_0}\int_0^{T_0} A^2\cos^2(\omega_0 t + \phi)\,dt = \frac{A^2}{T_0}\int_0^{T_0}\frac{1 + \cos(2\omega_0 t + 2\phi)}{2}\,dt = \frac{A^2}{2}. \]

The cosine term integrates to zero over a whole number of its periods. The power of a sinusoid of amplitude \(A\) is \(A^2/2\) whatever its frequency and phase, which is why the root-mean-square value of a sinusoid is \(A/\sqrt{2}\). For example \(5\cos(10t + \pi/3)\) has power \(12.5\).

Example 1.7 A geometric sequence

Find the energy of \(x[n] = (0.8)^n u[n]\), where \(u[n]\) is 1 for \(n \ge 0\) and 0 otherwise.

\[ E_x = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (0.8)^{2n} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (0.64)^n = \frac{1}{1 - 0.64} = 2.778, \]

using the geometric series \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} r^n = 1/(1 - r)\) for \(|r| < 1\). This series appears in almost every discrete-time calculation in the book; it is worth remembering together with its finite form \(\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} r^n = (1 - r^N)/(1 - r)\) for \(r \ne 1\).

The unit step \(u(t)\) has infinite energy but power \(\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{2T}\int_0^T 1\,dt = \frac{1}{2}\): it is a power signal.

Signal Energy Power Type \(Ae^{-at}u(t)\), \(a > 0\) \(A^2/(2a)\) 0 energy rectangular pulse, height \(A\), width \(\tau\) \(A^2\tau\) 0 energy \(A\cos(\omega_0 t + \phi)\) \(\infty\) \(A^2/2\) power \(Ae^{j\omega_0 t}\) \(\infty\) \(\lvert A\rvert^2\) power \(u(t)\) \(\infty\) \(1/2\) power \(t\,u(t)\) \(\infty\) \(\infty\) neither

Table 1.2. Energy and power of some common signals.

docs.title: Checking the numbers with NumPy
docs.text:
Sums like these are easy to check numerically. The script below computes the energy of Example 1.7, the power of a discrete sinusoid, and the even and odd parts of a short sequence.

import numpy as np

# Energy of x[n] = 0.8^n u[n]: sum enough terms that the tail is negligible
n = np.arange(0, 200)
x = 0.8 ** n
E = np.sum(np.abs(x) ** 2)
print(f"energy of 0.8^n u[n]    : {E:.4f}   formula 1/(1-0.64) = {1/(1-0.64):.4f}")

# Average power of y[n] = 3 cos(pi n / 4), averaged over -N..N
N = 1000
n = np.arange(-N, N + 1)
y = 3 * np.cos(np.pi * n / 4)
P = np.sum(y ** 2) / (2 * N + 1)
print(f"power of 3 cos(pi n/4)  : {P:.4f}   formula 9/2 = 4.5")

# Even and odd parts of a short sequence on n = -3..3
n = np.arange(-3, 4)
x = np.array([0, 0, 0, 4, 2, 1, 0.5])
xr = x[::-1]                     # x[-n], because n runs symmetrically
xe = 0.5 * (x + xr)
xo = 0.5 * (x - xr)
print("n  :", n)
print("x_e:", xe)
print("x_o:", xo)
print("x_e + x_o equals x:", np.allclose(xe + xo, x))

energy of 0.8^n u[n]    : 2.7778   formula 1/(1-0.64) = 2.7778
power of 3 cos(pi n/4)  : 4.5022   formula 9/2 = 4.5
n  : [-3 -2 -1  0  1  2  3]
x_e: [0.25 0.5  1.   4.   1.   0.5  0.25]
x_o: [-0.25 -0.5  -1.    0.    1.    0.5   0.25]
x_e + x_o equals x: True

The power is not exactly 4.5 because 2001 samples are not a whole number of periods of 8; the estimate approaches 4.5 as \(N\) grows. Notice the trick in the last part: reversing the array gives \(x[-n]\) only because the index runs symmetrically from \(-3\) to \(3\). With an unsymmetric index range you must build \(x[-n]\) explicitly.

Read the signal before computing

Before integrating, ask what kind of signal you have. If it is periodic, it cannot be an energy signal (unless it is zero); compute the power over one period. If it decays at least as fast as an exponential, it is an energy signal. A quick classification catches most algebra slips.

docs.title: 1.8 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • A signal is a function of an independent variable, usually time; a system maps an input signal to an output signal.
  • Continuous-time signals \(x(t)\) are defined for all real \(t\); discrete-time signals \(x[n]\) only at integers. Sampling gives \(x[n] = x_c(nT_s)\). Quantization of amplitude makes a signal digital.
  • Euler's formula \(e^{j\theta} = \cos\theta + j\sin\theta\) links sinusoids and complex exponentials; polar form makes multiplication easy.
  • Every signal splits uniquely into even and odd parts, \(x_e = \tfrac12[x(t) + x(-t)]\) and \(x_o = \tfrac12[x(t) - x(-t)]\).
  • A CT sinusoid is always periodic with \(T_0 = 2\pi/\omega_0\); a sum of periodic signals is periodic only if the ratio of periods is rational. A DT sinusoid \(\cos\Omega_0 n\) is periodic only if \(\Omega_0/2\pi\) is rational, and DT frequencies repeat every \(2\pi\).
  • Energy is \(\int|x|^2\) (or \(\sum|x|^2\)); power is its time average. Energy signals have zero power; power signals have infinite energy; some signals are neither.

docs.title: 1.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1.1

Write \(z = 3 - 3j\) in polar form, and find \(z^4\).

Answer

\(|z| = \sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}\) and the point is in the fourth quadrant, so \(\angle z = -\pi/4\). Then \(z^4 = (3\sqrt{2})^4 e^{-j\pi} = 324 \cdot (-1) = -324\).

Exercise 1.2

Find the even and odd parts of \(x[n] = \{1, 2, 3\}\) for \(n = 0, 1, 2\) (and zero elsewhere).

Answer

\(x[-n]\) is 3, 2, 1 at \(n = -2, -1, 0\). So on \(n = -2, \ldots, 2\): \(x_e[n] = \{1.5, 1, 1, 1, 1.5\}\) and \(x_o[n] = \{-1.5, -1, 0, 1, 1.5\}\). Their sum is \(\{0, 0, 1, 2, 3\}\), which is \(x[n]\).

Exercise 1.3

Is \(x(t) = \sin(4\pi t) + \cos(6\pi t)\) periodic? If so, find its fundamental period.

Answer

The periods are \(1/2\) and \(1/3\). Their ratio \(3/2\) is rational, and the least common multiple is \(1\). So \(T_0 = 1\) second.

Exercise 1.4

Find the fundamental period of \(x[n] = \cos(0.3\pi n)\), or show that it is not periodic.

Answer

20. Here \(\Omega_0/2\pi = 0.15 = 3/20\) in lowest terms, so \(N_0 = 20\) (three cycles in 20 samples).

Exercise 1.5

Is \(x[n] = \sin(2n)\) periodic?

Answer

No. \(\Omega_0/2\pi = 1/\pi\) is irrational, so no integer \(N\) makes \(2N\) a multiple of \(2\pi\).

Exercise 1.6

Compute the energy of the rectangular pulse \(x(t) = 4\) for \(0 \le t \le 3\) and zero elsewhere.

Answer

48. \(E = \int_0^3 16\,dt = 48\).

Exercise 1.7

Find the power of \(x(t) = 2 + 3\cos(5t)\).

Answer

\(|x|^2 = 4 + 12\cos 5t + 9\cos^2 5t\). Averaged over a period the middle term vanishes and \(\cos^2\) averages to \(1/2\), so \(P = 4 + 4.5 = 8.5\). (The powers of a constant and a sinusoid at a non-zero frequency simply add.)

Exercise 1.8

Classify as energy, power or neither: (a) \(e^{-3|t|}\); (b) \(e^{j5t}\); (c) \((1/2)^n u[n]\); (d) \(n\,u[n]\).

Answer

(a) Energy: \(E = 2\int_0^\infty e^{-6t}dt = 1/3\). (b) Power: \(|x|^2 = 1\), so \(P = 1\). (c) Energy: \(E = 1/(1 - 1/4) = 4/3\). (d) Neither: both energy and power are infinite.

Exercise 1.9

Show that the energy of a signal is the sum of the energies of its even and odd parts, for a real signal with finite energy.

Answer

\(E_x = \int (x_e + x_o)^2 dt = \int x_e^2\,dt + \int x_o^2\,dt + 2\int x_e x_o\,dt\). The product \(x_e x_o\) is odd, so its integral over the whole line is zero. Hence \(E_x = E_{x_e} + E_{x_o}\).

Exercise 1.10

A sequence is formed by sampling \(x_c(t) = \cos(2\pi \cdot 50\,t)\) at \(f_s = 400\) samples per second. Write \(x[n]\) and find its fundamental period.

Answer

\(x[n] = \cos(2\pi \cdot 50\,n/400) = \cos(\pi n/4)\). Then \(\Omega_0/2\pi = 1/8\), so \(N_0 = 8\): eight samples per cycle of the 50 Hz cosine.

docs.title: 1.10 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 1

Exercise 1

Which of these discrete-time signals is periodic?

  1. cos(2n)
  2. cos(πn/6)
  3. sin(n/3)
  4. cos(√2 n)
Answer

cos(πn/6)

Ω0/2π = 1/12 is rational, so N0 = 12. For the others Ω0/2π is irrational.

Exercise 2

What is the average power of 4cos(7t + 1)?

Answer

8 / 8.0

A sinusoid of amplitude A has power A²/2 = 16/2 = 8.

Exercise 3

An energy signal has average power equal to

  1. zero
  2. its energy
  3. infinity
  4. one half
Answer

zero

Finite energy averaged over infinite time gives zero power.

Exercise 4

A signal with x(−t) = −x(t) for all t is called ___.

Answer

odd / an odd signal

Reversing time changes its sign; it must also be zero at t = 0.

Exercise 5

What is the fundamental period, in samples, of cos(3πn/8)?

Answer

16

Ω0/2π = 3/16 in lowest terms, so N0 = 16.

Exercise 6

Match each signal with its type.

ABe^(−2t)u(t)power signalu(t)neithert u(t)energy signal Answer

e^(−2t)u(t) — energy signal; u(t) — power signal; t u(t) — neither

Exercise 7

Which discrete-time frequency gives the fastest-changing sequence?

  1. Ω = π/2
  2. Ω = π
  3. Ω = 3π/2
  4. Ω = 2π
Answer

Ω = π

Ω = π gives (−1)^n. Frequencies repeat every 2π, so 3π/2 behaves like −π/2 and 2π like 0.

docs.title: Chapter 13: State-Space Models
docs.text:
An internal description of systems: state equations, their solution, transfer functions and a first look at state feedback

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • explain what the state of a system is and why an internal description is useful;
  • write state equations for mechanical and electrical systems and for a transfer function in canonical form;
  • compute the transfer function \(C(sI - A)^{-1}B + D\) and identify the poles as eigenvalues of \(A\);
  • solve the state equations using the matrix exponential, and decide stability from the eigenvalues;
  • write and solve discrete-time state equations, and discretise a continuous-time model exactly for a piecewise-constant input;
  • place the poles of a simple system by state feedback.

docs.title: 13.1 Why describe the inside of a system?
docs.text:
Everything so far has described LTI systems from the outside: by an impulse response, a frequency response or a transfer function, each of which relates the output to the input and says nothing about what happens inside. This external view is powerful, but it has limits:

  • it assumes the system starts at rest, while real systems often start with stored energy;
  • it is awkward for systems with several inputs and several outputs;
  • it hides internal variables (a current inside a circuit, the velocity of a motor) that may matter in their own right, for example because they must not exceed a limit;
  • it does not extend to nonlinear or time-varying systems, while numerical simulation of such systems is naturally written in terms of internal variables.

The state-space description addresses all four. It is the language of modern control engineering and of numerical simulation, and it connects signals and systems with linear algebra.

The state of a system at time \(t_0\) is the smallest set of numbers that, together with the input for \(t \ge t_0\), determines the output for all \(t \ge t_0\). For a mass on a spring, the state is the position and the velocity: knowing both now, and the force from now on, fixes the whole future motion. In a circuit, the state is the set of capacitor voltages and inductor currents, the quantities that store energy. The number of state variables is the order of the system, and it equals the number of independent energy stores.

docs.title: 13.2 State equations
docs.text:
A continuous-time LTI system with input \(u(t)\), output \(y(t)\) and state vector \(\mathbf{x}(t)\) of \(N\) components is described by

\[ \dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) = A\,\mathbf{x}(t) + B\,u(t), \qquad y(t) = C\,\mathbf{x}(t) + D\,u(t). \]

The first is the state equation: \(N\) first-order differential equations, telling how the state changes. The second is the output equation, telling how the output is read from the state. \(A\) is \(N\times N\), \(B\) is \(N\times1\), \(C\) is \(1\times N\) and \(D\) is a scalar (with several inputs and outputs, \(B\), \(C\) and \(D\) become matrices of the appropriate sizes, and nothing else changes). The input of this chapter is called \(u\), following the custom of control engineering, because \(\mathbf{x}\) is now the state.

Figure 13.1 The state-space block diagram. Block diagram of the state equations. The input u is multiplied by B and added to A x to form ẋ, which a bank of integrators turns into the state x. The output y is C x plus a direct term D u.

Example 13.1 A mass-spring-damper

A mass \(m\) on a spring of stiffness \(k\) with a damper of coefficient \(c\), pushed by a force \(u(t)\), has position \(y(t)\) obeying \(m\ddot{y} + c\dot{y} + ky = u\). Choose the state variables \(x_1 = y\) (position) and \(x_2 = \dot{y}\) (velocity). Then

\[ \dot{x}_1 = x_2, \qquad \dot{x}_2 = -\frac{k}{m}x_1 - \frac{c}{m}x_2 + \frac{1}{m}u, \]

or, in matrices, with the output \(y = x_1\):

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -k/m & -c/m \end{bmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1/m \end{bmatrix}, \quad C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad D = 0 . \]

With \(m = 1\), \(c = 3\) and \(k = 2\) (the system of Example 10.9), \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\).

Figure 13.2 A mass-spring-damper and its state trajectory. Left: a mass m attached to a wall by a spring k and a damper c, pushed by a force u(t), with position y(t). Right: the path of the state (position, velocity) for a lightly damped system released from rest at y = 1: the state spirals in to the origin.

The pair \((x_1, x_2)\) can be drawn as a point in the state space (here a plane, the phase plane). As time passes the point traces a trajectory. For a damped oscillator released from rest away from equilibrium, the trajectory spirals in to the origin (Figure 13.2): the position and the velocity oscillate a quarter-cycle out of step while the damper removes energy.

Example 13.2 An RLC circuit

A series circuit of a resistor \(R\), an inductor \(L\) and a capacitor \(C_0\), driven by a voltage \(u(t)\), with the capacitor voltage as output. The energy stores are the inductor (current \(i\)) and the capacitor (voltage \(v\)). The element laws give \(C_0\dot{v} = i\) and \(L\dot{i} = u - Ri - v\). With \(\mathbf{x} = [v, i]^T\):

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1/C_0 \\ -1/L & -R/L \end{bmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1/L \end{bmatrix}, \quad C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad D = 0 . \]

The structure is the same as for the mass-spring-damper, which is why the two systems behave alike: inductance plays the part of mass, resistance of damping, and the reciprocal of capacitance of stiffness.

docs.title: 13.3 From a transfer function to state equations
docs.text:
Any proper rational transfer function can be turned into state equations; the result is called a realisation. One standard form, the controllable canonical form, reads the matrices off the coefficients. For

\[ H(s) = \frac{b_2s^2 + b_1s + b_0}{s^3 + a_2s^2 + a_1s + a_0}, \]

a realisation is

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -a_0 & -a_1 & -a_2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad C = \begin{bmatrix} b_0 & b_1 & b_2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad D = 0 . \]

The pattern extends to any order: ones above the diagonal, the negated denominator coefficients in the last row, the numerator coefficients in \(C\). (If the numerator has the same degree as the denominator, divide first; the constant quotient becomes \(D\).) The state variables are the output of a chain of integrators driven by an auxiliary signal, which is why this form is also called the phase-variable form. Example 13.1 is this form for \(H(s) = \frac{1}{s^2 + 3s + 2}\).

Realisations are not unique. If \(T\) is any invertible matrix, the new state \(\mathbf{z} = T\mathbf{x}\) obeys equations with matrices \(TAT^{-1}\), \(TB\), \(CT^{-1}\) and \(D\), and gives exactly the same input-output behaviour. Choosing a good set of state variables (physical ones, or ones that decouple the equations) is part of the engineer's craft.

docs.title: 13.4 From state equations to the transfer function
docs.text:
Take Laplace transforms of the state equations with zero initial state: \(s\mathbf{X}(s) = A\mathbf{X}(s) + BU(s)\), so \((sI - A)\mathbf{X}(s) = BU(s)\) and

\[ H(s) = \frac{Y(s)}{U(s)} = C\,(sI - A)^{-1}B + D . \]

The inverse \((sI - A)^{-1}\) equals the adjugate of \(sI - A\) divided by its determinant, so the denominator of \(H(s)\) is \(\det(sI - A)\), the characteristic polynomial of \(A\). Hence:

Key idea

The poles of the transfer function are eigenvalues of \(A\). (Every pole is an eigenvalue; an eigenvalue can fail to appear as a pole only if it is cancelled by a zero, which happens when part of the state cannot be affected by the input or cannot be seen in the output.)

Example 13.3 Transfer function of the mass-spring-damper

With \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\):

\[ sI - A = \begin{bmatrix} s & -1 \\ 2 & s + 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad (sI - A)^{-1} = \frac{1}{s^2 + 3s + 2}\begin{bmatrix} s + 3 & 1 \\ -2 & s \end{bmatrix}. \]

Then \(C(sI - A)^{-1}B\) picks the \((1, 2)\) entry: \(H(s) = \dfrac{1}{s^2 + 3s + 2}\), as expected. The eigenvalues of \(A\) are the roots of \(s^2 + 3s + 2\), namely \(-1\) and \(-2\).

docs.title: 13.5 Solving the state equations
docs.text:
For a scalar equation \(\dot{x} = ax + bu\), the solution is \(x(t) = e^{at}x(0) + \int_0^te^{a(t - \tau)}bu(\tau)\,d\tau\). The matrix equation has the same solution with the matrix exponential in place of \(e^{at}\):

\[ \mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At}\mathbf{x}(0) + \int_0^t e^{A(t - \tau)}B\,u(\tau)\,d\tau , \]

where

\[ e^{At} = I + At + \frac{(At)^2}{2!} + \frac{(At)^3}{3!} + \cdots . \]

The first term is the zero-input response, the free motion from the initial state; the second is the zero-state response, a convolution of the input with \(e^{At}B\). The output is \(y = C\mathbf{x} + Du\), and the impulse response is \(h(t) = Ce^{At}B\,u(t) + D\delta(t)\).

There are two practical ways to compute \(e^{At}\):

  • By Laplace transform: \(e^{At}\) is the inverse transform of \((sI - A)^{-1}\), entry by entry.
  • By eigenvalues: if \(A = V\Lambda V^{-1}\) with distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\) on the diagonal of \(\Lambda\), then \(e^{At} = V\,\mathrm{diag}(e^{\lambda_it})\,V^{-1}\). Each entry of \(e^{At}\) is a combination of the modes \(e^{\lambda_it}\).

Example 13.4 Free response of the mass-spring-damper

Inverting the entries of \((sI - A)^{-1}\) from Example 13.3 by partial fractions:

\[ e^{At} = \begin{bmatrix} 2e^{-t} - e^{-2t} & e^{-t} - e^{-2t} \\ -2e^{-t} + 2e^{-2t} & -e^{-t} + 2e^{-2t} \end{bmatrix}. \]

At \(t = 0\) this is the identity, as it must be. Released from \(y = 1\) at rest, \(\mathbf{x}(0) = [1, 0]^T\), the position is the first entry of \(e^{At}\mathbf{x}(0)\): \(y(t) = 2e^{-t} - e^{-2t}\). It starts at 1 with zero slope and decays without oscillating, because both modes are real.

docs.title: Stability
docs.text: Since every entry of \(e^{At}\) is a combination of the modes \(e^{\lambda_it}\) (times powers of \(t\) for repeated eigenvalues), the free response decays to zero from every initial state if and only if every eigenvalue of \(A\) has a negative real part. This internal stability implies BIBO stability; the converse fails only when an unstable mode is hidden by a pole-zero cancellation, which is precisely the kind of danger that the state-space view exposes and the transfer function conceals.

docs.title: 13.6 Discrete-time state equations
docs.text:
A DT LTI system has the state equations

\[ \mathbf{x}[n + 1] = A\,\mathbf{x}[n] + B\,u[n], \qquad y[n] = C\,\mathbf{x}[n] + D\,u[n]. \]

They need no calculus: starting from \(\mathbf{x}[0]\), iterate. The solution is

\[ \mathbf{x}[n] = A^n\mathbf{x}[0] + \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}A^{n-1-k}B\,u[k], \]

the transfer function is \(H(z) = C(zI - A)^{-1}B + D\), and the system is internally stable if and only if every eigenvalue of \(A\) lies strictly inside the unit circle, because the free response is built from the modes \(\lambda_i^n\).

Any difference equation can be put in this form; the delay elements of a block diagram hold the state, just as integrators do in continuous time.

docs.title: Exact discretisation
docs.text:
Digital controllers and simulators update a continuous system every \(T\) seconds, holding the input constant in between (a zero-order hold, Section 9.4). Over one interval, the CT solution with constant \(u\) gives exactly

\[ \mathbf{x}[n+1] = A_d\,\mathbf{x}[n] + B_d\,u[n], \qquad A_d = e^{AT}, \qquad B_d = \left(\int_0^Te^{A\tau}\,d\tau\right)B , \]

where \(\mathbf{x}[n] = \mathbf{x}(nT)\). When \(A\) is invertible, \(B_d = A^{-1}(e^{AT} - I)B\). The eigenvalues of \(A_d\) are \(e^{\lambda_iT}\): the mapping \(z = e^{sT}\) of Chapter 11 once more, sending stable CT modes to stable DT modes. Unlike a crude approximation such as Euler's method (\(A_d \approx I + AT\)), this discretisation is exact at the sampling instants for any \(T\).

docs.title: 13.7 A first look at state feedback
docs.text:
If all the state variables can be measured, the input can be computed from them: \(u = -K\mathbf{x} + r\), where \(K\) is a row of gains and \(r\) a reference input. Substituting into the state equation,

\[ \dot{\mathbf{x}} = (A - BK)\,\mathbf{x} + B\,r . \]

The closed-loop dynamics are governed by the eigenvalues of \(A - BK\), and for a system in controllable canonical form (or any controllable system, one whose every state can be steered by the input) the gains can place these eigenvalues anywhere we like.

Example 13.5 Placing the poles of a double integrator

A mass with no spring or damping, pushed by a force, obeys \(\ddot{y} = u\) (with \(m = 1\)). With \(\mathbf{x} = [y, \dot{y}]^T\), \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Both eigenvalues are 0: left alone, the mass drifts.

With \(K = [k_1, k_2]\), \(A - BK = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -k_1 & -k_2 \end{bmatrix}\), whose characteristic polynomial is \(s^2 + k_2s + k_1\). To place the poles at \(-2 \pm 2j\), match \(s^2 + 4s + 8\): \(k_1 = 8\), \(k_2 = 4\). The controller pushes back in proportion to the position (a virtual spring) and to the velocity (a virtual damper), giving \(\omega_n = \sqrt8\) and \(\zeta = 1/\sqrt2\).

When not every state can be measured, an observer estimates the state from the output; the dual notion of observability (whether the state can be deduced from the output) decides when this is possible. These topics belong to a course in control, and Chapter 14 shows the setting in which they are used.

docs.title: 13.8 State-space computations in NumPy
docs.text:
The program below builds the model of Example 13.1, checks its eigenvalues and transfer function, discretises it exactly with \(T = 0.1\) s, simulates the step response, and compares the result with the formula \(y(t) = \frac12 - e^{-t} + \frac12e^{-2t}\) of Example 10.9. Finally it checks the pole placement of Example 13.5.

import numpy as np

# Mass-spring-damper y'' + 3y' + 2y = u as a state-space model, x = [y, y']
A = np.array([[0.0, 1.0], [-2.0, -3.0]])
B = np.array([[0.0], [1.0]])
C = np.array([[1.0, 0.0]])
D = 0.0

print("eigenvalues of A:", np.linalg.eigvals(A))

# Transfer function C (sI - A)^-1 B + D at s = 2j, compared with 1 / (s^2 + 3s + 2)
s = 2j
H = (C @ np.linalg.solve(s * np.eye(2) - A, B))[0, 0] + D
print("H(j2) from state space:", np.round(H, 4), "  from formula:", np.round(1 / (s**2 + 3 * s + 2), 4))

def expm(M):
    """Matrix exponential by eigen-decomposition (fine when M has distinct eigenvalues)."""
    w, V = np.linalg.eig(M)
    return (V @ np.diag(np.exp(w)) @ np.linalg.inv(V)).real

# Exact discretisation for a piecewise-constant input (zero-order hold), T = 0.1 s
T = 0.1
Ad = expm(A * T)
Bd = np.linalg.solve(A, Ad - np.eye(2)) @ B          # A^-1 (e^{AT} - I) B
print("Ad =", np.round(Ad, 5).tolist())
print("Bd =", np.round(Bd.ravel(), 5).tolist())

# Step response by iterating x[n+1] = Ad x[n] + Bd u[n], against y(t) = 1/2 - e^-t + e^-2t / 2
x = np.zeros((2, 1))
ys = []
for n in range(51):
    ys.append((C @ x)[0, 0])
    x = Ad @ x + Bd * 1.0
for t in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0):
    exact = 0.5 - np.exp(-t) + 0.5 * np.exp(-2 * t)
    print(f"t = {t:3.1f}: simulated {ys[int(round(t / T))]:.6f}, exact {exact:.6f}")

# State feedback u = -K x on the double integrator y'' = u: place poles at -2 +/- 2j
A2 = np.array([[0.0, 1.0], [0.0, 0.0]])
K = np.array([[8.0, 4.0]])                            # from s^2 + 4s + 8
print("closed-loop eigenvalues:", np.linalg.eigvals(A2 - B @ K))

eigenvalues of A: [-1.+0.j -2.+0.j]
H(j2) from state space: (-0.05-0.15j)   from formula: (-0.05-0.15j)
Ad = [[0.99094, 0.08611], [-0.17221, 0.73262]]
Bd = [0.00453, 0.08611]
t = 0.5: simulated 0.077409, exact 0.077409
t = 1.0: simulated 0.199788, exact 0.199788
t = 2.0: simulated 0.373823, exact 0.373823
t = 5.0: simulated 0.493285, exact 0.493285
closed-loop eigenvalues: [-2.+2.j -2.-2.j]

The simulated and exact values agree to all six decimals, because the discretisation is exact for a step input, which is constant between samples. The eigen-decomposition expm is adequate here; for general matrices (repeated eigenvalues, or nearly so) use scipy.linalg.expm, which is numerically robust.

docs.title: 13.9 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • The state is the smallest set of variables that, with future inputs, fixes the future; physically, the energy stores.
  • CT state equations \(\dot{\mathbf{x}} = A\mathbf{x} + Bu\), \(y = C\mathbf{x} + Du\); DT state equations \(\mathbf{x}[n+1] = A\mathbf{x}[n] + Bu[n]\).
  • A transfer function can be realised in controllable canonical form; realisations are not unique (\(TAT^{-1}\), \(TB\), \(CT^{-1}\)).
  • \(H(s) = C(sI - A)^{-1}B + D\); the poles are eigenvalues of \(A\).
  • \(\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At}\mathbf{x}(0) + \int_0^te^{A(t-\tau)}Bu(\tau)d\tau\); the modes are \(e^{\lambda_it}\). Internal stability: all eigenvalues in the left half-plane (CT) or inside the unit circle (DT).
  • Exact ZOH discretisation: \(A_d = e^{AT}\), \(B_d = A^{-1}(e^{AT} - I)B\); eigenvalues map by \(z = e^{sT}\).
  • State feedback \(u = -K\mathbf{x} + r\) moves the eigenvalues to those of \(A - BK\).

docs.title: 13.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 13.1

Write state equations for \(\ddot{y} + 5\dot{y} + 6y = 2u\) with \(x_1 = y\), \(x_2 = \dot{y}\).

Answer

\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -6 & -5 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\), \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), \(D = 0\).

Exercise 13.2

Find the eigenvalues of the \(A\) in Exercise 13.1 and decide stability.

Answer

\(\det(sI - A) = s^2 + 5s + 6 = (s + 2)(s + 3)\): eigenvalues \(-2\) and \(-3\). Stable.

Exercise 13.3

Give a controllable canonical realisation of \(H(s) = \dfrac{s + 4}{s^2 + 2s + 10}\).

Answer

\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -10 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(D = 0\).

Exercise 13.4

Compute \(H(s)\) for \(A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), \(D = 0\).

Answer

\(A\) is diagonal, so \((sI - A)^{-1} = \mathrm{diag}\left(\frac{1}{s+1}, \frac{1}{s+4}\right)\) and \(H(s) = \frac{2}{s + 1} + \frac{3}{s + 4} = \frac{5s + 11}{(s + 1)(s + 4)}\).

Exercise 13.5

For the diagonal \(A\) of Exercise 13.4, write \(e^{At}\) and the free response from \(\mathbf{x}(0) = [1, -1]^T\), with output \(y = C\mathbf{x}\).

Answer

\(e^{At} = \mathrm{diag}(e^{-t}, e^{-4t})\), so \(\mathbf{x}(t) = [e^{-t}, -e^{-4t}]^T\) and \(y(t) = 2e^{-t} - 3e^{-4t}\).

Exercise 13.6

A DT system has \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0.8 \end{bmatrix}\). Is it stable?

Answer

\(A\) is triangular, so its eigenvalues are 0.5 and 0.8, both inside the unit circle: stable.

Exercise 13.7

Iterate \(\mathbf{x}[n+1] = A\mathbf{x}[n]\) with \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -0.5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) from \(\mathbf{x}[0] = [1, 0]^T\) for two steps.

Answer

\(\mathbf{x}[1] = [0, -0.5]^T\); \(\mathbf{x}[2] = [-0.5, -0.5]^T\).

Exercise 13.8

A scalar CT system \(\dot{x} = -2x + u\) is discretised with \(T = 0.5\) s and a zero-order hold. Find \(A_d\) and \(B_d\).

Answer

\(A_d = e^{-1} \approx 0.368\); \(B_d = \frac{e^{-1} - 1}{-2} = \frac{1 - e^{-1}}{2} \approx 0.316\).

Exercise 13.9

For the double integrator of Example 13.5, find the gains that place both closed-loop poles at \(-3\).

Answer

Match \(s^2 + k_2s + k_1 = (s + 3)^2 = s^2 + 6s + 9\): \(k_1 = 9\), \(k_2 = 6\).

Exercise 13.10

Show that the similarity transformation \(\mathbf{z} = T\mathbf{x}\) does not change the transfer function.

Answer

\(CT^{-1}(sI - TAT^{-1})^{-1}TB = CT^{-1}\left[T(sI - A)T^{-1}\right]^{-1}TB = CT^{-1}T(sI - A)^{-1}T^{-1}TB = C(sI - A)^{-1}B\).

docs.title: 13.11 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 13

Exercise 1

For a mass on a spring, a suitable state is

  1. position and velocity
  2. force and mass
  3. position only
  4. acceleration only
Answer

position and velocity

Exercise 2

The poles of H(s) = C(sI − A)⁻¹B + D are

  1. eigenvalues of A
  2. entries of B
  3. zeros of C
  4. always real
Answer

eigenvalues of A

Exercise 3

How many state variables does a series RLC circuit need?

Answer

2 / two

One for each energy store: the capacitor voltage and the inductor current.

Exercise 4

A discrete-time state-space system is stable when every eigenvalue of A

  1. lies inside the unit circle
  2. has negative real part
  3. is real
  4. equals 1
Answer

lies inside the unit circle

Exercise 5

With state feedback u = −Kx + r, the closed-loop dynamics are set by the eigenvalues of

  1. A − BK
  2. A + K
  3. BK
  4. C − K
Answer

A − BK

Exercise 6

The exact discretisation of ẋ = Ax + Bu with a zero-order hold has A_d = e^(___).

Answer

AT / A T

Exercise 7

What is e^(At) at t = 0?

Answer

I / the identity / identity matrix / the identity matrix

docs.title: Chapter 3: Systems and Their Properties
docs.text:
Memory, causality, stability, invertibility, time invariance and linearity, and how to test for each

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • describe a system by an input-output rule, a block diagram, or a differential or difference equation;
  • combine systems in series, in parallel and with feedback;
  • decide whether a given system is memoryless, causal, BIBO stable, invertible, time-invariant and linear, giving a proof or a counterexample;
  • compute the output of a simple recursive difference equation by iteration from rest.

docs.title: 3.1 What a system is
docs.text:
A system transforms an input signal \(x\) into an output signal \(y\). We write

\[ y(t) = T\{x(t)\} \qquad\text{or}\qquad y[n] = T\{x[n]\}, \]

where \(T\) stands for the rule. The notation is a little loose: \(T\{x(t)\}\) means "apply \(T\) to the whole signal \(x\), then read the result at time \(t\)". The output at one instant may depend on the input at many instants.

A continuous-time system has CT input and output: an electric circuit, a mechanical suspension, a loudspeaker. A discrete-time system has DT input and output: a program that processes a list of samples. Mixed systems exist too: a sampler takes a CT input and produces a DT output, and Chapter 9 studies it.

Systems are described in several ways, and a skilled engineer moves between them easily:

  • by an explicit formula, such as \(y(t) = x(t - 2)\) or \(y[n] = \frac{1}{3}(x[n] + x[n-1] + x[n-2])\);
  • by a differential equation (CT) or difference equation (DT) that relates the output and its derivatives or past values to the input, such as \(RC\,\frac{dy}{dt} + y = x\);
  • by a block diagram made of simple parts: gains, adders, integrators, delays;
  • by the response to one special input, the impulse, from which (for the systems of Chapter 4) everything else follows;
  • by a frequency response or a transfer function (Chapters 5 to 12).

Some simple systems recur so often that they deserve names. The identity \(y = x\). The ideal delay \(y(t) = x(t - t_0)\) or \(y[n] = x[n - n_0]\). The amplifier \(y = Kx\). The integrator \(y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{t} x(\tau)\,d\tau\) and its discrete partner the accumulator \(y[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{n} x[k]\). The differentiator \(y = dx/dt\) and the first difference \(y[n] = x[n] - x[n-1]\). The moving average \(y[n] = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{k=0}^{M-1}x[n-k]\).

docs.title: 3.2 Interconnections of systems
docs.text:
Large systems are built from small ones joined in three standard ways (Figure 3.1).

Figure 3.1 Interconnections. Three interconnections. Series: x passes through T₁ to give w, which passes through T₂ to give y. Parallel: x feeds T₁ and T₂ and their outputs are added. Feedback: the output y passes through T₂ and is subtracted from the input before entering T₁.
  • Series (or cascade): the output of \(T_1\) is the input of \(T_2\), so \(y = T_2\{T_1\{x\}\}\). A microphone preamplifier followed by an equaliser.
  • Parallel: the same input drives both systems and their outputs are added, \(y = T_1\{x\} + T_2\{x\}\). A loudspeaker crossover splits the signal into bass and treble paths.
  • Feedback: the output is passed back through \(T_2\) and subtracted from the input, so that \(T_1\) acts on the error \(e = x - T_2\{y\}\). Feedback is the basis of control: a thermostat compares the room temperature with the setting and drives the heater with the difference.

In general the order of a series connection matters: \(T_2\{T_1\{x\}\}\) need not equal \(T_1\{T_2\{x\}\}\). For instance, squaring and then adding 1 gives \(x^2 + 1\); adding 1 and then squaring gives \((x+1)^2\). Chapter 4 shows that for linear time-invariant systems the order does not matter, a fact used constantly in practice.

docs.title: 3.3 Memory
docs.text:
A system is memoryless (or static) if the output at each time depends only on the input at the same time. Otherwise it has memory (it is dynamic).

  • \(y(t) = 3x(t)\), \(y(t) = x^2(t)\) and \(y[n] = \cos(x[n])\) are memoryless.
  • \(y[n] = x[n-1]\), \(y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{t}x(\tau)\,d\tau\) and \(y[n] = x[n] + x[n+1]\) have memory.

A resistor is memoryless: its current depends on the present voltage. A capacitor has memory: its voltage depends on all the current that has flowed into it in the past. A system with memory needs some kind of storage, physical (charge on a capacitor, the position of a mass) or digital (a delay register).

docs.title: 3.4 Causality
docs.text:
A system is causal if the output at any time depends only on the input at the present time and in the past, never in the future. Equivalently, if two inputs agree up to time \(t_0\), the outputs of a causal system also agree up to time \(t_0\).

  • \(y[n] = x[n] - x[n-1]\) is causal.
  • \(y[n] = x[n+1] - x[n]\) is not causal: to compute \(y[0]\) we need \(x[1]\).
  • \(y(t) = x(-t)\) is not causal: \(y(-2) = x(2)\) depends on the future. (For \(t > 0\) it uses the past, but one counterexample is enough.)
  • \(y(t) = x(t)\cos(t+1)\) is causal: the factor \(\cos(t+1)\) is not the input, just a known function of time.
  • Every memoryless system is causal.

Physical systems that work in real time are causal: no circuit can respond to a voltage before it is applied. Non-causal systems are still useful when the whole signal is recorded before processing, as when smoothing yesterday's measurements or processing a photograph, where the "independent variable" is position and has no past or future.

docs.title: 3.5 Stability
docs.text:
Many definitions of stability exist. The one used for signals and systems is bounded-input, bounded-output (BIBO) stability: a system is BIBO stable if every bounded input produces a bounded output. In symbols, if \(|x(t)| \le B_x < \infty\) for all \(t\), then there must be a finite \(B_y\) with \(|y(t)| \le B_y\) for all \(t\).

To prove stability, assume a bound on the input and derive one on the output. To disprove it, find one bounded input whose output is unbounded.

Example 3.1 Testing stability

(a) \(y[n] = \frac{1}{3}(x[n] + x[n-1] + x[n-2])\). If \(|x[n]| \le B\) then \(|y[n]| \le \frac{1}{3}(B + B + B) = B\). Stable.

(b) The accumulator \(y[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{n}x[k]\). Take the bounded input \(x[n] = u[n]\). The output is \(y[n] = (n+1)u[n]\), which grows without limit. Unstable.

(c) \(y(t) = e^{x(t)}\). If \(|x(t)| \le B\) then \(|y(t)| \le e^{B}\). Stable, although nonlinear.

(d) \(y(t) = t\,x(t)\). The bounded input \(x(t) = 1\) gives \(y(t) = t\), unbounded. Unstable.

Stable is not the same as 'output usually bounded'

The integrator gives a bounded output for many inputs, such as a short pulse. That does not make it stable. BIBO stability demands a bounded output for every bounded input, so a single bad input (here the step) settles the question.

docs.title: 3.6 Invertibility
docs.text:
A system is invertible if distinct inputs always give distinct outputs. Then there is an inverse system \(T^{-1}\) that recovers the input: \(T^{-1}\{T\{x\}\} = x\).

  • \(y(t) = 2x(t)\) is invertible; the inverse is \(x(t) = \frac{1}{2}y(t)\).
  • The accumulator \(y[n] = \sum_{k\le n}x[k]\) is invertible; the inverse is the first difference \(x[n] = y[n] - y[n-1]\).
  • \(y(t) = x^2(t)\) is not invertible: \(x\) and \(-x\) give the same output.
  • \(y[n] = x[2n]\) (decimation) is not invertible: the odd samples are lost.
  • \(y(t) = 0\) for every input is not invertible.

Invertibility matters in communications, where a receiver tries to undo the distortion of the channel (equalisation), and in measurement, where an instrument's own response is removed from a recording (deconvolution).

docs.title: 3.7 Time invariance
docs.text:
A system is time-invariant if delaying the input simply delays the output by the same amount, and changes nothing else. A resistor behaves the same today and tomorrow; a battery that is running down does not.

Formally: let \(y(t) = T\{x(t)\}\). Feed the system the delayed input \(x_1(t) = x(t - t_0)\) and call its response \(y_1(t)\). The system is time-invariant if, for every input and every \(t_0\),

\[ y_1(t) = y(t - t_0). \]

The test has three steps, and it pays to write them out every time:

  1. Compute the response \(y_1\) to the shifted input \(x(t - t_0)\): substitute \(x(t - t_0)\) for every occurrence of the input, but leave the explicit \(t\) alone.
  2. Compute the shifted output \(y(t - t_0)\): replace every \(t\) in the formula for \(y(t)\) by \(t - t_0\).
  3. Compare.

Example 3.2 Testing time invariance

(a) \(y(t) = \sin(x(t))\). Step 1: \(y_1(t) = \sin(x(t - t_0))\). Step 2: \(y(t - t_0) = \sin(x(t - t_0))\). Equal: time-invariant.

(b) \(y[n] = n\,x[n]\). Step 1: \(y_1[n] = n\,x[n - n_0]\). Step 2: \(y[n - n_0] = (n - n_0)\,x[n - n_0]\). Different: time-varying. The gain \(n\) grows with time, so the same input applied later is amplified more.

(c) \(y(t) = x(2t)\). Step 1: the input \(x_1(t) = x(t - t_0)\) gives \(y_1(t) = x_1(2t) = x(2t - t_0)\). Step 2: \(y(t - t_0) = x(2(t - t_0)) = x(2t - 2t_0)\). Different: time-varying. A compressor squeezes delays as well as the signal.

(d) \(y(t) = x(-t)\). Step 1: \(y_1(t) = x_1(-t) = x(-t - t_0)\). Step 2: \(y(t - t_0) = x(-(t - t_0)) = x(-t + t_0)\). Different: time-varying. Reflection turns a delay into an advance.

Cases (c) and (d) catch many students. In step 1 the new input \(x_1\) replaces the old one, and the system's rule ("evaluate the input at \(2t\)") is then applied to \(x_1\): \(x_1(2t) = x(2t - t_0)\), not \(x(2(t - t_0))\).

A useful shortcut: a system is time-varying if time appears explicitly in its formula outside the argument of the input (as the \(n\) in \(n\,x[n]\) or the \(\cos t\) in \(x(t)\cos t\)), or if the argument of the input is anything other than \(t\) minus a constant (as in \(x(2t)\), \(x(-t)\), \(x(t^2)\)).

docs.title: 3.8 Linearity
docs.text:
A system is linear if it obeys the principle of superposition: the response to a weighted sum of inputs is the same weighted sum of the individual responses. If \(x_1 \mapsto y_1\) and \(x_2 \mapsto y_2\), then for all constants \(a\) and \(b\)

\[ a\,x_1 + b\,x_2 \;\mapsto\; a\,y_1 + b\,y_2 . \]

The condition combines two simpler ones: additivity (\(x_1 + x_2 \mapsto y_1 + y_2\)) and homogeneity or scaling (\(a x_1 \mapsto a y_1\)). Linearity is the property that makes analysis possible: if we can split a complicated input into simple pieces whose responses we know, we can add the responses.

A quick necessary condition follows from homogeneity with \(a = 0\): a linear system must give zero output for zero input. If the zero input gives a non-zero output, the system is not linear.

Example 3.3 Testing linearity

(a) \(y[n] = n\,x[n]\). The input \(a x_1 + b x_2\) gives \(n(a x_1[n] + b x_2[n]) = a\,n x_1[n] + b\,n x_2[n] = a y_1 + b y_2\). Linear (though time-varying).

(b) \(y(t) = x^2(t)\). The input \(a x_1\) gives \(a^2x_1^2 \ne a\,x_1^2\) in general. Nonlinear.

(c) \(y[n] = 2x[n] + 3\). Zero input gives \(y = 3 \ne 0\). Nonlinear. Such a system is called incrementally linear: the difference between two outputs depends linearly on the difference between the inputs. It is a linear system plus a constant offset.

(d) \(y(t) = \mathrm{Re}\{x(t)\}\) for complex inputs. Additive, but scaling by \(a = j\) fails: the input \(jx\) with \(x = 1\) gives \(\mathrm{Re}\{j\} = 0\), while \(j\,\mathrm{Re}\{1\} = j\). Nonlinear over complex inputs. Additivity alone is not enough.

docs.title: Linearity and initial conditions
docs.text: A circuit with a charged capacitor gives an output even when its input is zero. Is it linear? By the strict test above, no. The standard way out is to split the output of such a system into two parts: the zero-input response, due to the initial stored energy alone, and the zero-state response, due to the input with all initial conditions zero. Each part is linear in its own cause. Throughout most of this book we assume that systems are initially at rest: no stored energy before the input starts. Then the output is the zero-state response and the system is linear in the strict sense.

Systems that are both linear and time-invariant (LTI) occupy the rest of this book. They are not the only systems that matter, but they are the ones for which a complete theory exists, and many real systems are LTI to a good approximation over their normal range of operation.

docs.title: 3.10 Systems described by differential and difference equations
docs.text:
Most physical LTI systems are described by linear constant-coefficient differential equations. A resistor \(R\) in series with a capacitor \(C\), driven by a voltage \(x(t)\), has a capacitor voltage \(y(t)\) satisfying

\[ RC\,\frac{dy(t)}{dt} + y(t) = x(t). \]

The general form for a CT system of order \(N\) is

\[ \sum_{k=0}^{N} a_k\,\frac{d^k y(t)}{dt^k} = \sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k\,\frac{d^k x(t)}{dt^k}. \]

The DT counterpart is the linear constant-coefficient difference equation

\[ \sum_{k=0}^{N} a_k\,y[n - k] = \sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k\,x[n - k]. \]

An equation alone does not fix the output: we also need auxiliary conditions, such as the initial values of the output. With the condition of initial rest (if \(x\) is zero before some time, so is \(y\)) such a system is linear, time-invariant and causal. Chapters 10 and 11 solve these equations systematically with the Laplace and z-transforms; here we look at the discrete case, which can be solved by plain arithmetic.

docs.title: Solving a difference equation by iteration
docs.text:
A difference equation with \(a_0 \ne 0\) can be rearranged to give the present output in terms of past outputs and inputs:

\[ y[n] = \frac{1}{a_0}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k\,x[n-k] - \sum_{k=1}^{N} a_k\,y[n-k]\right). \]

A system that uses past outputs is called recursive. Given the input and the starting values, we can compute \(y[0], y[1], y[2], \ldots\) one after another. This is exactly how a digital filter runs on a processor.

Example 3.4 Impulse response by iteration

Find the output of \(y[n] = x[n] + 0.5\,y[n-1]\) for \(x[n] = \delta[n]\), with the system initially at rest (\(y[n] = 0\) for \(n < 0\)).

\(n\) \(x[n]\) \(0.5\,y[n-1]\) \(y[n]\) 0 1 0 1 1 0 0.5 0.5 2 0 0.25 0.25 3 0 0.125 0.125

Table 3.2. Iterating the recursion.

The pattern is \(y[n] = (0.5)^n u[n]\). A single input sample produces an output that lasts forever, decaying geometrically. Such a system is said to have an infinite impulse response (IIR). The moving average, by contrast, has a finite impulse response (FIR): its response to \(\delta[n]\) is \(\frac13\) for \(n = 0, 1, 2\) and zero afterwards.

If the coefficient were 2 instead of 0.5, the response would be \(2^n u[n]\), which grows without bound: the system would be unstable. The size of the feedback coefficient decides stability, a theme that returns with the poles of Chapters 10 and 11.

docs.title: 3.11 Testing properties numerically
docs.text:
A computer cannot prove that a system is linear (that needs algebra), but it can quickly find a counterexample. The program below feeds random inputs to four systems and checks superposition and time invariance.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
L = 50
n = np.arange(L)

def delay(x, k):
    """Delay a finite sequence by k samples, filling with zeros."""
    return np.concatenate([np.zeros(k), x[:-k]])

systems = {
    "y[n] = x[n] + x[n-1]": lambda x: x + delay(x, 1),
    "y[n] = n x[n]":        lambda x: n * x,
    "y[n] = x[n]^2":        lambda x: x ** 2,
    "y[n] = 2 x[n] + 3":    lambda x: 2 * x + 3,
}

for name, T in systems.items():
    x1, x2 = rng.standard_normal(L), rng.standard_normal(L)
    x1[:5] = x2[:5] = 0            # start at rest so that delays are clean
    a, b = 2.0, -0.7
    linear = np.allclose(T(a * x1 + b * x2), a * T(x1) + b * T(x2))
    k = 3
    tinv = np.allclose(T(delay(x1, k))[k:], delay(T(x1), k)[k:])
    print(f"{name:22s} linear: {str(linear):5s}  time-invariant: {tinv}")

y[n] = x[n] + x[n-1]   linear: True   time-invariant: True
y[n] = n x[n]          linear: True   time-invariant: False
y[n] = x[n]^2          linear: False  time-invariant: True
y[n] = 2 x[n] + 3      linear: False  time-invariant: True

The results agree with Table 3.1. A "True" here means only that one random test passed; a "False" is a genuine counterexample.

docs.title: 3.12 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • A system maps an input signal to an output signal. It can be given by a formula, a differential or difference equation, a block diagram or (for LTI systems) its impulse or frequency response.
  • Systems combine in series, parallel and feedback.
  • Memoryless: output depends only on the present input. Causal: output never depends on future inputs. BIBO stable: every bounded input gives a bounded output. Invertible: distinct inputs give distinct outputs.
  • Time-invariant: a delayed input gives an equally delayed output. Test by comparing the response to \(x(t - t_0)\) with \(y(t - t_0)\). Explicit time factors, compression and reflection break time invariance.
  • Linear: superposition holds. Zero input must give zero output. A system with an offset is incrementally linear, not linear.
  • Linear constant-coefficient differential and difference equations with initial rest describe causal LTI systems. Recursive difference equations can be solved by iteration; their impulse response may last forever (IIR).

docs.title: 3.13 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 3.1

Is \(y[n] = x[n] + x[n - 2]\) memoryless? causal? stable?

Answer

It has memory (uses \(x[n-2]\)), it is causal (no future values) and it is stable (\(|y| \le 2B\)).

Exercise 3.2

Is \(y(t) = x(t/3)\) causal?

Answer

No. For negative \(t\), \(t/3 > t\); for example \(y(-3) = x(-1)\), a later value of the input. (For \(t > 0\) it uses past values, but one counterexample settles it.)

Exercise 3.3

Show that \(y(t) = x(t)\cos(\omega_c t)\) (a modulator) is linear but time-varying.

Answer

Linear: \((a x_1 + b x_2)\cos\omega_c t = a\,x_1\cos\omega_c t + b\,x_2\cos\omega_c t\). Time-varying: the response to \(x(t - t_0)\) is \(x(t - t_0)\cos\omega_c t\), but \(y(t - t_0) = x(t - t_0)\cos(\omega_c(t - t_0))\); these differ in general.

Exercise 3.4

Is \(y[n] = x[n]\,x[n-1]\) linear? time-invariant?

Answer

Nonlinear: doubling the input quadruples the output. Time-invariant: the response to \(x[n - n_0]\) is \(x[n - n_0]x[n - n_0 - 1] = y[n - n_0]\).

Exercise 3.5

Is \(y(t) = \int_{t-1}^{t} x(\tau)\,d\tau\) stable? Is it causal?

Answer

Stable: if \(|x| \le B\) then \(|y| \le \int_{t-1}^{t}B\,d\tau = B\). Causal: it uses the input only over the last second, up to the present.

Exercise 3.6

Find the inverse of the system \(y[n] = x[n] - 0.5\,x[n-1]\) in the form of a recursive equation.

Answer

Solve for \(x\): \(x[n] = y[n] + 0.5\,x[n-1]\). The inverse system takes \(y\) as input and produces \(x\) recursively. (Its impulse response is \((0.5)^n u[n]\), which is the system of Example 3.4.)

Exercise 3.7

Iterate \(y[n] = x[n] - 0.8\,y[n-1]\) from rest for \(x[n] = \delta[n]\), for \(n = 0, \ldots, 3\), and give the general term.

Answer

\(y[0] = 1\), \(y[1] = -0.8\), \(y[2] = 0.64\), \(y[3] = -0.512\). In general \(y[n] = (-0.8)^n u[n]\): a decaying, alternating response.

Exercise 3.8

Find the step response (the output for \(x[n] = u[n]\)) of \(y[n] = x[n] + 0.5\,y[n-1]\), from rest, for \(n = 0, 1, 2, 3\), and its limit as \(n \to \infty\).

Answer

\(y[0] = 1\), \(y[1] = 1.5\), \(y[2] = 1.75\), \(y[3] = 1.875\). In general \(y[n] = 2 - (0.5)^n\), which tends to 2. In steady state \(y = 1 + 0.5y\), so \(y = 2\).

Exercise 3.9

Two systems are each linear. Show that their series connection is linear.

Answer

\(T_2\{T_1\{a x_1 + b x_2\}\} = T_2\{a T_1\{x_1\} + b T_1\{x_2\}\} = a T_2\{T_1\{x_1\}\} + b T_2\{T_1\{x_2\}\}\), using the linearity of \(T_1\) and then of \(T_2\).

Exercise 3.10

Is the system \(y(t) = x(t) + 1\) invertible? Is it linear?

Answer

Invertible, with inverse \(x(t) = y(t) - 1\). Not linear: zero input gives output 1. It is incrementally linear.

docs.title: 3.14 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 3

Exercise 1

Which system is time-varying?

  1. y(t) = 3x(t − 1)
  2. y(t) = x(t)²
  3. y(t) = t x(t)
  4. y(t) = dx/dt
Answer

y(t) = t x(t)

The explicit factor t changes the gain over time.

Exercise 2

Which system is not BIBO stable?

  1. y[n] = x[n] − x[n−1]
  2. the accumulator y[n] = Σ x[k] for k ≤ n
  3. y(t) = e^(x(t))
  4. y(t) = cos(x(t))
Answer

the accumulator y[n] = Σ x[k] for k ≤ n

A unit step input gives a ramp output, which is unbounded.

Exercise 3

A system gives output 3 when the input is identically zero. It must be

  1. nonlinear
  2. non-causal
  3. unstable
  4. time-varying
Answer

nonlinear

A linear system maps zero input to zero output.

Exercise 4

y(t) = x(2t) is

  1. linear and time-invariant
  2. linear and time-varying
  3. nonlinear and time-invariant
  4. nonlinear and time-varying
Answer

linear and time-varying

Exercise 5

From rest, iterate y[n] = x[n] + 0.5 y[n−1] with x[n] = δ[n]. What is y[3]?

Answer

0.125 / 1/8

Exercise 6

A system whose output never depends on future input values is called ___.

Answer

causal

Exercise 7

Match each system with its inverse.

ABy = 4xfirst differenceaccumulatorx(t) = y(t + 2)y(t) = x(t − 2)x = y/4 Answer

y = 4x — x = y/4; accumulator — first difference; y(t) = x(t − 2) — x(t) = y(t + 2)
