docs.text:
The spectrum of an aperiodic signal, its properties, and filtering as multiplication

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • obtain the Fourier transform as the limit of the Fourier series of a periodic signal whose period grows without bound;
  • compute the transforms of the standard signals and use a table of pairs;
  • apply the properties (shift, scaling, duality, differentiation, convolution, modulation, Parseval) to find transforms without integrating;
  • use the frequency response \(H(j\omega)\) to find the output of an LTI system;
  • represent periodic signals by impulses in frequency, and explain the trade-off between duration and bandwidth.

docs.title: 6.1 From series to transform
docs.text:
The Fourier series describes periodic signals. Most signals of interest are not periodic: a spoken word, a radar pulse, the response of a circuit to a switch being closed. The trick for extending Fourier's idea to them is to regard an aperiodic signal as a periodic one whose period is infinitely long.

Take a pulse \(x(t)\) that is zero outside some interval, and build a periodic signal \(\tilde{x}(t)\) by repeating it every \(T_0\) seconds, with \(T_0\) long enough that the copies do not overlap. Its Fourier coefficients are

\[ a_k = \frac{1}{T_0}\int_{-T_0/2}^{T_0/2}\tilde{x}(t)\,e^{-jk\omega_0 t}\,dt = \frac{1}{T_0}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)\,e^{-jk\omega_0 t}\,dt , \]

because within one period \(\tilde{x}\) equals \(x\), and \(x\) is zero elsewhere. Define the function

\[ X(j\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)\,e^{-j\omega t}\,dt . \]

Then \(a_k = \frac{1}{T_0}X(jk\omega_0)\): the Fourier coefficients are samples of one fixed function, spaced \(\omega_0 = 2\pi/T_0\) apart, scaled by \(1/T_0\). We saw exactly this in Figure 5.1, where the coefficients of a pulse train sat on a sinc envelope. The synthesis equation becomes

\[ \tilde{x}(t) = \sum_k \frac{1}{T_0}X(jk\omega_0)\,e^{jk\omega_0 t} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_k X(jk\omega_0)\,e^{jk\omega_0 t}\,\omega_0 . \]

As \(T_0 \to \infty\), \(\tilde{x}\) becomes \(x\), the spacing \(\omega_0\) becomes an infinitesimal \(d\omega\), the samples \(k\omega_0\) become a continuous variable \(\omega\), and the sum becomes an integral. The result is the Fourier transform pair.

docs.title: 6.2 The Fourier transform pair
docs.text:
\[ X(j\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)\,e^{-j\omega t}\,dt \qquad\text{(analysis, or forward transform)} \] \[ x(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} X(j\omega)\,e^{j\omega t}\,d\omega \qquad\text{(synthesis, or inverse transform)} \]

We write \(x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)\). The function \(X(j\omega)\) is the spectrum of \(x\). The synthesis equation says that \(x\) is a continuous superposition of complex exponentials \(e^{j\omega t}\); the amount at frequency \(\omega\) is \(\frac{1}{2\pi}X(j\omega)\,d\omega\). Unlike the line spectrum of a periodic signal, the spectrum of an aperiodic signal is spread continuously over frequency, and \(X(j\omega)\) is a density: it has the units of the signal multiplied by time.

The notation \(X(j\omega)\), rather than \(X(\omega)\), is chosen to match the Laplace transform \(X(s)\) of Chapter 10, which equals the Fourier transform on the line \(s = j\omega\). Some books use the frequency \(f\) in hertz instead of \(\omega\); then \(X(f) = \int x(t)e^{-j2\pi ft}dt\) and \(x(t) = \int X(f)e^{j2\pi ft}df\), with no \(2\pi\) in front. The two conventions are related by \(\omega = 2\pi f\). Formulas in this book use \(\omega\).

Existence. The transform exists (as an ordinary function) if \(x\) is absolutely integrable, \(\int|x(t)|\,dt < \infty\), and satisfies Dirichlet-type conditions like those of Section 5.5. It also exists, in the energy sense, for every finite-energy signal. Signals such as constants, sinusoids and the step are neither absolutely integrable nor of finite energy, but they have transforms if we allow impulses in frequency (Section 6.6). Growing signals such as \(e^{t}u(t)\) have no Fourier transform; for them we need the Laplace transform.

docs.title: 6.3 Standard transform pairs
docs.text:
Example 6.1 The decaying exponential

For \(x(t) = e^{-at}u(t)\) with \(a > 0\):

\[ X(j\omega) = \int_0^{\infty}e^{-at}e^{-j\omega t}dt = \left[\frac{-e^{-(a + j\omega)t}}{a + j\omega}\right]_0^{\infty} = \frac{1}{a + j\omega}. \]

The upper limit vanishes because \(|e^{-(a+j\omega)t}| = e^{-at} \to 0\). The magnitude and phase are

\[ |X(j\omega)| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^2 + \omega^2}}, \qquad \angle X(j\omega) = -\arctan\frac{\omega}{a}. \]

The magnitude is largest at \(\omega = 0\) and falls to \(1/\sqrt2\) of its peak at \(\omega = a\); the phase goes from \(0\) to \(-\pi/2\) (Figure 6.1). A faster decay (larger \(a\)) means a wider spectrum.

Figure 6.1 Transform of a decaying exponential. Magnitude (left) and phase (right) of the transform of e^(−at)u(t). The magnitude peaks at 1/a at ω = 0 and falls to 0.707/a at ω = ±a. The phase falls from π/2 to −π/2, passing −π/4 at ω = a.

Example 6.2 The rectangular pulse

For a pulse of height 1 and width \(\tau\) centred at the origin, \(x(t) = \mathrm{rect}(t/\tau)\):

\[ X(j\omega) = \int_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2}e^{-j\omega t}dt = \frac{e^{j\omega\tau/2} - e^{-j\omega\tau/2}}{j\omega} = \frac{2\sin(\omega\tau/2)}{\omega} = \tau\,\mathrm{sinc}\!\left(\frac{\omega\tau}{2\pi}\right). \]

The spectrum is real (the pulse is real and even), equal to \(\tau\) (the pulse area) at \(\omega = 0\), and zero at \(\omega = 2\pi m/\tau\) for every non-zero integer \(m\). The main lobe extends from \(-2\pi/\tau\) to \(2\pi/\tau\), so its width is inversely proportional to the pulse width.

Figure 6.2 The pulse and the sinc. A rectangular pulse of width τ (left) and its Fourier transform, a sinc function with peak τ at ω = 0 and zeros at every non-zero multiple of 2π/τ (right).

Example 6.3 The impulse

\(\delta(t) \leftrightarrow \int\delta(t)e^{-j\omega t}dt = 1\). An impulse contains every frequency in equal amount. This is why striking a system with a hammer (an approximate impulse) reveals its whole frequency response, and why a lightning flash causes crackles across the whole radio band.

Table 6.1 collects the pairs used most often. The entries with impulses in frequency are justified in Section 6.6.

\(x(t)\) \(X(j\omega)\) Condition \(\delta(t)\) \(1\) \(\delta(t - t_0)\) \(e^{-j\omega t_0}\) \(1\) \(2\pi\delta(\omega)\) \(e^{j\omega_0 t}\) \(2\pi\delta(\omega - \omega_0)\) \(\cos\omega_0 t\) \(\pi[\delta(\omega - \omega_0) + \delta(\omega + \omega_0)]\) \(\sin\omega_0 t\) \(\dfrac{\pi}{j}[\delta(\omega - \omega_0) - \delta(\omega + \omega_0)]\) \(u(t)\) \(\dfrac{1}{j\omega} + \pi\delta(\omega)\) \(\mathrm{sgn}(t)\) \(\dfrac{2}{j\omega}\) \(e^{-at}u(t)\) \(\dfrac{1}{a + j\omega}\) \(a > 0\) \(t\,e^{-at}u(t)\) \(\dfrac{1}{(a + j\omega)^2}\) \(a > 0\) \(e^{-a\lvert t\rvert}\) \(\dfrac{2a}{a^2 + \omega^2}\) \(a > 0\) \(\mathrm{rect}(t/\tau)\) \(\tau\,\mathrm{sinc}(\omega\tau/2\pi)\) \(\dfrac{\sin Wt}{\pi t}\) \(1\) for \(\lvert\omega\rvert < W\), \(0\) otherwise \(e^{-t^2/(2\sigma^2)}\) \(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}\,e^{-\sigma^2\omega^2/2}\) \(\sigma > 0\) \(\sum_n \delta(t - nT)\) \(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}\sum_k\delta\!\left(\omega - \dfrac{2\pi k}{T}\right)\)

Table 6.1. Common Fourier transform pairs.

The Gaussian is special: its transform is another Gaussian. It is the signal with the smallest possible product of duration and bandwidth (Section 6.7). The last row, the impulse train, transforms into another impulse train; it is the mathematical heart of sampling (Chapter 9).

docs.title: 6.4 Properties of the Fourier transform
docs.text:
The properties are the working tools of Fourier analysis. With a short table of pairs and the properties below, most transforms can be found without integrating. Let \(x \leftrightarrow X\) and \(y \leftrightarrow Y\).

Property Signal Transform Linearity \(ax(t) + by(t)\) \(aX(j\omega) + bY(j\omega)\) Time shift \(x(t - t_0)\) \(e^{-j\omega t_0}X(j\omega)\) Frequency shift \(e^{j\omega_0 t}x(t)\) \(X(j(\omega - \omega_0))\) Time scaling \(x(at)\) \(\dfrac{1}{\lvert a\rvert}X\!\left(\dfrac{j\omega}{a}\right)\) Time reversal \(x(-t)\) \(X(-j\omega)\) Conjugation \(x^*(t)\) \(X^*(-j\omega)\) Duality \(X(jt)\) \(2\pi\,x(-\omega)\) Differentiation in time \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}\) \(j\omega\,X(j\omega)\) Integration \(\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{t}x(\tau)\,d\tau\) \(\dfrac{X(j\omega)}{j\omega} + \pi X(0)\delta(\omega)\) Differentiation in frequency \(t\,x(t)\) \(j\dfrac{dX(j\omega)}{d\omega}\) Convolution \(x(t) * y(t)\) \(X(j\omega)\,Y(j\omega)\) Multiplication \(x(t)\,y(t)\) \(\dfrac{1}{2\pi}X(j\omega) * Y(j\omega)\) Real signal \(x\) real \(X(-j\omega) = X^*(j\omega)\) Parseval \(\displaystyle\int\lvert x(t)\rvert^2dt\) \(\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\displaystyle\int\lvert X(j\omega)\rvert^2d\omega\)

Table 6.2. Properties of the continuous-time Fourier transform.

A few deserve comment.

Time shift. Delaying a signal does not change \(|X|\); it adds a phase \(-\omega t_0\), a straight line through the origin with slope \(-t_0\). A system that delays all frequencies equally therefore has linear phase, a property prized in audio and data transmission because it preserves the shape of waveforms.

Scaling. Compressing a signal in time (\(a > 1\)) stretches its spectrum in frequency and lowers it. Playing a recording at double speed raises every pitch by an octave. This is the first sign of the time-bandwidth trade-off: a signal cannot be both short and narrow-band.

Duality. The forward and inverse transforms differ only in the sign of the exponent and the factor \(2\pi\), so every pair has a dual. Since \(\mathrm{rect}(t/\tau) \leftrightarrow \tau\,\mathrm{sinc}(\omega\tau/2\pi)\), a sinc in time has a rectangular spectrum: that is the pair \(\frac{\sin Wt}{\pi t} \leftrightarrow\) (1 for \(|\omega| < W\)) in Table 6.1. Since \(\delta(t) \leftrightarrow 1\), the constant \(1 \leftrightarrow 2\pi\delta(\omega)\).

Real signals. Conjugate symmetry \(X(-j\omega) = X^*(j\omega)\) means that the magnitude spectrum of a real signal is even and the phase spectrum is odd. The negative frequencies carry no new information; they are the mirror images that make the sum real.

Example 6.4 Using properties instead of integrals

Find the transform of \(y(t) = e^{-2(t - 3)}u(t - 3)\) and of \(z(t) = e^{-3|t|}\cos(10t)\).

For \(y\): it is \(x(t - 3)\) with \(x(t) = e^{-2t}u(t) \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{2 + j\omega}\). By the time-shift property, \(Y(j\omega) = \dfrac{e^{-j3\omega}}{2 + j\omega}\).

For \(z\): write \(\cos 10t = \frac12(e^{j10t} + e^{-j10t})\) and use \(e^{-3|t|} \leftrightarrow \frac{6}{9 + \omega^2}\) with the frequency-shift property:

\[ Z(j\omega) = \frac{3}{9 + (\omega - 10)^2} + \frac{3}{9 + (\omega + 10)^2}. \]

The spectrum of \(e^{-3|t|}\), centred at zero, has been moved to \(\pm10\) and halved.

Example 6.5 Duality and the ideal low-pass filter

The ideal low-pass filter passes all frequencies below \(W\) unchanged and removes all others: \(H(j\omega) = 1\) for \(|\omega| < W\) and \(0\) otherwise. Its impulse response is

\[ h(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-W}^{W}e^{j\omega t}\,d\omega = \frac{\sin Wt}{\pi t}. \]

This \(h(t)\) is non-zero for \(t < 0\), so the ideal low-pass filter is not causal: it would have to respond before the input arrives. It is also not absolutely integrable (it decays only as \(1/t\)), so it is not BIBO stable. Ideal filters are a reference point, not something that can be built. Chapter 12 designs practical filters that approximate them.

docs.title: 6.5 The convolution property and the frequency response
docs.text:
The most important property is that convolution in time becomes multiplication in frequency:

\[ y(t) = x(t) * h(t) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Y(j\omega) = X(j\omega)\,H(j\omega). \]

Proof. \(Y(j\omega) = \int\!\!\int x(\tau)h(t - \tau)\,d\tau\,e^{-j\omega t}dt\). Substitute \(t = \tau + \sigma\) and separate: \(\int x(\tau)e^{-j\omega\tau}d\tau\int h(\sigma)e^{-j\omega\sigma}d\sigma = X(j\omega)H(j\omega)\).

The transform of the impulse response, \(H(j\omega)\), is the frequency response of the system: it is exactly the eigenvalue of Section 4.8 for \(s = j\omega\). Writing \(H(j\omega) = |H(j\omega)|e^{j\angle H(j\omega)}\), the system multiplies the amplitude of each frequency component by the gain \(|H(j\omega)|\) and shifts its phase by \(\angle H(j\omega)\). In terms of magnitudes and phases,

\[ |Y(j\omega)| = |X(j\omega)|\,|H(j\omega)|, \qquad \angle Y(j\omega) = \angle X(j\omega) + \angle H(j\omega). \]

This gives a second route to the output of an LTI system: transform the input, multiply by \(H\), and transform back. For systems described by differential equations, the route is especially simple. Transforming \(\sum a_k \frac{d^k y}{dt^k} = \sum b_k\frac{d^k x}{dt^k}\) term by term with the differentiation property gives

\[ H(j\omega) = \frac{Y(j\omega)}{X(j\omega)} = \frac{\sum_k b_k(j\omega)^k}{\sum_k a_k(j\omega)^k}, \]

a ratio of polynomials in \(j\omega\) that can be written down by inspection.

Example 6.6 Response of a first-order system

The system \(\frac{dy}{dt} + 2y = x(t)\) is driven by \(x(t) = e^{-t}u(t)\). Find \(y(t)\), assuming initial rest.

By inspection, \(H(j\omega) = \dfrac{1}{j\omega + 2}\), and \(X(j\omega) = \dfrac{1}{j\omega + 1}\). So

\[ Y(j\omega) = \frac{1}{(j\omega + 1)(j\omega + 2)} = \frac{1}{j\omega + 1} - \frac{1}{j\omega + 2}, \]

by partial fractions (check: the right side is \(\frac{(j\omega + 2) - (j\omega + 1)}{(j\omega+1)(j\omega+2)}\)). Each term is in the table, so \(y(t) = (e^{-t} - e^{-2t})u(t)\). Compare Exercise 4.6, where a similar result came from a convolution integral; here only algebra was needed.

docs.title: 6.6 Periodic signals and the modulation property
Fourier transforms of periodic signals
docs.text:
Since \(1 \leftrightarrow 2\pi\delta(\omega)\), the frequency-shift property gives \(e^{j\omega_0 t} \leftrightarrow 2\pi\delta(\omega - \omega_0)\): a single complex exponential has all its "spectral mass" at one frequency. A periodic signal is a sum of such exponentials, so

\[ x(t) = \sum_k a_k e^{jk\omega_0 t} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X(j\omega) = \sum_k 2\pi a_k\,\delta(\omega - k\omega_0). \]

The transform of a periodic signal is a train of impulses at the harmonic frequencies, with areas \(2\pi a_k\). In this way the Fourier transform includes the Fourier series as a special case, and periodic and aperiodic signals can be handled with one tool. The cosine and sine entries of Table 6.1 are the cases with only \(a_{\pm1}\) non-zero.

docs.title: Modulation
docs.text:
The multiplication property says that multiplying two signals in time convolves their spectra (divided by \(2\pi\)). The most important case is multiplication by a sinusoid, called modulation. With \(\cos\omega_c t = \frac12(e^{j\omega_c t} + e^{-j\omega_c t})\) and the frequency-shift property,

\[ x(t)\cos\omega_c t \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac12 X(j(\omega - \omega_c)) + \frac12 X(j(\omega + \omega_c)). \]

The spectrum of \(x\) is copied to \(\pm\omega_c\) at half height (Figure 6.3). Radio works this way. A speech signal occupies frequencies up to a few kilohertz, which cannot be radiated efficiently and would collide with every other speech signal. Multiplying by a carrier at, say, 1 MHz moves the speech spectrum up to 1 MHz, where an antenna of reasonable size radiates it, and different stations can be placed at different carriers. Chapter 14 returns to this.

Figure 6.3 The modulation property. Left: the spectrum of a message, a triangle extending from −W to W. Right: the spectrum of the message multiplied by cos ω_c t, two half-height copies of the triangle centred at −ω_c and ω_c.

Example 6.7 Recovering a modulated message

A receiver multiplies the modulated signal \(y(t) = x(t)\cos\omega_c t\) by \(\cos\omega_c t\) again. What does it obtain?

\(y(t)\cos\omega_c t = x(t)\cos^2\omega_c t = \frac12 x(t) + \frac12 x(t)\cos 2\omega_c t\). The first term is the message (at half amplitude); the second is the message moved to \(\pm 2\omega_c\). If \(\omega_c > W\) the two do not overlap in frequency, and a low-pass filter with cut-off between \(W\) and \(2\omega_c - W\) keeps the message and removes the rest. This is synchronous demodulation.

docs.title: 6.7 Energy, bandwidth and the time-bandwidth trade-off
docs.text:
Parseval's relation for the transform,

\[ E_x = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|^2dt = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|X(j\omega)|^2d\omega , \]

says that energy can be computed in either domain. The function \(|X(j\omega)|^2\) is the energy spectral density: \(\frac{1}{2\pi}|X(j\omega)|^2d\omega\) is the energy in the band \(d\omega\). For \(x(t) = e^{-2t}u(t)\), the energy is \(\frac14\) by direct integration (Example 1.5), and \(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\frac{d\omega}{4 + \omega^2} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac14\) in frequency.

The bandwidth of a signal is the width of the band of frequencies that contains most of its energy. There are several definitions (the half-power or 3 dB bandwidth, the width of the main lobe, the band containing 99% of the energy), and which is used depends on the application. Whatever the definition, the scaling property guarantees that duration and bandwidth are inversely proportional: compress a signal by a factor \(a\) and its bandwidth grows by \(a\). The product of duration and bandwidth cannot be made arbitrarily small. With duration and bandwidth measured as root-mean-square widths of \(|x(t)|^2\) and \(|X(j\omega)|^2\), the product is at least \(\frac12\), with equality only for the Gaussian; this is the signal-processing form of the uncertainty principle.

The trade-off has practical consequences everywhere. A radar that must resolve two targets close together needs short pulses, and therefore wide bandwidth. A data link that sends more symbols per second needs shorter symbols, and therefore more bandwidth. A musician who wants to hear the exact pitch of a note needs to listen for long enough.

docs.title: 6.8 Computing transforms numerically
docs.text:
The analysis integral can be approximated numerically for any signal that decays fast enough. The program below does this with the trapezoidal rule for two signals and compares the results with the formulas of Examples 6.1 and 6.2, then checks Parseval's relation. (np.trapezoid is the NumPy 2 name of the trapezoidal-rule function.)

import numpy as np

def ctft(x, t, w):
    """Approximate X(jw) = integral x(t) e^{-jwt} dt by the trapezoidal rule."""
    return np.array([np.trapezoid(x * np.exp(-1j * wk * t), t) for wk in w])

t = np.linspace(-20, 20, 400_001)
w = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0])

# x(t) = e^{-2t} u(t)  <->  1 / (2 + jw)
x = np.where(t >= 0, np.exp(-2 * t), 0.0)
X = ctft(x, t, w)
for wk, Xk in zip(w, X):
    exact = 1 / (2 + 1j * wk)
    print(f"w = {wk:3.0f}: |X| = {abs(Xk):.4f} (exact {abs(exact):.4f}), "
          f"angle = {np.degrees(np.angle(Xk)):7.2f} deg (exact {np.degrees(np.angle(exact)):7.2f})")

# rect pulse of width 1  <->  sin(w/2) / (w/2) = sinc(w / 2pi)
p = (np.abs(t) <= 0.5).astype(float)
P = ctft(p, t, np.array([np.pi, 2 * np.pi, 3 * np.pi]))
print("rect at w = pi, 2pi, 3pi:", np.round(P.real, 4), " exact:", np.round(np.sinc(np.array([0.5, 1, 1.5])), 4))

# Parseval for e^{-2t}u(t): energy 1/4 in time, (1/2pi) * integral |X|^2 dw in frequency
wf = np.linspace(-2000, 2000, 2_000_001)
E_freq = np.trapezoid(1 / (4 + wf ** 2), wf) / (2 * np.pi)
print(f"energy: time {np.trapezoid(x ** 2, t):.4f}, frequency {E_freq:.4f}")

w =   0: |X| = 0.5001 (exact 0.5000), angle =    0.00 deg (exact    0.00)
w =   1: |X| = 0.4473 (exact 0.4472), angle =  -26.56 deg (exact  -26.57)
w =   2: |X| = 0.3536 (exact 0.3536), angle =  -44.99 deg (exact  -45.00)
w =   5: |X| = 0.1857 (exact 0.1857), angle =  -68.18 deg (exact  -68.20)
rect at w = pi, 2pi, 3pi: [ 6.366e-01 -1.000e-04 -2.122e-01]  exact: [ 0.6366  0.     -0.2122]
energy: time 0.2501, frequency 0.2498

The small errors (in the fourth decimal place) come from the jumps of the signals: the trapezoidal rule treats a jump as a steep ramp one step wide. In the frequency-domain energy, the error comes from cutting the integral off at \(|\omega| = 2000\); the missing tail is about \(\frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{2}{2000} \approx 0.00016\). For signals given only as samples, Chapter 8 shows how the FFT computes many values of the spectrum at once.

docs.title: 6.9 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • The Fourier transform \(X(j\omega) = \int x(t)e^{-j\omega t}dt\) and its inverse \(x(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int X(j\omega)e^{j\omega t}d\omega\) describe an aperiodic signal as a continuous superposition of exponentials. It is the limit of the Fourier series as the period grows.
  • Key pairs: \(e^{-at}u(t) \leftrightarrow 1/(a + j\omega)\); \(\mathrm{rect}(t/\tau) \leftrightarrow \tau\,\mathrm{sinc}(\omega\tau/2\pi)\); \(\delta(t) \leftrightarrow 1\); \(1 \leftrightarrow 2\pi\delta(\omega)\); \(\cos\omega_0 t \leftrightarrow \pi[\delta(\omega - \omega_0) + \delta(\omega + \omega_0)]\).
  • A delay adds linear phase; compression widens the spectrum; differentiation multiplies by \(j\omega\); duality swaps the roles of time and frequency.
  • Convolution in time is multiplication in frequency: \(Y = XH\). For a differential equation, \(H(j\omega)\) is a ratio of polynomials in \(j\omega\) written down by inspection.
  • Periodic signals have impulsive spectra \(\sum 2\pi a_k\delta(\omega - k\omega_0)\). Multiplying by \(\cos\omega_c t\) shifts the spectrum to \(\pm\omega_c\).
  • Parseval: energy is the same in both domains. Duration and bandwidth are inversely proportional.

docs.title: 6.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 6.1

Find the Fourier transform of \(x(t) = e^{-3t}u(t) + e^{3t}u(-t)\).

Answer

This is \(e^{-3|t|}\), so \(X(j\omega) = \dfrac{6}{9 + \omega^2}\). (Or add \(\frac{1}{3 + j\omega}\) and \(\frac{1}{3 - j\omega}\), using time reversal for the second.)

Exercise 6.2

Find the transform of a rectangular pulse of height 2 lasting from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 4\).

Answer

It is \(2\,\mathrm{rect}((t - 2)/4)\). So \(X(j\omega) = 2\cdot4\,\mathrm{sinc}(2\omega/\pi)\,e^{-j2\omega} = \dfrac{4\sin 2\omega}{\omega}e^{-j2\omega}\).

Exercise 6.3

Use differentiation in frequency to find the transform of \(t e^{-at}u(t)\).

Answer

\(t\,x(t) \leftrightarrow j\frac{d}{d\omega}\frac{1}{a + j\omega} = j\cdot\frac{-j}{(a + j\omega)^2} = \frac{1}{(a + j\omega)^2}\).

Exercise 6.4

A signal has \(X(j\omega) = 1\) for \(|\omega| < 5\) and 0 otherwise. Find \(x(t)\) and its value at \(t = 0\).

Answer

\(x(t) = \dfrac{\sin 5t}{\pi t}\), and \(x(0) = 5/\pi \approx 1.59\) (the area under \(X\) divided by \(2\pi\)).

Exercise 6.5

Find the frequency response of the system \(\frac{d^2y}{dt^2} + 3\frac{dy}{dt} + 2y = \frac{dx}{dt} + x\), and simplify it.

Answer

\(H(j\omega) = \dfrac{j\omega + 1}{(j\omega)^2 + 3j\omega + 2} = \dfrac{j\omega + 1}{(j\omega + 1)(j\omega + 2)} = \dfrac{1}{j\omega + 2}\).

Exercise 6.6

Find the output of the system with \(H(j\omega) = \frac{1}{2 + j\omega}\) for the input \(x(t) = \cos 2t\).

Answer

\(H(j2) = \frac{1}{2 + 2j} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt2}e^{-j\pi/4}\). So \(y(t) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt2}\cos(2t - \pi/4) \approx 0.354\cos(2t - \pi/4)\).

Exercise 6.7

Find the energy of \(x(t) = \dfrac{\sin 3t}{\pi t}\) using Parseval's relation.

Answer

\(X = 1\) for \(|\omega| < 3\), so \(E = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-3}^{3}1\,d\omega = \frac{6}{2\pi} = \frac{3}{\pi}\).

Exercise 6.8

The signal \(x(t)\) has bandwidth 4 kHz. What is the bandwidth of \(x(3t)\), and of \(x(t/2)\)?

Answer

12 kHz and 2 kHz. Compressing by 3 stretches the spectrum by 3; expanding by 2 compresses it by 2.

Exercise 6.9

Find the Fourier transform of the periodic signal \(x(t) = 1 + \cos(4t)\).

Answer

\(X(j\omega) = 2\pi\delta(\omega) + \pi\delta(\omega - 4) + \pi\delta(\omega + 4)\).

Exercise 6.10

A message with spectrum confined to \(|\omega| < 2\pi\cdot 5000\) rad/s is multiplied by \(\cos(2\pi\cdot 10^5 t)\). Between which frequencies (in kHz) does the spectrum of the product lie (for positive frequencies)?

Answer

From 95 kHz to 105 kHz: the message band, 5 kHz wide on each side, is centred on the 100 kHz carrier.

docs.title: Chapter 8: The DFT and the FFT
docs.text:
The Fourier transform a computer can calculate, and the algorithm that makes it fast

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • define the \(N\)-point DFT and its inverse, and compute small DFTs by hand;
  • relate the DFT to samples of the DTFT and to the coefficients of the DTFS;
  • use circular shift and circular convolution, and use zero-padding to obtain linear convolution;
  • convert DFT bin numbers to frequencies in hertz, and explain resolution, zero-padding, leakage and windowing;
  • derive the radix-2 decimation-in-time FFT and count its operations;
  • analyse real signals with np.fft.

docs.title: 8.1 Why we need the DFT
docs.text: The DTFT of Chapter 7 is a function of a continuous frequency, and it is defined by an infinite sum. A computer can do neither: it holds a finite list of numbers and can produce only a finite list of numbers. The discrete Fourier transform (DFT) is the version of Fourier analysis that is finite in both domains. It takes \(N\) samples and returns \(N\) frequency values, exactly, with no approximation in the transform itself. Combined with a fast algorithm, the fast Fourier transform (FFT), it is the workhorse of digital signal processing: spectrum analysers, audio and image compression, radar, wireless communication and the solution of differential equations all use it.

docs.title: 8.2 Definition
docs.text:
For a sequence \(x[n]\), \(n = 0, 1, \ldots, N-1\), the \(N\)-point DFT is

\[ X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n]\,e^{-j2\pi kn/N}, \qquad k = 0, 1, \ldots, N-1, \]

and the inverse DFT is

\[ x[n] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} X[k]\,e^{j2\pi kn/N}, \qquad n = 0, 1, \ldots, N-1. \]

It is customary to write \(W_N = e^{-j2\pi/N}\), a complex \(N\)th root of unity, so that \(X[k] = \sum_n x[n]W_N^{kn}\). The index \(k\) is the bin number. The inverse formula works because the vectors \(e^{j2\pi kn/N}\), \(k = 0, \ldots, N-1\), are orthogonal, with the same finite geometric sum that made the DTFS work in Section 5.8. Indeed, comparing definitions, the DFT is \(N\) times the DTFS of the periodic sequence obtained by repeating \(x[n]\) with period \(N\): \(X[k] = N a_k\).

Example 8.1 A four-point DFT by hand

Compute the DFT of \(x = [1, 2, 0, -1]\). For \(N = 4\), \(W_4 = e^{-j\pi/2} = -j\), so \(W_4^{kn}\) takes only the values \(1, -j, -1, j\).

\[ \begin{aligned} X[0] &= 1 + 2 + 0 - 1 = 2,\\ X[1] &= 1 + 2(-j) + 0(-1) + (-1)(j) = 1 - 3j,\\ X[2] &= 1 + 2(-1) + 0(1) + (-1)(-1) = 0,\\ X[3] &= 1 + 2(j) + 0(-1) + (-1)(-j) = 1 + 3j. \end{aligned} \]

Notice \(X[3] = X[1]^*\): for a real sequence, \(X[N - k] = X^*[k]\). \(X[0]\) is the sum of the samples (the DC term), and \(X[2]\), at \(k = N/2\), is the alternating sum \(x[0] - x[1] + x[2] - x[3]\).

In matrix form the DFT is \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}\), where \(\mathbf{W}\) is the \(N\times N\) matrix with entries \(W_N^{kn}\). The inverse matrix is \(\frac{1}{N}\mathbf{W}^*\) (the conjugate, scaled). Computing the DFT straight from the definition needs \(N^2\) complex multiplications.

docs.title: Samples of the DTFT
docs.text:
If \(x[n]\) is zero outside \(0 \le n \le N-1\), its DTFT is \(X(e^{j\Omega}) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-j\Omega n}\). Setting \(\Omega = 2\pi k/N\) gives the DFT. So

\[ X[k] = X(e^{j\Omega})\Big|_{\Omega = 2\pi k/N} : \]

the DFT samples the DTFT at \(N\) equally spaced frequencies around the unit circle, from \(\Omega = 0\) up to (but not including) \(2\pi\). Bins \(k\) near 0 and near \(N\) are low frequencies; bins near \(N/2\) are high. Bins \(k > N/2\) represent negative frequencies \(\Omega = 2\pi k/N - 2\pi\), which is why np.fft.fftfreq lists them as negative.

Figure 8.1 The DFT samples the DTFT. The dashed curve is the magnitude of the DTFT of a pulse of four ones. Left: an 8-point DFT gives eight samples of it. Right: padding with zeros to 32 points gives 32 samples of the same curve, filling in its shape.

docs.title: Frequencies in hertz
docs.text:
When \(x[n]\) was obtained by sampling at \(f_s\) samples per second, bin \(k\) corresponds to the frequency

\[ f_k = \frac{k}{N}f_s \quad\text{for } 0 \le k \le N/2, \qquad f_k = \frac{k - N}{N}f_s \quad\text{for } N/2 < k < N . \]

The bin spacing is \(\Delta f = f_s/N = 1/(NT_s)\), the reciprocal of the duration of the record. One second of data gives 1 Hz bins, whatever the sampling rate. The highest frequency represented is \(f_s/2\), at bin \(N/2\).

Example 8.2 Locating a tone

A signal is sampled at 8 kHz and a 256-point DFT is taken. A peak appears in bin 40. What is its frequency?

\(\Delta f = 8000/256 = 31.25\) Hz, so bin 40 is at \(40 \times 31.25 = 1250\) Hz. Because the signal is real, a matching peak appears in bin \(256 - 40 = 216\), which represents \(-1250\) Hz.

docs.title: Zero-padding
docs.text: Appending zeros to a sequence before taking the DFT (Figure 8.1, right) gives more samples of the same DTFT, so the plot looks smoother and peaks can be located more precisely. It does not improve the ability to separate two close frequencies, called the resolution. Resolution is set by the length of the actual data: the DTFT of \(L\) samples cannot show details narrower than about \(2\pi/L\), however finely it is sampled.

docs.title: 8.4 Properties of the DFT
docs.text:
The DFT inherits the properties of the DTFS, with one essential twist: because both \(x[n]\) and \(X[k]\) are implicitly periodic with period \(N\), shifts are circular. A circular shift by \(m\) moves each sample \(m\) places to the right, and samples that fall off the end reappear at the beginning. We write \(x[(n - m)_N]\), where \((\cdot)_N\) means "modulo \(N\)".

Property Sequence (length \(N\)) DFT Linearity \(ax[n] + by[n]\) \(aX[k] + bY[k]\) Circular time shift \(x[(n - m)_N]\) \(W_N^{km}X[k]\) Circular frequency shift \(W_N^{-ln}x[n]\) \(X[(k - l)_N]\) Circular convolution \(\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}x[m]\,y[(n - m)_N]\) \(X[k]\,Y[k]\) Multiplication \(x[n]\,y[n]\) \(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{l=0}^{N-1}X[l]\,Y[(k - l)_N]\) Real sequence \(x\) real \(X[(N - k)_N] = X^*[k]\) Parseval \(\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\lvert x[n]\rvert^2\) \(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\lvert X[k]\rvert^2\)

Table 8.1. Properties of the N-point DFT.

docs.title: Circular versus linear convolution
docs.text:
Multiplying two DFTs corresponds to circular convolution, not the linear convolution of Chapter 4. In circular convolution, the tail of the linear result that would extend beyond \(N - 1\) wraps around and adds to the beginning. For example, the linear convolution of \([1, 2, 3]\) with \([1, 1, 1]\) is \([1, 3, 6, 5, 3]\); the 3-point circular convolution adds the last two values onto the first two, giving \([1 + 5, 3 + 3, 6] = [6, 6, 6]\).

To get linear convolution from DFTs, pad both sequences with zeros to a length of at least \(L + M - 1\), where \(L\) and \(M\) are their lengths. Then the linear result fits in the frame and nothing wraps around. This is the basis of fast convolution: for long sequences, computing two FFTs, a product and an inverse FFT is much faster than evaluating the convolution sum directly. Very long signals, such as audio streams, are cut into blocks and convolved block by block (the overlap-add and overlap-save methods).

docs.title: 8.5 Leakage and windows
docs.text:
Suppose a signal contains a single sinusoid. If an exact whole number of its cycles fits into the \(N\)-sample record, its frequency falls exactly on a bin, and the DFT shows a single clean line (and its mirror). If not, the energy leaks into all the other bins. The reason is that the DFT implicitly repeats the record periodically; when the record does not hold whole cycles, the repetition has a jump at the joins, and a jump needs many frequencies. Equivalently, taking \(N\) samples multiplies the signal by a rectangular window, which convolves its spectrum with the Dirichlet kernel of Example 7.3, whose side lobes decay slowly.

The remedy is to multiply the record by a window that tapers smoothly to zero at both ends before taking the DFT. The Hann window \(w[n] = 0.5 - 0.5\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi n}{N - 1}\right)\) (in the symmetric form used by np.hanning) is a common choice. Its side lobes are far lower than those of the rectangle, so distant leakage drops dramatically. The price is a wider main lobe, which spreads each tone over two or three bins and slightly worsens resolution. Chapter 12 uses the same windows to design filters.

Figure 8.2 Leakage and windowing. The spectrum, in decibels, of a 50.5 Hz tone analysed with 1 Hz bins. With a rectangular window (blue) the tone leaks into every bin, still about −35 dB twenty bins away. With a Hann window (orange) the main peak is two bins wide but the leakage falls below −80 dB within twenty bins.

Reading amplitudes from a DFT

For a real sinusoid of amplitude \(A\) that falls exactly on bin \(k\) (not 0 or \(N/2\)), \(|X[k]| = AN/2\). So the amplitude is \(2|X[k]|/N\). With a window \(w\), divide by \(\sum w[n]\) instead of \(N\). If the tone falls between bins, the peak reads low (by up to about 36% with no window, as the program in Section 8.7 shows), which is another reason to window.

docs.title: 8.6 The fast Fourier transform
docs.text: The direct DFT costs \(N^2\) complex multiplications. For \(N = 1024\) that is over a million; for the \(N = 2^{20}\) points of a long recording, about \(10^{12}\). The FFT computes exactly the same numbers with about \(\frac{N}{2}\log_2 N\) multiplications, which for \(N = 1024\) is 5,120, two hundred times fewer, and for \(N = 2^{20}\) is about ten million, a hundred thousand times fewer. The algorithm was published by Cooley and Tukey in 1965 and is one of the most important algorithms of the twentieth century; the essential idea had been used, by hand, much earlier.

docs.title: Decimation in time
docs.text:
Let \(N\) be a power of 2. Split the sum into even-indexed and odd-indexed samples, \(n = 2r\) and \(n = 2r + 1\):

\[ X[k] = \sum_{r=0}^{N/2-1}x[2r]\,W_N^{2rk} + W_N^{k}\sum_{r=0}^{N/2-1}x[2r+1]\,W_N^{2rk}. \]

Since \(W_N^2 = e^{-j4\pi/N} = W_{N/2}\), each sum is an \(N/2\)-point DFT:

\[ X[k] = E[k] + W_N^{k}\,O[k], \]

where \(E\) is the DFT of the even samples and \(O\) the DFT of the odd samples. Both \(E\) and \(O\) have period \(N/2\), and \(W_N^{k + N/2} = -W_N^{k}\), so for \(k = 0, 1, \ldots, N/2 - 1\):

\[ X[k] = E[k] + W_N^{k}O[k], \qquad X[k + N/2] = E[k] - W_N^{k}O[k]. \]

This pair of equations is the butterfly: one multiplication by the twiddle factor \(W_N^k\), one addition and one subtraction produce two outputs.

docs.title: Counting operations
docs.text:
One \(N\)-point DFT has been replaced by two \(N/2\)-point DFTs plus \(N/2\) butterflies. Each half can be split in the same way, and so on until the DFTs have one point (and a one-point DFT is the sample itself). There are \(\log_2 N\) stages, each with \(N/2\) butterflies, for a total of \(\frac{N}{2}\log_2 N\) complex multiplications.

\(N\) Direct DFT, \(N^2\) FFT, \(\frac{N}{2}\log_2 N\) Ratio 8 64 12 5 256 65,536 1,024 64 1,024 1,048,576 5,120 205 65,536 about \(4.3\times10^9\) 524,288 8,192

Table 8.2. Complex multiplications for the direct DFT and the radix-2 FFT.

The splitting reorders the input: after all the stages, the samples enter in bit-reversed order (for \(N = 8\): 0, 4, 2, 6, 1, 5, 3, 7). Other FFT algorithms split the output instead (decimation in frequency), use other radices, or handle lengths that are not powers of two. Library routines such as np.fft.fft choose among them automatically and work for any \(N\), though lengths with only small prime factors are fastest.

The inverse DFT is computed with the same algorithm, by conjugating the twiddle factors and dividing by \(N\) (or by using \(x = \frac{1}{N}\left(\mathrm{DFT}\{X^*\}\right)^*\)).

docs.title: 8.7 The DFT in NumPy
docs.text:
The first program checks Example 8.1, implements the radix-2 FFT exactly as derived, and demonstrates circular and linear convolution.

import numpy as np

# The 4-point DFT by its matrix, compared with np.fft.fft
N = 4
n = np.arange(N)
W = np.exp(-2j * np.pi * np.outer(n, n) / N)     # W[k, n] = e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}
x = np.array([1, 2, 0, -1])
print("matrix DFT :", np.round(W @ x, 4))
print("np.fft.fft :", np.round(np.fft.fft(x), 4))

# A radix-2 decimation-in-time FFT in a few lines
def fft_radix2(x):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=complex)
    N = len(x)
    if N == 1:
        return x
    E = fft_radix2(x[0::2])                      # DFT of even-indexed samples
    O = fft_radix2(x[1::2])                      # DFT of odd-indexed samples
    tw = np.exp(-2j * np.pi * np.arange(N // 2) / N) * O
    return np.concatenate([E + tw, E - tw])      # the butterflies

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
v = rng.standard_normal(1024)
print("radix-2 FFT matches np.fft.fft:", np.allclose(fft_radix2(v), np.fft.fft(v)))

# Circular versus linear convolution
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([1, 1, 1])
circ = np.fft.ifft(np.fft.fft(a) * np.fft.fft(b)).real
L = len(a) + len(b) - 1
lin = np.fft.ifft(np.fft.fft(a, L) * np.fft.fft(b, L)).real
print("3-point circular :", np.round(circ, 4))
print("5-point (padded) :", np.round(lin, 4), "  np.convolve:", np.convolve(a, b))

matrix DFT : [2.+0.j 1.-3.j 0.+0.j 1.+3.j]
np.fft.fft : [2.+0.j 1.-3.j 0.+0.j 1.+3.j]
radix-2 FFT matches np.fft.fft: True
3-point circular : [6. 6. 6.]
5-point (padded) : [1. 3. 6. 5. 3.]   np.convolve: [1 3 6 5 3]

The second argument of np.fft.fft(a, L) pads a with zeros to length L. The second program analyses a sampled signal containing tones at 50 Hz and 120 Hz, then shows leakage and the effect of a Hann window on a tone at 50.5 Hz, which falls halfway between bins. For real signals, np.fft.rfft returns only the bins \(k = 0, \ldots, N/2\), since the others are conjugates, and np.fft.rfftfreq gives their frequencies in hertz.

import numpy as np

fs = 1000                      # sampling rate, Hz
N = 1000                       # one second of data, so bins are 1 Hz apart
t = np.arange(N) / fs
x = 1.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 50 * t) + 0.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 120 * t)

X = np.fft.rfft(x)             # bins k = 0 .. N/2 for a real signal
f = np.fft.rfftfreq(N, d=1 / fs)
amp = 2 * np.abs(X) / N        # single-sided amplitude
for k in np.argsort(amp)[-2:][::-1]:
    print(f"peak at {f[k]:6.1f} Hz, amplitude {amp[k]:.3f}")

# A tone that falls between bins leaks into its neighbours; a Hann window reduces far leakage
y = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 50.5 * t)
Y_rect = 2 * np.abs(np.fft.rfft(y)) / N
w = np.hanning(N)
Y_hann = 2 * np.abs(np.fft.rfft(y * w)) / np.sum(w)
for name, Y in (("rectangular", Y_rect), ("Hann", Y_hann)):
    print(f"{name:11s}: peak {Y.max():.3f}, level at 60 Hz {Y[60]:.4f}, at 100 Hz {Y[100]:.5f}")

peak at   50.0 Hz, amplitude 1.000
peak at  120.0 Hz, amplitude 0.500
rectangular: peak 0.640, level at 60 Hz 0.0307, at 100 Hz 0.00442
Hann       : peak 0.849, level at 60 Hz 0.0004, at 100 Hz 0.00000

With whole numbers of cycles in the record, the amplitudes come out exactly. With the 50.5 Hz tone and no window, the peak reads 0.640 instead of 1 (the worst case for a tone exactly between bins), and 50 bins away the leakage is still 0.4% of the amplitude. The Hann window reads 0.849 at the peak, and its leakage at the same distance is too small to show in five decimals.

docs.title: 8.8 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • The \(N\)-point DFT \(X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-j2\pi kn/N}\) and its inverse are exact, finite and invertible. The DFT is \(N\) times the DTFS of the periodically repeated sequence.
  • For a sequence of length at most \(N\), \(X[k]\) samples the DTFT at \(\Omega = 2\pi k/N\). Bin \(k\) is at \(kf_s/N\) Hz (negative for \(k > N/2\)); bins are \(f_s/N\) apart.
  • Zero-padding samples the DTFT more finely but does not improve resolution, which depends on the record length.
  • Shifts and convolution are circular. Pad to at least \(L + M - 1\) points to obtain linear convolution.
  • A tone that does not fit a whole number of cycles leaks across bins; tapering windows such as Hann reduce leakage at the cost of a wider peak.
  • The radix-2 FFT splits a DFT into even and odd halves recursively, using butterflies \(E[k] \pm W_N^kO[k]\), for \(\frac{N}{2}\log_2 N\) multiplications instead of \(N^2\).

docs.title: 8.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 8.1

Compute the 4-point DFT of \(x = [1, 1, 1, 1]\) and of \(x = [1, 0, 0, 0]\).

Answer

\([1, 1, 1, 1] \to [4, 0, 0, 0]\): a constant has only DC. \([1, 0, 0, 0] \to [1, 1, 1, 1]\): an impulse has all frequencies equally.

Exercise 8.2

Compute the 4-point DFT of \(x = [0, 1, 0, -1]\), and identify the sinusoid it represents.

Answer

\(X[0] = 0\); \(X[1] = (-j) - (j) = -2j\); \(X[2] = -1 - (-1) = 0\); \(X[3] = j - (-j) = 2j\). The sequence is \(\sin(\pi n/2)\), a sinusoid at bin 1: \(X[1] = N/(2j) = -2j\) as expected.

Exercise 8.3

A 2048-point FFT is computed on data sampled at 44.1 kHz. What is the bin spacing, and which bin is nearest to 1 kHz?

Answer

\(\Delta f = 44100/2048 \approx 21.53\) Hz. \(1000/21.53 \approx 46.4\), so bin 46 (at about 990.5 Hz).

Exercise 8.4

How long must a record be to give a bin spacing of 0.5 Hz?

Answer

2 seconds. The bin spacing is the reciprocal of the record duration, whatever the sampling rate.

Exercise 8.5

Find the 4-point circular convolution of \([1, 2, 3, 4]\) with \([1, 1, 0, 0]\), and the linear convolution.

Answer

Linear: \([1, 3, 5, 7, 4]\). Circular (wrap the fifth value onto the first): \([1 + 4, 3, 5, 7] = [5, 3, 5, 7]\).

Exercise 8.6

Sequences of lengths 300 and 50 are to be convolved with FFTs. What is the smallest power-of-two FFT length that avoids wrap-around?

Answer

The linear result has \(300 + 50 - 1 = 349\) samples, so the FFT length must be at least 349; the smallest power of two is 512.

Exercise 8.7

For a real sequence of length 16, \(X[3] = 2 - 5j\). What is \(X[13]\)?

Answer

\(X[13] = X[16 - 3] = X^*[3] = 2 + 5j\).

Exercise 8.8

How many complex multiplications does a radix-2 FFT need for \(N = 4096\), and how many does the direct DFT need?

Answer

FFT: \(\frac{4096}{2}\times12 = 24{,}576\). Direct: \(4096^2 = 16{,}777{,}216\), about 683 times more.

Exercise 8.9

Two tones at 1000 Hz and 1003 Hz are to be distinguished in a DFT. Roughly how long must the record be?

Answer

The resolution is about the reciprocal of the record length, so at least about \(1/3\) second; in practice a little longer, especially with a window, whose main lobe is wider. Zero-padding a shorter record does not help.

Exercise 8.10

Verify Parseval's relation for the DFT of Example 8.1.

Answer

Time: \(1 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 6\). Frequency: \(\frac14(4 + 10 + 0 + 10) = 6\).

docs.title: 8.10 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 8

Exercise 1

Data sampled at 1000 Hz is analysed with a 500-point DFT. What is the bin spacing in hertz?

Answer

2 / 2 Hz

Exercise 2

Multiplying two N-point DFTs corresponds in time to

  1. linear convolution
  2. circular convolution
  3. multiplication
  4. correlation
Answer

circular convolution

Exercise 3

Zero-padding a record before the DFT

  1. improves frequency resolution
  2. samples the same DTFT more finely
  3. removes leakage
  4. changes the DTFT
Answer

samples the same DTFT more finely

Exercise 4

What is X[0] for x = [3, −1, 2, 4]?

Answer

8

X[0] is the sum of the samples.

Exercise 5

Approximately how many complex multiplications does a radix-2 FFT of length N need?

  1. N²
  2. (N/2) log₂ N
  3. N
  4. 2^N
Answer

(N/2) log₂ N

Exercise 6

Why are windows such as Hann applied before a DFT?

  1. to reduce leakage
  2. to increase the sampling rate
  3. to make the DFT exact
  4. to remove the DC component
Answer

to reduce leakage

Exercise 7

In the FFT, the operation X[k] = E[k] ± W^k O[k] is called a ___.

Answer

butterfly

docs.title: Chapter 7: The Discrete-Time Fourier Transform
docs.text:
Spectra of sequences, frequency responses of digital systems, and the family of four Fourier representations

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • define the DTFT and its inverse, and explain why the DTFT is periodic with period \(2\pi\);
  • compute the DTFT of impulses, exponentials and rectangular sequences;
  • use the properties of the DTFT, especially time shift, convolution and modulation;
  • find the frequency response of a system described by a difference equation and evaluate it at chosen frequencies;
  • place the CTFS, CTFT, DTFS and DTFT in one picture and state the duality between periodicity and discreteness.

docs.title: 7.1 Definition
docs.text:
The discrete-time Fourier transform (DTFT) of a sequence \(x[n]\) is

\[ X(e^{j\Omega}) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n]\,e^{-j\Omega n}, \]

and the inverse DTFT is

\[ x[n] = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{2\pi} X(e^{j\Omega})\,e^{j\Omega n}\,d\Omega , \]

where the integral is over any interval of length \(2\pi\), usually \(-\pi\) to \(\pi\). As in the continuous case, the synthesis equation expresses \(x[n]\) as a superposition of complex exponentials \(e^{j\Omega n}\), and \(X(e^{j\Omega})\) gives the density of each frequency. The frequency \(\Omega\) is measured in radians per sample.

The notation \(X(e^{j\Omega})\) looks heavy but is chosen deliberately: it is the z-transform \(X(z)\) of Chapter 11 evaluated on the unit circle \(z = e^{j\Omega}\), just as \(X(j\omega)\) is the Laplace transform on the imaginary axis.

docs.title: Why the DTFT is periodic
docs.text:
Because \(n\) is an integer, \(e^{-j(\Omega + 2\pi)n} = e^{-j\Omega n}\). Every term of the sum is unchanged when \(\Omega\) increases by \(2\pi\), so

\[ X(e^{j(\Omega + 2\pi)}) = X(e^{j\Omega}). \]

The DTFT is always periodic with period \(2\pi\). This is the frequency-domain face of a fact met in Section 1.6: discrete-time exponentials whose frequencies differ by \(2\pi\) are identical sequences. All the information is in one period, and the inverse transform integrates over one period only.

Within a period, the low frequencies are near \(\Omega = 0\) (and, equivalently, near \(\pm2\pi\)), and the highest frequency is \(\Omega = \pm\pi\), where \(e^{j\pi n} = (-1)^n\) alternates in sign at every sample. A spectrum concentrated near \(\Omega = 0\) belongs to a slowly varying sequence; one concentrated near \(\pm\pi\) belongs to a rapidly alternating one.

When \(x[n]\) comes from sampling a CT signal every \(T_s\) seconds, a continuous frequency \(\omega\) (rad/s) appears in the sequence at \(\Omega = \omega T_s\) (rad/sample). So \(\Omega = \pi\) corresponds to \(\omega = \pi/T_s\), which is half the sampling rate. Chapter 9 explains why nothing above that frequency can be represented.

docs.title: Convergence
docs.text: The DTFT sum converges absolutely, to a continuous function of \(\Omega\), if \(x\) is absolutely summable: \(\sum|x[n]| < \infty\). It converges in the energy sense if \(x\) has finite energy. Sequences such as \(u[n]\) and \(\cos\Omega_0 n\) need impulses in frequency, as in Section 7.5. Growing sequences have no DTFT; they need the z-transform.

docs.title: 7.2 Standard DTFT pairs
docs.text:
Example 7.1 The impulse and the shifted impulse

\(\delta[n] \leftrightarrow 1\) and \(\delta[n - n_0] \leftrightarrow e^{-j\Omega n_0}\). A single sample contains all frequencies equally; a delay of \(n_0\) samples adds a phase \(-\Omega n_0\), linear in frequency.

Example 7.2 The exponential

For \(x[n] = a^n u[n]\) with \(|a| < 1\):

\[ X(e^{j\Omega}) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(ae^{-j\Omega}\right)^n = \frac{1}{1 - ae^{-j\Omega}}, \]

a geometric series with ratio of magnitude \(|a| < 1\). Its squared magnitude is

\[ |X(e^{j\Omega})|^2 = \frac{1}{(1 - a\cos\Omega)^2 + a^2\sin^2\Omega} = \frac{1}{1 - 2a\cos\Omega + a^2}. \]

At \(\Omega = 0\) the magnitude is \(\frac{1}{1 - a}\); at \(\Omega = \pi\) it is \(\frac{1}{1 + a}\). For \(a = 0.8\) these are 5 and 0.556: the sequence, which decays smoothly, is concentrated at low frequencies. For \(a = -0.8\) they swap: the sequence alternates in sign, and its spectrum is concentrated near \(\pi\) (Figure 7.1).

Example 7.3 The rectangular sequence

Let \(x[n] = 1\) for \(0 \le n \le N - 1\) and 0 otherwise. Using the finite geometric series,

\[ X(e^{j\Omega}) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}e^{-j\Omega n} = \frac{1 - e^{-j\Omega N}}{1 - e^{-j\Omega}}. \]

Factor \(e^{-j\Omega N/2}\) from the numerator and \(e^{-j\Omega/2}\) from the denominator:

\[ X(e^{j\Omega}) = e^{-j\Omega(N-1)/2}\,\frac{\sin(\Omega N/2)}{\sin(\Omega/2)}. \]

The ratio of sines is the Dirichlet kernel, the discrete-time cousin of the sinc. It equals \(N\) at \(\Omega = 0\) and is zero at \(\Omega = 2\pi k/N\) for \(k = 1, \ldots, N-1\). The phase factor is linear: the sequence is symmetric about \(n = (N-1)/2\), which acts as a delay of \((N-1)/2\) samples. As with the CT pulse, a longer sequence has a narrower main lobe, of width \(4\pi/N\).

Figure 7.2 The rectangular sequence. Left: the rectangular sequence equal to 1 for n = 0 to 4. Right: the magnitude of its DTFT over one period, the Dirichlet kernel with peak 5 at Ω = 0 and zeros at Ω = ±2π/5 and ±4π/5.

Example 7.4 The ideal discrete-time low-pass filter

An ideal low-pass filter with cut-off \(W\) (\(0 < W < \pi\)) has \(H(e^{j\Omega}) = 1\) for \(|\Omega| < W\) and 0 for \(W < |\Omega| \le \pi\), repeated with period \(2\pi\). Its impulse response is

\[ h[n] = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-W}^{W}e^{j\Omega n}\,d\Omega = \frac{\sin Wn}{\pi n}, \qquad h[0] = \frac{W}{\pi}. \]

As in continuous time, this impulse response extends to \(n = -\infty\) and decays only as \(1/n\): the ideal filter is neither causal nor stable. Truncating and windowing this sequence is the basis of FIR filter design in Chapter 12.

\(x[n]\) \(X(e^{j\Omega})\) (one period, or for all \(\Omega\)) \(\delta[n]\) \(1\) \(\delta[n - n_0]\) \(e^{-j\Omega n_0}\) \(a^n u[n]\), \(\lvert a\rvert < 1\) \(\dfrac{1}{1 - ae^{-j\Omega}}\) \((n + 1)a^n u[n]\), \(\lvert a\rvert < 1\) \(\dfrac{1}{(1 - ae^{-j\Omega})^2}\) \(a^{\lvert n\rvert}\), \(\lvert a\rvert < 1\) \(\dfrac{1 - a^2}{1 - 2a\cos\Omega + a^2}\) \(1\) for \(0 \le n \le N-1\) \(e^{-j\Omega(N-1)/2}\dfrac{\sin(\Omega N/2)}{\sin(\Omega/2)}\) \(\dfrac{\sin Wn}{\pi n}\), \(0 < W < \pi\) \(1\) for \(\lvert\Omega\rvert < W\), \(0\) for \(W < \lvert\Omega\rvert \le \pi\) \(1\) \(2\pi\sum_k\delta(\Omega - 2\pi k)\) \(e^{j\Omega_0 n}\) \(2\pi\sum_k\delta(\Omega - \Omega_0 - 2\pi k)\) \(\cos\Omega_0 n\) \(\pi\sum_k[\delta(\Omega - \Omega_0 - 2\pi k) + \delta(\Omega + \Omega_0 - 2\pi k)]\) \(u[n]\) \(\dfrac{1}{1 - e^{-j\Omega}} + \pi\sum_k\delta(\Omega - 2\pi k)\)

Table 7.1. Common DTFT pairs.

docs.title: 7.3 Properties of the DTFT
docs.text:
The properties closely parallel those of the CT transform, with differences where the integer nature of \(n\) matters (there is no simple time scaling, for instance). Let \(x \leftrightarrow X\) and \(y \leftrightarrow Y\).

Property Sequence DTFT Linearity \(ax[n] + by[n]\) \(aX(e^{j\Omega}) + bY(e^{j\Omega})\) Time shift \(x[n - n_0]\) \(e^{-j\Omega n_0}X(e^{j\Omega})\) Frequency shift \(e^{j\Omega_0 n}x[n]\) \(X(e^{j(\Omega - \Omega_0)})\) Time reversal \(x[-n]\) \(X(e^{-j\Omega})\) Conjugation \(x^*[n]\) \(X^*(e^{-j\Omega})\) Differencing \(x[n] - x[n-1]\) \((1 - e^{-j\Omega})X(e^{j\Omega})\) Accumulation \(\sum_{k=-\infty}^{n}x[k]\) \(\dfrac{X(e^{j\Omega})}{1 - e^{-j\Omega}} + \pi X(e^{j0})\sum_k\delta(\Omega - 2\pi k)\) Differentiation in frequency \(n\,x[n]\) \(j\dfrac{dX(e^{j\Omega})}{d\Omega}\) Expansion by \(L\) \(x[n/L]\) for \(n\) a multiple of \(L\), else 0 \(X(e^{jL\Omega})\) Convolution \(x[n] * y[n]\) \(X(e^{j\Omega})\,Y(e^{j\Omega})\) Multiplication \(x[n]\,y[n]\) \(\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\displaystyle\int_{2\pi}X(e^{j\theta})Y(e^{j(\Omega - \theta)})\,d\theta\) Real sequence \(x\) real \(X(e^{-j\Omega}) = X^*(e^{j\Omega})\) Parseval \(\displaystyle\sum_n\lvert x[n]\rvert^2\) \(\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\displaystyle\int_{2\pi}\lvert X(e^{j\Omega})\rvert^2d\Omega\)

Table 7.2. Properties of the DTFT.

Two entries differ visibly from the CT versions. Multiplication gives a periodic convolution of the spectra, an integral over one period only, because both spectra are periodic. Expansion (inserting \(L - 1\) zeros between samples) compresses the spectrum by \(L\), so that \(L\) copies of the original period now fit into \(2\pi\); the extra copies are called images, and removing them is the job of the interpolation filter in Chapter 9.

The frequency-shift property with \(\Omega_0 = \pi\) is worth noting: multiplying by \((-1)^n = e^{j\pi n}\) shifts the spectrum by \(\pi\), turning low frequencies into high and vice versa. It turns a low-pass filter into a high-pass one: if \(h[n]\) is low-pass, \((-1)^n h[n]\) is high-pass. Figure 7.1 shows exactly this, since \((-0.8)^n = (-1)^n(0.8)^n\).

Example 7.5 Using properties

Find the DTFT of \(y[n] = (0.5)^{n-2}u[n - 2]\) and of \(z[n] = n(0.5)^n u[n]\).

\(y\) is \(x[n - 2]\) with \(x[n] = 0.5^n u[n]\), so \(Y(e^{j\Omega}) = \dfrac{e^{-j2\Omega}}{1 - 0.5e^{-j\Omega}}\).

For \(z\), use differentiation in frequency: \(j\frac{d}{d\Omega}\left(1 - 0.5e^{-j\Omega}\right)^{-1} = j\cdot\frac{-0.5je^{-j\Omega}}{(1 - 0.5e^{-j\Omega})^2} = \dfrac{0.5e^{-j\Omega}}{(1 - 0.5e^{-j\Omega})^2}\).

docs.title: 7.4 Frequency response of discrete-time systems
docs.text:
For a DT LTI system with impulse response \(h[n]\), the convolution property gives \(Y(e^{j\Omega}) = H(e^{j\Omega})X(e^{j\Omega})\), where the frequency response \(H(e^{j\Omega})\) is the DTFT of \(h[n]\). By the eigenfunction property, the input \(e^{j\Omega_0 n}\) produces \(H(e^{j\Omega_0})e^{j\Omega_0 n}\), and for a real system the input \(\cos(\Omega_0 n + \phi)\) produces

\[ y[n] = |H(e^{j\Omega_0})|\cos\!\left(\Omega_0 n + \phi + \angle H(e^{j\Omega_0})\right). \]

For a system described by the difference equation \(\sum_{k=0}^{N}a_k y[n-k] = \sum_{k=0}^{M}b_k x[n-k]\), the time-shift property turns each delay into a factor \(e^{-j\Omega}\):

\[ H(e^{j\Omega}) = \frac{\sum_{k=0}^{M}b_k e^{-jk\Omega}}{\sum_{k=0}^{N}a_k e^{-jk\Omega}}. \]

As in continuous time, the frequency response is read off the coefficients of the equation.

Example 7.6 The three-point moving average

\(y[n] = \frac13(x[n] + x[n-1] + x[n-2])\) has

\[ H(e^{j\Omega}) = \frac13\left(1 + e^{-j\Omega} + e^{-j2\Omega}\right) = \frac13 e^{-j\Omega}\left(e^{j\Omega} + 1 + e^{-j\Omega}\right) = \frac{1 + 2\cos\Omega}{3}\,e^{-j\Omega}. \]

The magnitude \(|1 + 2\cos\Omega|/3\) is 1 at \(\Omega = 0\), \(\frac23\) at \(\Omega = \pi/3\), zero at \(\Omega = 2\pi/3\) and \(\frac13\) at \(\Omega = \pi\). The filter passes slow variations, completely removes the frequency \(2\pi/3\) (a sequence with period 3, which averages to zero over any three samples), and attenuates other high frequencies. The phase is \(-\Omega\) (with an extra \(\pi\) where \(1 + 2\cos\Omega < 0\)): a delay of one sample, the centre of the averaging window.

Example 7.7 Response of a recursive filter to a sinusoid

The system \(y[n] = 0.8\,y[n-1] + x[n]\) receives \(x[n] = 2\cos(\pi n/2)\). Find the steady-state output.

\(H(e^{j\Omega}) = \dfrac{1}{1 - 0.8e^{-j\Omega}}\). At \(\Omega = \pi/2\), \(e^{-j\pi/2} = -j\), so \(H = \dfrac{1}{1 + 0.8j}\), with \(|H| = 1/\sqrt{1.64} = 0.781\) and \(\angle H = -\arctan 0.8 = -0.675\) rad (\(-38.7°\)). Therefore

\[ y[n] = 1.562\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi n}{2} - 0.675\right). \]

docs.title: 7.5 Periodic sequences
docs.text:
A periodic sequence with DTFS coefficients \(a_k\) (Section 5.8) has the DTFT

\[ X(e^{j\Omega}) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} 2\pi a_k\,\delta\!\left(\Omega - \frac{2\pi k}{N}\right), \]

a train of impulses at the harmonic frequencies \(2\pi k/N\). Since \(a_k\) is periodic in \(k\) with period \(N\), the impulse train repeats every \(2\pi\), as every DTFT must. The constant and cosine entries of Table 7.1 are special cases.

docs.title: 7.6 The four Fourier representations
docs.text:
We now have four Fourier tools, one for each combination of continuous or discrete time and periodic or aperiodic signal.

Periodic in time Aperiodic in time Continuous time CTFS: \(a_k = \frac{1}{T_0}\int_{T_0}x(t)e^{-jk\omega_0t}dt\)spectrum discrete, aperiodic CTFT: \(X(j\omega) = \int x(t)e^{-j\omega t}dt\)spectrum continuous, aperiodic Discrete time DTFS: \(a_k = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{\langle N\rangle}x[n]e^{-jk2\pi n/N}\)spectrum discrete, periodic DTFT: \(X(e^{j\Omega}) = \sum x[n]e^{-j\Omega n}\)spectrum continuous, periodic

Table 7.3. The four Fourier representations.

The table displays a beautiful duality:

  • Periodic in one domain means discrete in the other. Periodic signals have line spectra (CTFS, DTFS); periodic spectra belong to discrete-time signals (DTFS, DTFT).
  • Aperiodic in one domain means continuous in the other. Aperiodic signals have continuous spectra (CTFT, DTFT); continuous-time signals have aperiodic spectra (CTFS, CTFT).

The DTFS is the only one of the four in which both domains are discrete and finite: \(N\) numbers in, \(N\) numbers out. That is the one a computer can calculate exactly, and it is the subject of the next chapter, under the name of the discrete Fourier transform.

Key idea

Sampling in one domain makes the other domain periodic. Sampling a CT signal in time makes its spectrum periodic (the DTFT); sampling a spectrum in frequency makes the signal periodic (the Fourier series). Chapter 9 makes the first statement precise.

docs.title: 7.7 Evaluating the DTFT numerically
docs.text:
For a finite sequence the DTFT is a finite sum, which can be evaluated at any frequency. For an infinite but decaying sequence, truncating the sum gives an approximation whose error is the size of the neglected tail. The program below evaluates the frequency responses of Examples 7.6 and 7.2 at four frequencies and confirms the \(2\pi\) periodicity.

import numpy as np

def dtft(x, n, W):
    """X(e^{jW}) = sum_n x[n] e^{-jWn} for a finite sequence x on indices n."""
    return np.array([np.sum(x * np.exp(-1j * w * n)) for w in W])

W = np.array([0, np.pi / 3, 2 * np.pi / 3, np.pi])

# Three-point moving average h[n] = 1/3, n = 0, 1, 2
n = np.arange(3)
H = dtft(np.ones(3) / 3, n, W)
print("moving average |H|  :", np.round(np.abs(H), 4))
print("formula |1+2cos W|/3:", np.round(np.abs(1 + 2 * np.cos(W)) / 3, 4))

# First-order recursive system: h[n] = 0.8^n u[n] (truncated at 200 terms)
n = np.arange(200)
H1 = dtft(0.8 ** n, n, W)
exact = 1 / (1 - 0.8 * np.exp(-1j * W))
print("recursive |H|       :", np.round(np.abs(H1), 4))
print("formula             :", np.round(np.abs(exact), 4))

# Periodicity: the DTFT repeats every 2 pi
print("H(e^{j0.5}) - H(e^{j(0.5+2pi)}) =", abs(dtft(0.8 ** n, n, [0.5])[0] - dtft(0.8 ** n, n, [0.5 + 2 * np.pi])[0]))

moving average |H|  : [1.     0.6667 0.     0.3333]
formula |1+2cos W|/3: [1.     0.6667 0.     0.3333]
recursive |H|       : [5.     1.0911 0.6402 0.5556]
formula             : [5.     1.0911 0.6402 0.5556]
H(e^{j0.5}) - H(e^{j(0.5+2pi)}) = 4.965068306494546e-16

The truncation at 200 terms is invisible: the neglected tail of \(0.8^n\) is about \(0.8^{200}/0.2 \approx 10^{-19}\). The periodicity check differs from zero only by rounding error. The library SciPy offers scipy.signal.freqz, which evaluates the frequency response of a difference equation on a grid of frequencies in one call; writing the sum out, as here, shows what it does.

docs.title: 7.8 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • The DTFT \(X(e^{j\Omega}) = \sum_n x[n]e^{-j\Omega n}\) is periodic in \(\Omega\) with period \(2\pi\); the inverse integrates over one period. Low frequencies are near \(\Omega = 0\), the highest at \(\Omega = \pm\pi\).
  • \(a^n u[n] \leftrightarrow 1/(1 - ae^{-j\Omega})\); the rectangular sequence gives the Dirichlet kernel \(\sin(\Omega N/2)/\sin(\Omega/2)\) with linear phase; the ideal low-pass filter has \(h[n] = \sin(Wn)/(\pi n)\).
  • Shifts add linear phase, convolution becomes multiplication, multiplication becomes periodic convolution, and multiplying by \((-1)^n\) shifts the spectrum by \(\pi\).
  • A difference equation gives \(H(e^{j\Omega})\) as a ratio of polynomials in \(e^{-j\Omega}\). A sinusoid at \(\Omega_0\) is scaled by \(|H(e^{j\Omega_0})|\) and shifted by \(\angle H(e^{j\Omega_0})\).
  • Across CTFS, CTFT, DTFS and DTFT: periodic in one domain means discrete in the other, and aperiodic means continuous.

docs.title: 7.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 7.1

Find the DTFT of \(x[n] = \delta[n] + 2\delta[n-1] + \delta[n-2]\) and write it as a real function times a linear-phase factor.

Answer

\(X = 1 + 2e^{-j\Omega} + e^{-j2\Omega} = e^{-j\Omega}(e^{j\Omega} + 2 + e^{-j\Omega}) = 2(1 + \cos\Omega)\,e^{-j\Omega}\). It is zero at \(\Omega = \pi\): a low-pass filter.

Exercise 7.2

Find the DTFT of \(x[n] = (0.5)^{|n|}\) and its value at \(\Omega = 0\).

Answer

\(X = \dfrac{1 - 0.25}{1 - \cos\Omega + 0.25} = \dfrac{0.75}{1.25 - \cos\Omega}\). At \(\Omega = 0\): \(0.75/0.25 = 3\), which equals \(\sum_n 0.5^{|n|} = 1 + 2\cdot1 = 3\).

Exercise 7.3

A sequence is real. Its DTFT at \(\Omega = 0.3\pi\) is \(2 - j\). What is its DTFT at \(\Omega = -0.3\pi\)? At \(\Omega = 1.7\pi\)?

Answer

Conjugate symmetry gives \(X(e^{-j0.3\pi}) = 2 + j\). Periodicity gives \(X(e^{j1.7\pi}) = X(e^{-j0.3\pi}) = 2 + j\).

Exercise 7.4

Find the frequency response of \(y[n] = x[n] - x[n-1]\) and describe it.

Answer

\(H = 1 - e^{-j\Omega} = e^{-j\Omega/2}\cdot 2j\sin(\Omega/2)\). \(|H| = 2|\sin(\Omega/2)|\): zero at \(\Omega = 0\), 2 at \(\Omega = \pi\). A high-pass filter that blocks constants, the discrete analogue of a differentiator.

Exercise 7.5

Find the steady-state output of the three-point moving average for \(x[n] = 4 + 3\cos(2\pi n/3) + \cos(\pi n)\).

Answer

\(H(e^{j0}) = 1\), \(H(e^{j2\pi/3}) = 0\), \(H(e^{j\pi}) = \frac{1 + 2(-1)}{3}e^{-j\pi} = \frac13\) (since \(-\frac13 e^{-j\pi} = \frac13\)). So \(y[n] = 4 + \frac13\cos(\pi n)\).

Exercise 7.6

Use Parseval's relation to find the energy of \(h[n] = \dfrac{\sin(\pi n/4)}{\pi n}\).

Answer

\(H = 1\) for \(|\Omega| < \pi/4\), so \(E = \frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac14\).

Exercise 7.7

If \(h[n]\) is an ideal low-pass filter with cut-off \(\pi/4\), describe the filter with impulse response \((-1)^n h[n]\).

Answer

Its frequency response is \(H(e^{j(\Omega - \pi)})\): it passes \(|\Omega - \pi| < \pi/4\), that is \(3\pi/4 < |\Omega| \le \pi\). An ideal high-pass filter with cut-off \(3\pi/4\).

Exercise 7.8

Find the DTFT of \(x[n] = \cos(\pi n/4)\) over one period.

Answer

For \(-\pi < \Omega \le \pi\): \(X(e^{j\Omega}) = \pi\delta(\Omega - \pi/4) + \pi\delta(\Omega + \pi/4)\), repeated every \(2\pi\).

Exercise 7.9

A sequence \(x[n]\) has DTFT \(X(e^{j\Omega})\). Express the DTFT of \(x[n] * x[-n]\) in terms of \(X\), for a real \(x\).

Answer

\(X(e^{j\Omega})X(e^{-j\Omega}) = X(e^{j\Omega})X^*(e^{j\Omega}) = |X(e^{j\Omega})|^2\): real and non-negative. (This is the autocorrelation of \(x\).)

Exercise 7.10

A CT signal is sampled at 8000 samples per second. Which value of \(\Omega\) corresponds to 1000 Hz? Which frequency in hertz corresponds to \(\Omega = \pi\)?

Answer

\(\Omega = 2\pi\cdot1000/8000 = \pi/4\). \(\Omega = \pi\) corresponds to 4000 Hz, half the sampling rate.

docs.title: Chapter 10: The Laplace Transform
docs.text:
Exponentials of every kind, regions of convergence, transfer functions, and differential equations with initial conditions

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • define the bilateral Laplace transform, relate it to the Fourier transform, and find the region of convergence (ROC) of a transform;
  • draw pole-zero plots and state the properties of the ROC;
  • invert rational transforms by partial fractions, including repeated and complex poles, using the ROC to choose each term;
  • use the properties of the transform, including the initial and final value theorems;
  • find the transfer function of a system, and decide causality and stability from its poles and ROC;
  • solve linear differential equations with initial conditions using the unilateral transform;
  • describe second-order systems by natural frequency and damping ratio, and predict overshoot.

docs.title: 10.1 Beyond the Fourier transform
docs.text:
The Fourier transform analyses signals into pure oscillations \(e^{j\omega t}\). It fails for signals that grow, such as \(e^{t}u(t)\), and for unstable systems, whose impulse responses grow, because the Fourier integral does not converge. Yet growing signals matter: an engineer must be able to analyse an unstable system in order to stabilise it. The cure is to allow the exponentials of Section 4.8 in full generality, \(e^{st}\) with complex \(s = \sigma + j\omega\).

The (bilateral) Laplace transform of \(x(t)\) is

\[ X(s) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)\,e^{-st}\,dt, \qquad s = \sigma + j\omega . \]

Writing \(e^{-st} = e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}\) shows what it does:

\[ X(\sigma + j\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left[x(t)e^{-\sigma t}\right]e^{-j\omega t}\,dt = \mathcal{F}\{x(t)e^{-\sigma t}\}. \]

The Laplace transform is the Fourier transform of \(x(t)\) multiplied by a real exponential \(e^{-\sigma t}\). A suitable \(\sigma\) tames a growing signal (for \(e^{t}u(t)\), any \(\sigma > 1\) makes \(e^{(1-\sigma)t}u(t)\) decay), so the transform exists for many signals that have no Fourier transform. On the imaginary axis \(\sigma = 0\), the Laplace transform becomes the Fourier transform: \(X(s)|_{s = j\omega} = X(j\omega)\), which explains the notation of Chapter 6.

The variable \(s\) lives in the complex s-plane, with \(\sigma\) on the horizontal axis and \(\omega\) on the vertical axis. The inverse transform is a contour integral in this plane,

\[ x(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi j}\int_{\sigma - j\infty}^{\sigma + j\infty}X(s)\,e^{st}\,ds , \]

taken along a vertical line inside the region of convergence. In practice we almost never evaluate it: for the rational transforms that arise from circuits and mechanical systems, partial fractions and a table suffice.

docs.title: 10.2 The region of convergence
docs.text:
Example 10.1 A right-sided exponential

For \(x(t) = e^{-at}u(t)\) (with \(a\) real or complex):

\[ X(s) = \int_0^{\infty}e^{-(s + a)t}\,dt = \left[\frac{-e^{-(s+a)t}}{s + a}\right]_0^{\infty} = \frac{1}{s + a}, \]

provided the upper limit vanishes, which needs \(\mathrm{Re}\{s + a\} > 0\), that is \(\mathrm{Re}\{s\} > -\mathrm{Re}\{a\}\). So \(e^{-at}u(t) \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{s+a}\) with ROC \(\mathrm{Re}\{s\} > -a\) (for real \(a\)). The ROC is the half-plane to the right of the point \(s = -a\).

Example 10.2 A left-sided exponential

For \(x(t) = -e^{-at}u(-t)\):

\[ X(s) = -\int_{-\infty}^{0}e^{-(s + a)t}\,dt = -\left[\frac{-e^{-(s+a)t}}{s + a}\right]_{-\infty}^{0} = \frac{1}{s + a}, \]

provided the lower limit vanishes, which needs \(\mathrm{Re}\{s\} < -a\). The ROC is the half-plane to the left of \(s = -a\).

The two examples give the same algebraic expression for two different signals. The expression alone does not determine the signal: the ROC is part of the transform. Figure 10.1 shows the two regions.

Figure 10.1 Regions of convergence. The s-plane with a pole (cross) at s = −a. Left: the ROC of e^(−at)u(t) is the half-plane to the right of the pole. Right: the ROC of −e^(−at)u(−t) is the half-plane to the left of the pole. The two transforms have the same formula, 1/(s + a).

The ROC has a simple structure, which follows from the observation that convergence depends only on \(\sigma = \mathrm{Re}\{s\}\):

  1. The ROC consists of vertical strips in the s-plane (a strip, a half-plane, or the whole plane).
  2. For a rational transform, the ROC contains no poles, and it is bounded by poles or extends to infinity.
  3. If \(x\) is of finite duration (and absolutely integrable), the ROC is the entire s-plane.
  4. If \(x\) is right-sided, the ROC is a right half-plane: to the right of the rightmost pole.
  5. If \(x\) is left-sided, the ROC is a left half-plane: to the left of the leftmost pole.
  6. If \(x\) is two-sided, the ROC is a strip between two poles, or empty.
  7. The Fourier transform of \(x\) exists (as a function) if and only if the ROC includes the \(j\omega\) axis.

Example 10.3 A two-sided signal

Find the transform of \(x(t) = e^{-2t}u(t) + e^{3t}u(-t)\).

The first term gives \(\frac{1}{s + 2}\) with \(\mathrm{Re}\{s\} > -2\). The second is \(-(-e^{3t}u(-t))\), so by Example 10.2 with \(a = -3\) it gives \(-\frac{1}{s - 3}\) with \(\mathrm{Re}\{s\} < 3\). Both must converge, so the ROC is the strip \(-2 < \mathrm{Re}\{s\} < 3\), and

\[ X(s) = \frac{1}{s + 2} - \frac{1}{s - 3} = \frac{-5}{(s + 2)(s - 3)}. \]

The strip contains the \(j\omega\) axis, so this signal (which decays in both directions) has a Fourier transform, \(X(j\omega)\).

docs.title: Poles and zeros
docs.text: Most transforms in practice are rational: \(X(s) = N(s)/D(s)\), a ratio of polynomials. The roots of \(N\) are the zeros (where \(X = 0\)), and the roots of \(D\) are the poles (where \(X\) is infinite). A pole-zero plot marks poles with crosses and zeros with circles. Apart from a constant gain factor, the poles, the zeros and the ROC determine the transform completely.

docs.text:
